<meta>This page begins the formal dedication of the work. The author, writing under a pseudonym, addresses a close friend to introduce his commentary on the works of the famous Swiss occultist and physician Paracelsus.</meta>

# LEO SUAVIUS
<note>Leo Suavius was the pseudonym of Jacques Gohory (1520–1576), a French scholar, alchemist, and physician who was instrumental in introducing Paracelsian thought to France.</note>

## TO THE NOBLE MAN
### RENÉ PERROT
### OF LE MANS,
<note>René Perrot (Renatus Perotus) was a contemporary of Gohory and a fellow enthusiast of the "New Philosophy" or alchemy.</note>

### GREETINGS.

To whose trust should I sooner commit these books of commentaries on Paracelsus’s *On Long Life* than to yours? They are like children recently born to me; yet, by whatever right they are mine, they are also yours by right of ownership and bond, my sweetest friend, since among friends all things are held in common. Because these writings are imbued with Philosophy, they are rightly dedicated to you, who are most devoted to its study, so that you may be chosen as the judge, as it were, of their initiation into the world.

Let us leave those haughty dedications to Princes to the ambitious writers of our age, who use such names to decorate the frontispieces of their works as if they were the facades of their own houses. For us—who delight in the leisure of literature and have long since withdrawn from the company of the Great—it is more fitting to offer our works to those endowed with virtue than to chase after empty little glory through a prideful dedication.

There are many who are devoid of all learning—

<summary>In this dedication, Jacques Gohory (as Leo Suavius) presents his commentaries on Paracelsus to his friend René Perrot, arguing that true intellectual work belongs with virtuous friends rather than powerful patrons.</summary>
<keywords>Jacques Gohory, René Perrot, Paracelsus, On Long Life, alchemy, Renaissance humanism, friendship, patronage</keywords>

--- Page 8 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedication from page 3. The text concludes a sentence describing the "unlearned" masses who cannot appreciate intellectual work, before pivoting to praise the recipient, René Perrot, and the subject of the commentary, Paracelsus.</meta>

## LETTER.

—ing: with what boldness do you hope they will receive a gift when they are utterly ignorant of what it even is? Why do you offer pearls to a sow <note>original: *sui*; a reference to the biblical proverb "neither cast ye your pearls before swine."</note>, which would prefer a grain of barley to the great pearl of Cleopatra <note>A famous ancient anecdote recounts Cleopatra dissolving a priceless pearl (an *unio*) in vinegar to win a bet about the most expensive meal; here, it represents the highest value which the ignorant cannot perceive.</note>? Wretched me, who spent so many sleepless nights polishing these pages! Even though I knew these people were unskilled in the sciences, I still trusted that they would honor the virtue they saw in others, even if they lacked it themselves.

Indeed, this treatment of such hidden subjects—matters to which very few turn their attention today—is completely foreign to those who have not gained knowledge through the common arts. But it is worthy of you, Perrot. Although your fortune and wealth would allow you to spend your life in luxury and ease, you hold nothing more precious, nothing more vital <note>original: *antiquius*, literally "more ancient," but used here to imply a thing of higher priority or more venerable status.</note>, than the knowledge of the finest things.

As for this author <note>Referring to the Swiss physician and alchemist Paracelsus (1493–1541), whose work *On Long Life* Gohory is editing.</note>, to tell you what I truly think: in our age, I have seen no physician more serious, nor any philosopher more profound <note>original: *subtiliorem*, meaning more subtle, keen-witted, or precise.</note>. Since I saw that he was so pleasing to you, and because I measure the dedication of all good men by your judgment, I decided to explain a few of his more obscure passages: sometimes through notes <term>scholia (explanatory comments written in the margins or between lines)</term>, sometimes through paraphrase, occasionally with formal arguments, and at other times with a simple list of words—

<meta>catchword: —rum (completing "vocabulorum," meaning "of words")</meta>

<summary>Gohory laments that the uneducated cannot appreciate his work, comparing it to "pearls before swine," but praises René Perrot’s dedication to wisdom and introduces his plan to clarify Paracelsus's difficult writings.</summary>
<keywords>Jacques Gohory, René Perrot, Paracelsus, philosophy, physician, Cleopatra's pearl, Renaissance education, alchemy, scholarship</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dedicatory epistle to René Perrot. ## LETTER.

—by the interpretation of his new works. For diligent men, and those studious of hidden things (for whom alone this work is forged), will, as the Poet says <note>original: *vt Poeta dicit*; referring to Virgil, *Aeneid* II, 65: *ab uno disce omnes*—"from one learn all."</note>, learn all things from one; and the light that is brought into one place will be transmitted to other things likewise surrounded by the same darkness. 

As for the abundance of the books of Paracelsus, I hear from the Germans that nearly three hundred are counted. <margin>Paracelsus wrote three hundred books.</margin> O, fertility of genius! Regarding his medical and surgical work, beyond his treatments of daily illnesses, he wished to give a specimen of his most excellent art at Nuremberg: twelve lepers <margin>He restored twelve lepers.</margin> presented from the public were restored to their former health. This is a matter indeed beyond the belief of many, yet not incredible to those who consider his rare and unheard-of remedies made from the flower of Wallflower <note>original: *Cheiri*; likely *Cheiranthus cheiri*, used in Paracelsian medicine.</note> and Rosemary <note>original: *Anthos*; from the Greek for "flower," often specifically used by Paracelsus to refer to the essence of rosemary.</note>, the secret of coral <note>original: *arcano corallino*; a chemical preparation of coral believed to have cardiotonic or cooling properties.</note>, the essence of gold, the mystery of Antimony <margin>Wonders concerning Antimony and others.</margin>, and very many of this kind, which are not even known by name to common physicians. 

If only these arts were pleasing to our Kings—for, as Cicero says, "honor nourishes the arts" <note>original: *honos alit artes*; a classic defense of patronage from Cicero's *Tusculan Disputations*.</note>, and we are all kindled to our studies by glory—just as they were to the great King Francis <note>Francis I of France (reigned 1515–1547), renowned as a "Renaissance Prince" and patron of learning.</note>, for nature does not...

->A 3<-

<summary>Gohory praises the prolific output and miraculous healing powers of Paracelsus, specifically citing his cure of twelve lepers in Nuremberg using chemical remedies. He laments the lack of royal patronage for such arts compared to the era of King Francis I.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Jacques Gohory’s letter to René Perrot. The previous page discussed the vast number of Paracelsus's works and his miraculous healings at Nuremberg using chemical medicines like antimony and the "flower of wallflower," lamenting that these arts were not better known.</meta>

## LETTER.

—brought forth, nor is our region so barren of talent that there was no hope that knowledge of the greatest and most useful things (which the ancient Magi and Poets wove in such great veils <note>original: *involucris*; referring to the allegorical or "wrapped" nature of ancient wisdom and myths.</note>) and truth itself, as if unearthed from the well of Democritus <note>The Greek philosopher Democritus famously stated that "truth lies at the bottom of a well," meaning it is difficult to find and deeply hidden.</note>, would be revealed in our times as well. Meanwhile, as you yourself know, after long travels undertaken for the sake of knowledge—having consumed my wealth following the example of that philosopher <note>referring again to Democritus, who was said to have spent his inheritance on travel to learn from foreign sages.</note>—I finally rest in the suburban gardens of my city, entirely absorbed in the contemplation of the most beautiful things in nature. In this, I am like the Virgilian Iapyx <note>A character from Virgil's *Aeneid* (Book XII) who, though offered the gifts of prophecy and music by Apollo, chose instead to learn the "silent arts" of medicine to save his father.</note>, who indeed:

> *Preferred to know the powers of herbs and the practice of healing,*
> *And to ply the silent arts without glory:*

or like Menetes, for whom:

> *His art was his home, a poor one, nor did he know the gifts of the powerful;*
> *He sowed his herbs on rented land.* <note>These verses are adapted from Virgil, describing a life of humble, honest labor in nature rather than the pursuit of political power.</note>

For although I might have had some assistance from talent and fortune for conducting public affairs, yet mindful of the human condition, I have willingly renounced the pursuit and service of princes.

Farewell. From <term>Lutetia</term> <note>The Latin name for Paris.</note>, August 6th, in the year [15]66.

<meta>catchword: OF THE LION</meta>

<meta>This page transitions from Jacques Gohory’s introductory letter to René Perrot into a formal biographical preface written under Gohory’s pseudonym, "Leo Suavius." It begins to document the life, titles, and bibliography of Paracelsus.</meta>

PREFACE

## BY LEO SUAVIUS
### ON THE LIFE AND WORKS OF THE AUTHOR.

->* * *<-

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'T' featuring a figure in robes standing amidst foliage and classical architectural elements.</image-desc>
THEOPHRASTUS Paracelsus von Hohenheim is called "The Hermit" <note>original: *Eremita*; a title derived from his birthplace, Maria-Einsiedeln, which means "Our Lady of the Hermits."</note> in several of his book titles, as well as by Erasmus of Rotterdam in a letter written to him—a letter which I have judged should be inserted here as a witness to his remarkable doctrine. By some, such as Adam von Bodenstein <note>A German physician and alchemist who was one of the earliest editors and promoters of Paracelsus's works.</note>, he is said to have been a Doctor of Philosophy and of *both Medicines* <note>original: *utriusque Medicinae*; referring to the traditional division between internal medicine (physic) and external medicine (surgery).</note>, so that they might include surgery under this name—fields which today, to the great misfortune of the public, are separated and distinguished. His book against physicians, *The Labyrinth of Wandering Doctors*, is extant. There also exists a book against surgeons regarding their impostures, but only in the German language; I hear this is now being translated into Latin by a German man. From his hands I received a prophecy <note>original: *prognosticon*</note> by the same author for twenty-three years, which, through certain riddles, threatened grave hardships for all of Europe. I shall write out for you a catalog of his other books of which knowledge has reached me. <margin>The homeland, lineage, and status of Paracelsus.</margin> He was German by nation, of a robust body but a keen intellect. "I was born," he says himself, "in Einsiedeln in the region of the Swiss." <note>original: *Heluetiorum*</note> "From my father, Wilhelm von Hohenheim, I received the foundations of the 'attained' philosophy." <note>original: *adeptae Philosophiae*; a term Paracelsus used for the practical, divinely inspired knowledge of nature and alchemy, as opposed to mere book learning.</note> And he is said by some to be noble in lineage, in all things...

<summary>This page introduces the biography of Paracelsus by Leo Suavius, citing his titles, his birth in Switzerland, and his goal of reuniting surgery with general medicine. It mentions his correspondence with Erasmus and lists some of his early published works and prophecies.</summary>
<keywords>Paracelsus, Leo Suavius, Erasmus of Rotterdam, Adam von Bodenstein, surgery vs medicine, Einsiedeln, Switzerland, Labyrinth of Wandering Doctors, prophecy, alchemy</keywords>

--- Page 12 ---
<meta>This page continues Leo Suavius’s biographical and bibliographical preface for Paracelsus. It follows from the discussion of his German origins and proceeds to list his published works and his use of "Spagyric" terminology.</meta>

->PREFACE.<-

...most expert in every branch of the sciences; however, because of the distance between places and the differences between regions, I am not familiar with the splendor of his noble lineage. That famous Adam von Bodenstein published several of his volumes, which he illustrated with his own prefaces, such as this one on *Long Life* <note>original: *de Vita longa*</note>, another on *Degrees and Compositions of Recipes and Natural Matters*, and another on *Tartar* <note>In Paracelsian medicine, "Tartar" refers to the stony deposits or toxins formed in the body, which he believed caused diseases like gout and stones.</note>, which was published with annotations taken directly from the mouth of the teacher at Basel. Adam indeed acted rightly, if only he had kept himself within the boundaries of a preface-writer, and had not proclaimed his "true and certain" knowledge of the **Philosopher’s Stone** <note>original: *lapidis philosophici*; the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and providing the elixir of life.</note> first to the Prince of Venice and later to the Lords Fugger <note>The Fuggers were an immensely wealthy and influential German banking family who funded emperors and kings.</note>. Wise men have never boasted of such a thing, and in their writings, they have condemned ostentation of this kind.

That Paracelsus was endowed with great skill in the **chemical art**, his own surviving works <note>original: *monumenta*</note> sufficiently testify, filled as they are with traditions regarding metallic matters, which he himself called by the new word <term>Spagyric</term> <note>A term coined by Paracelsus to describe alchemical medicine, derived from the Greek words for "to separate" and "to combine."</note>. Indeed, he openly affirms in this little book on *Long Life* that he was delighted by this novelty of words, by which he might keep the uninitiated <note>original: *prophanos*</note> from reading it, while attracting the students of wisdom. The greater part of these terms, sought from his other books through his own interpretation, I shall explain <note>original: *enucleabo*; literally "to take out the kernel."</note> here. 

<margin>Augurellus</margin> 
For, as Augurellus <note>Giovanni Aurelio Augurello (c. 1441–1524), an Italian humanist and poet famous for his alchemical poem *Chrysopoeia*.</note> sang concerning those hidden arts:

->—it is not right to speak of all things.—<-

<margin>From the *Book of Degrees*.</margin> 
Thus our Paracelsus wrote in the final book of *On Degrees*: 
"And these indeed are those <term>Magnalia</term> <note>Great wonders or "the great things of God."</note> in which I, not without cause, glory in through nature; and of these, there are yet even more."

However, he never confessed anywhere quite so openly, whether by divine favor or by the revelation of some philosopher...

<summary>This page discusses the publication of Paracelsus's works by Adam von Bodenstein and critiques Bodenstein for overstepping his role by claiming alchemical secrets. It introduces Paracelsus's "Spagyric" vocabulary and his intentional use of obscure language to protect sacred knowledge from the uninitiated.</summary>
<keywords>Adam von Bodenstein, Philosopher's Stone, Fugger family, Spagyric, alchemy, Augurellus, Magnalia, occult terminology</keywords>

--- Page 13 ---
<meta>This page continues Leo Suavius’s critical introduction to Paracelsus. It follows the previous discussion of Adam von Bodenstein’s prefaces, where Suavius critiqued Bodenstein for boasting about possessing the Philosopher's Stone. Here, Suavius uses a literary dialogue to contrast such boasting with the secrecy traditionally required of true alchemists.</meta>

->PREFACE.<-

<margin>In the dialogue *Chrysorrhoa*.</margin>
... (just as **Adam** [von Bodenstein] had) claimed to have attained a perfect knowledge of chemical philosophy. Indeed, that learned man who, in the dialogue *Chrysorrhoa* <note>The *Chrysorrhoa* ("River of Gold") was a popular 16th-century alchemical dialogue, often attributed to Johannes Aurifaber, featuring Paracelsus as a character.</note>, fashioned **Theophrastus** [Paracelsus] as the opening speaker, attributed to him this speech: "But that I have attempted anything for the sake of my own private gain can be seen by no one anywhere."

To which **Chrysophilus** <note>A character name meaning "Gold-lover."</note> replied to him: "By these words of yours I am made more certain that you dwell in the very inner chambers of absolute science. Have you not also frequently performed this very thing? Now indeed you deny it. Have you not brought aid to the most desperate diseases? Though you never entered the schools of physicians, yet by those ethereal qualities of yours and your abstract healing faculty alone, you surpass all the physicians of **Europe**; and they have long since yielded the palm of victory to you. Therefore, you cannot refuse me any longer without causing me grave offense." To whom **Theophrastus** replied: "Even if I were to acknowledge these things as true, you know it has been said by the wise: what you wish to remain hidden, tell to no one <note>original: *quod occultum esse vis, nemini dixeris*</note>. I confess that, both from the energy and efficacy of metals and metallic substances, I have discovered many things with the help of physics itself, the practice of which contributes greatly to public utility and to the very art of healing."

<margin>The destruction of Jason.</margin>
"But that I have attempted... etc." <note>This refers back to the beginning of the speech quoted above.</note> since I understand that this was the destruction of kings and of **Jason** <note>In alchemical literature, the myth of Jason and the Golden Fleece was often interpreted as a metaphor for the pursuit of the Philosopher's Stone; his tragic end served as a warning against the dangers of the work.</note> himself, who was utterly destroyed along with his children by his own wife—perhaps because he had handled this mystery too incautiously—and his books were burned along with the royal palace. Consider now, I pray, whether such a thing is to be desired by a wise man. Note here, **Adam**, and recognize that those who have attained this wisdom keep it in their hearts; the display of which [causes] great...

A 5

<summary>Suavius quotes an alchemical dialogue to demonstrate that true masters like Paracelsus emphasize secrecy and public utility over personal gain or boasting. He uses the tragedy of Jason as a cautionary tale for those who treat alchemical mysteries incautiously.</summary>

<keywords>Paracelsus, Adam von Bodenstein, Chrysorrhoa, alchemy, medical ethics, Jason and Medea, secrecy, chemical philosophy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Leo Suavius’s introduction. It completes the dialogue from the previous page where "Theophrastus" (Paracelsus) was speaking about the necessity of keeping alchemical secrets, contrasting his humility with the boasting of editors like Adam von Bodenstein. It then transitions into historical accounts of Paracelsus’s time in Basel.</meta>

->PREFACE.<-

...provide proof of your ignorance. For at the beginning of that dialogue, **Chrysophilus** <note>A character name meaning "Gold-lover."</note> says: "But I see **Theophrastus von Hohenheim** walking over there—a man who, if **Germany** ever produced one, is a perfect master of this art." To this effect, **Augurellus** sang:

<margin>I. **Augurellus** in his *Chrysopeia* <note>Giovanni Aurelio Augurello (c. 1441–1524) was an Italian humanist whose poem *Chrysopeia* sought to reconcile alchemy with classical poetry.</note>.</margin>

> But who, having a breast fortified with such brittle strength,
> Would not keep silent about those things that should never be repeated to anyone?
> For whom does the wisdom of things not forbid to speak
> Those matters which, once uttered, will immediately bring harm?
> By what virtue could he protect himself from snares
> Who would openly display that he hides
> Enormous riches in a small box? etc.
> Therefore, if anyone has already been able to assemble
> Such great treasures, let him keep them wonderfully under the cover of friendly silence.

Now, to return to our **Paracelsus** (a name which even the author of the *Dialogue* suppressed), he himself lectured at **Basel** on his book *On Tartar* <note>original: *de Tartaro*. Paracelsus’s "Tartaric" theory claimed that many diseases were caused by the "stone" or dregs of food and drink (like the tartar in a wine cask) precipitating inside the body.</note>, which he explains as all the dregs of the internal humors from which various diseases flow. There, he freed the distinguished printer **Frobenius** <note>Johann Froben (c. 1460–1527), the famous Swiss printer and publisher.</note> from a most dangerous illness. For this, the great **Erasmus**—renowned for his virtue and learning—gave thanks and even begged for help for his own failing health, offering clear testimony of **Paracelsus**’s rare and new skill in the healing art. 

For he established new foundations for the art and demolished and overthrew the old ones of the **Greeks**, **Hippocrates** and **Galen**, and the **Arabs**, **Avicenna**, **Rhazes**, and **Mesue** <note>These were the traditional authorities of ancient and medieval medicine. Paracelsus’s public burning of their books in Basel was a defining moment of the medical reformation.</note>. He drew the greatest part of his remedies from the metallic workshop <note>i.e., the alchemical laboratory</note>, as can be understood from his writings.

<meta>This page contains a famous letter from the great humanist scholar Erasmus of Rotterdam to the physician Paracelsus (here addressed as Theophrastus Eremita). It follows the previous page's introduction where the author was discussing Paracelsus’s time in Basel and his successful treatment of the printer Johannes Frobenius.</meta>

->P R E F A C E.<-

# TO THE MOST SKILLED IN THE MEDICAL ART,
## the physician Theophrastus the Hermit, <note>This is Paracelsus (Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim). "Eremita" likely refers to his family name "von Hohenheim" (High Home), sometimes associated with "Einsiedeln" meaning Hermitage.</note>
### Erasmus of Rotterdam.
->Greetings.<-

*It is not absurd to wish eternal health of the soul for a physician, through whom God supplies us with the health of the body.* <note>Erasmus plays on the Latin word "salutem," which means both physical "health" and spiritual "salvation."</note> *I wonder how you know me so deeply, having seen me only once. I recognize that your riddles* <note>original: "Aenigmata." Likely referring to Paracelsus's diagnostic predictions or his cryptic way of speaking.</note> *are most true, not from the medical art—which I have never learned—but from my own wretched sensations. In the region of the liver I have long felt pains, nor could I guess what might be the source of the evil. I observed fatty deposits from the kidneys in my urine* <term>urine (original: *lotio*)</term> *several years ago. What the third thing might be, I do not quite understand, yet it seems probable to me that what you said would be troublesome. In these last few days I have had no time to be treated, nor to be sick, nor to die: I am so overwhelmed by the labors of my studies. If, however, there is anything that can soothe my illness without the dissolution of my body, I ask that you share it. But if you are distracted, explain more fully in a few words those things which you noted more than concisely* <note>original: "plusquam laconice," a reference to the brief, blunt speech of the ancient Spartans of Laconia.</note>, *and prescribe other remedies that I might take when I am free. I cannot promise a reward equal to your art and zeal, but I certainly promise a grateful heart. You have recalled Frobenius* <note>Johannes Froben (c. 1460–1527), the famous Basel printer and close friend of Erasmus. Paracelsus famously saved him from a leg amputation.</note> *from the underworld; he is half of my soul. If you restore me as well, you will restore both of us in each of us. I wish it were your fortune to remain in Basel. I fear you may not be able to read these things, written in such haste.*

->Farewell.<-

->Erasmus of Rotterdam<-
->with his own hand.<-

<summary>A letter from Erasmus of Rotterdam to Paracelsus, confirming Paracelsus’s accurate diagnosis of Erasmus’s liver and kidney ailments and thanking him for curing the printer Johannes Froben.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the preface, shifting from the text of Erasmus's letter to a commentary on Paracelsus's identity, his time in Basel, and his intentionally cryptic writing style. The author defends Paracelsus against the charge of being too obscure while contrasting him with other scholars like Gesner and a figure named Adam.</meta>

->P R E F A C E.<-

In this address of the Letter, the surname Paracelsus is missing, just as it is in the Dialogue *Chrysorrhoas*: <note>original: "Chrysorrhoas," meaning "Stream of Gold." This refers to a specific alchemical or philosophical dialogue attributed to the circle of Paracelsus.</note> a name which he sometimes adopted, although his proper name was Bombast. <margin>Caution regarding the mysteries.</margin>

*WHEN I had run through, by reading, the books of the great philosopher and physician Theophrastus concerning medicine and philosophy written in Latin, as well as the writings of the Arabs, Chaldeans, and Greeks: I discovered that the writings of Theophrastus were far firmer, more certain, and more solid than the writings of Avicenna* <note>Ibn Sina, the Persian "Prince of Physicians" whose *Canon of Medicine* dominated medieval universities.</note>, *Hippocrates, and Galen* <note>The ancient Greek authorities whose theories of the four humors Paracelsus sought to overthrow.</note>. *Furthermore, his own recipes rest upon firmer and more certain reasons and experiences than those of Rhazes, Mesue* <note>Rhazes and Mesue were influential medieval Arabic medical authors.</note>, *and other ancient physicians. Indeed, the writings of Theophrastus are like silver tried by fire—most proven and most thoroughly examined. His opinions on medicine, which stand out in all his books, are not in conformity with or similar to the opinions of the ancient doctors; rather, his entire practice and theory embrace many singular things worthy of understanding. He is indeed a new physician, and a true inventor of medicine, who [draws] not from the writings of the ancients, but from a certain singular philosophical foundation (which is as white is to black* <note>original: *album ad nigrum*; a common idiom for things that are complete opposites or distinctly different.</note>)...

*...we took care to have them translated. Once the Greeks were informed about this, they called him the Eternal Monarch, certainly on account of his most acute and subtle writings, in which hardly a single word of his can be found that is worthy of blame or criticism.*

*However, because he did not follow the path of the ancients* <note>Referring to the traditional medical and philosophical authorities like Galen and Aristotle, whose "humoral" theories Paracelsus famously rejected</note>*, some judge his works only according to their own limited understanding. # CATALOGUE OF THOSE THINGS
## *which are contained in this work.*

### A COMPENDIUM <term>Compendium: A concise summary or collection of knowledge</term> of Universal Philosophy and Medicine by Ph. Theophrastus Paracelsus, authored by Leo Suavius, I. G. P. <note>original: "Leone Suauio I. G. P." Leo Suavius was the pseudonym of Jacques Gohory (1520–1576), a French scholar and physician who sought to bridge the gap between alchemy and mainstream medicine. "I. G. P." stands for Iacobus Gohorius Parisiensis (Jacques Gohory of Paris)</note>

### Four Books on Long Life <note>original: "De Vita longa"</note> by Ph. Theophrastus Paracelsus.

The first contains a general treatise on Long Life.

The second lists a singular method of healing, for the purpose of recovering a healthy life from diseases and preserving it in its entirety.

The third makes use of quintessences <term>Quintessence: The "fifth essence" or purest, most concentrated medicinal force extracted from a substance</term>, and completes the elixir secret <note>original: "arcanum Elixiricum"</note> for the use of that same healthy life.

The fourth, having laid the foundations in Book I of *Long Life*, puts on the finishing touch <note>original: "supremam manum imponit," a Latin idiom for completing or perfecting a work</note>: that is, for that life which exists beyond nature <note>This refers to "preternatural" longevity—the alchemical goal of extending human life far beyond its standard biological limits</note>.

## PHILIP THEOPHRASTUS
# PARACELSUS
## ON PHILOSOPHY
### AND UNIVERSAL MEDICINE:
### A COMPENDIUM.

->By the author Leo Suavius, I. G. P.<- <note>original: "Leone Suauio I. G. P." As noted previously, this is the pseudonym of the French scholar Jacques Gohory.</note>

ALTHOUGH I am well aware, O philosophers, that the ancients criticized the separation between the art of thinking rightly and the art of speaking rightly, and that this new Philosophy might have appeared before your eyes a little more polished and adorned (had my busy schedule permitted it); nevertheless, like a chaste maiden (who naturally recoils from makeup and curling irons), she preferred to present herself to you thus unadorned, with a "diligent negligence," <note>original: "diligenti negligentia." This is a rhetorical term suggesting that the work's lack of polish is intentional, focusing on substance over style.</note> at the earliest possible time. She hopes that even if she is seen naked, she may still awaken a marvelous love for herself.

<margin>Roger Bacon</margin>
Therefore, so that I may explain this marvelous book (insofar as it is permitted by the oath of the Philosophers), <note>This refers to the "Hermetic Oath" or the traditional vow of secrecy taken by alchemists and occult philosophers not to reveal the "Great Secret" to the uninitiated.</note> I shall gather together in a general way those things from various books by the same author which can, in a sense, awaken the reader's understanding. For no one seems to be a better interpreter of a man than the man himself—unless, perhaps, I insert a few things from Roger Bacon the Englishman, <note>Roger Bacon (c. 1214–1292) was a medieval friar and scientist known as "Doctor Mirabilis" for his focus on empirical study and alchemy.</note> from whom Paracelsus seems to have drawn a great many things. Indeed, Paracelsus agrees with him most strongly in all his opinions on hidden matters. As for the necessary secrecy regarding certain abstruse <term>Abstruse: Difficult to understand; obscure or specialized knowledge</term> works, he offers his judgment below.

# COMPENDIUM OF PHILOSOPHY
### Page 22

> ... whose birth or natural death no one has ever discovered or heard of. To understand these beings, we must first establish the foundations of that *Philosophy to the Athenians* <note>original: "Philosophia ad Athenienses," a major cosmological work by Paracelsus.</note>, which I have taken care to translate from the German language.

<margin>From the book, *Philosophy to the Athenians*.</margin>
He calls the first beginning of things the **Great Mystery** <note>original: "Mysterium magnum." In Paracelsian thought, this is the primordial "mother" of all things, a chaotic but divine source-matter.</note>, from which he claims all mysteries were created or established. The Eternal is the cause of all those things we see, and it is joined with perishable things. But eternity is unknown to us mortals; for this reason, the origin, arrival, and departure of the soul are likewise unknown. 

<margin>Diverse mysteries.</margin>
Eternal things are born, not begotten <note>This distinction implies they emerge directly from the divine essence rather than through biological reproduction.</note>. That **prime matter** is imperceptible to the senses, yet it is the beginning of all elements. That Great Mystery hands down to all things their own general mysteries; and just as various successive mysteries do not appear in the things that came before them, so all things are contained within the first mystery. All created things were made at once and at the same time; they existed within the uncreated just as an image exists within a block of wood <note>A favorite Paracelsian metaphor: the sculptor does not "create" the statue but reveals what was already latent in the wood.</note>. 

A rough example of these mysteries can be seen in **milk**, which is the "mystery" of cheese, butter, and similar things; and cheese is also the matter for the worms that are born within it. The Earth rests upon **archaltic columns** <term>archaltis: a Paracelsian term referring to the spiritual or "astral" foundations that support the physical earth</term>; the air is the chest of invisible things, and water is the chest of the Nymphs. The Earth provides the throne, the water provides **Turas**, and the Air provides **samies** <term>Turas and samies: specific Paracelsian terms for the vital or elemental essences belonging to water and air respectively</term>: and these are the **great works of God** <note>original: "magnalia Dei"</note>. 

The first separation of the Great Mystery resulted in the elements: the firmament was separated from the fire, and from that firmament the stars emerged like flowers from a plant; but their splendor comes from the **arcanum** <note>The "arcanum" refers to the secret, inner medicinal or spiritual virtue of a thing.</note>, not from the fire, as seen in the sun.

...and stars. In the element of earth there are Gnomes <note>original: "Gnomi." In Paracelsian thought, Gnomes are the "pygmies" or elemental spirits of the earth.</note>, wild men, night-women, and giants. In the element of fire, there are various species of fires of different degrees, from which comes the variety of colors. Moreover, all elements contain certain rational and irrational beings; thus, from the elements comes the separation of offspring, and from these offspring, the final mysteries. Furthermore, the four elements are just as many worlds.

Plutarch <note>A Greek-Roman philosopher and biographer</note> warns that loves and other occurrences similar to human affairs should be attributed to spirits, not to the eternal, holy, and immortal God. <margin>Paradoxes from Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim, the birth name of Paracelsus.</note></margin>

The "essate" anatomy <note>original: "Anatomia essata"; a Paracelsian term referring to the spiritual or essential blueprint of an organism that governs its health and form.</note> is the parent of diseases.
<margin>Native life, from the book *On Long Life*.</margin>
Here he touches upon a distinction, discussed in this first book, between "native life" and "long life" (or life beyond nature). To this I would add that this life resides in the heart, its source; as Aristotle rightly said, the heart is the "first thing to live and the last to die" <note>original: "primum viuens & vltimum moriens"</note>.
<margin>On blood leaping from a corpse.</margin>
From this principle proceeds that miracle of blood leaping from a body shortly after death when the person who committed the violence approaches. Levinus Lemnius <note>A 16th-century Dutch physician known for blending medicine with natural philosophy.</note> writes much on this in his book *On the Secret Miracles of Nature*. I myself was present at such a spectacle involving an infant whom we suspected had been suffocated by a drunken nurse. I twice saw blood flow from the nostrils, occurring both at the first and second meeting <note>The practice of "cruentation," a medieval legal test where a corpse was believed to bleed in the presence of its murderer.</note>. I concluded that this happens to those taken by a violent death, because in other deaths, the vital spirits exhale in their own due time.

<margin>The formation of man, and how he participates in minerals.</margin>
Since man, according to the opinion of the ancient sages, is called a **Microcosm** <note>Meaning "little world," the belief that the human body is a miniature reflection of the entire universe (the Macrocosm).</note>, the author compares the ailments of man to the impressions of the greater world. And since man was formed from the earth, the author assigns to him, by way of similarity, all species of **minerals**: which the "humoral" physicians <note>Traditional doctors who followed the system of Galen, focusing on the four "humors" or bodily fluids.</note> had only used lightly in relation to their humors. Thus, he identifies vitriol, alum, and nitre within the body, which he indeed determines consists of only three things: **sulfur, salt, and liquor** (or **mercury**). These three he borrowed from the Chemists <note>Alchemists.</note>, especially from **Johannes Valentianus**, who joined these three in a single French verse to this effect:

> *From whence flow sulfur, salt, and oil.* <note>original: "Vnde manat sulphur, sal, oleum."</note>

When any of those three is damaged, a destruction occurs in the body, which is removed by **secret tinctures** <note>Known as "arcana" in Paracelsian medicine; these were specialized chemical remedies believed to target the essence of a disease.</note>, rather than by **evacuation** <note>The traditional practice of purging or bloodletting.</note>, which only removes waste products. The aforementioned author affirms that while common doctors occupy themselves with these waste products, **Theophrastus** <note>Paracelsus.</note> alone deals with those fundamental substances.

**Bolus** (or clay) is the body in which no mineral has a place; in a similar way, the more principal organs do not suffer such things within themselves. **Corrosives** in the principal organs do not cause ulceration in the same way as they do in the external parts. **Diseases** are born from the body as if from a foundation, just as thorns and briars spring from the earth. The **fetus** flows from the bones, beginning first from the center of the seed.

# AND PARACELSIAN MEDICINE
### C

The active power <note>original: "virtutem"</note> must be extracted from **simples** <term>raw medicinal ingredients, typically plants or minerals</term>, while their physical body must be discarded. For the stomach of the sick person is overwhelmed by the dregs of these materials, and **tartar** <term>stony deposits or metabolic waste, likened to the crust in wine barrels</term> is left behind in the body, which is the cause of various diseases.

Doctors are greatly deluded regarding their **four humors** <note>The traditional medical system of Galen, which focused on balancing blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note> (which is the sole foundation of their art). The mixture of these humors in the human body is so complex that a disease cannot easily be attributed to any single one; especially since a "dominant" humor often cannot be identified when the mixture is nearly balanced. No diseases are incurable in themselves—neither epilepsy, nor dropsy <note>An old term for edema or swelling caused by fluid retention.</note>, and so on. Every individual domain of nature has its own appointed governor: the **light of nature** <note>The innate intelligence or divine wisdom found within the natural world.</note>.

Once the skilled master of medicine has recognized the **limit** <note>original: "terminum," referring to the specific stage, duration, or boundary of a disease</note> of a disease, he divides it into twelve parts. He takes the first and the second half for himself to heal, and the remaining ten and a half he quickly cuts away and drives off.

**Natural science** <note>original: "Physica"</note> is necessary for the doctor to understand the nature of things; **Chemistry** for their correct preparation; and **Astronomy** to calculate the proper timing in the administration of remedies, whether medical or surgical.

<margin>Three types of physicians.</margin>

There are three kinds of doctors: some arise from nature and the influence of the stars; some are given by God; and some are trained through formal study against their natural instinct. These latter practice medicine unhappily and ignorantly, as is recognized by their works. New diseases often descend from the heavens, which without astro... <note>The text cuts off here, likely continuing with "astrology" or "astronomy" on the next page.</note>

Gout, which is called "knotted" <note>original: "nodosa"</note>, ought to be called "granular."

# COMPENDIUM OF PHILOSOPHY

### *From the Labyrinth of Erring Physicians.* <note>original: "Ex Labyrintho medicorum errantium"; this refers to a famous work by the physician Paracelsus which critiques traditional medical practices and promotes his new chemical medicine.</note>

Just as a small cloud in a clear sky brings forth hail, rain, and lightning, so must one theorize regarding the nature of illnesses.

<margin>The guiding form.</margin>
The "form" is spiritual, invisible, and sidereal <note>meaning influenced by or derived from the stars and astral forces</note>. It is empty talk to speak of "directing agents"—such as claiming sage must be sent to the head, or marjoram and lavender to specific parts—for eyebright <note>original: "eufragia"; a plant traditionally used for eye ailments</note> does not need a vehicle to reach the eyes. Because of its ocular form <note>referring to the "Doctrine of Signatures," the belief that a plant's physical appearance reveals its healing purpose; eyebright flowers resemble eyes</note>, <margin>Human members in herbs</margin> it travels to that specific part of the body of its own accord. All human members—the heart, liver, and so on—are present in herbs; not in their physical shape, but in their essential properties. When the essence of a herb is taken into the body, the "heart" of the plant seeks out the heart of the man. <margin>Medicine for cancer.</margin> In this way, a draft of *dactiletus* <note>likely a preparation involving the "dactyl" or date-like signature</note> heals a cancer <note>or "canker," referring to spreading sores</note>, because its inner form is that of a "cancer." <note>Paracelsus believed that a medicine must possess the same "form" or character as the disease to overcome it.</note>

<margin>Dropsy.</margin>
In dropsy <term>hydropisis: an old medical term for edema or the swelling of tissues due to an accumulation of fluid</term>, a "meteoric seed" is present which dissolves into rain; this rain falls to the bottom of the body, and thus a "lake" is formed.

<margin>Evacuation of waste.</margin>
In human waste, sometimes it is not actual bile <note>original: "fel"</note> that is present, but merely the color of bile.

<margin>The powers of Comfrey, Sapphire, and Emerald.</margin>
Broken legs and other bones, as well as ruptures, are healed by Comfrey <note>original: "Symphyto"; from the Greek "symphyo" meaning to grow together</note>.
By experience, Sapphire heals carbuncles <note>original: "anthracem"; a severe, painful skin infection or ulcer</note>.
Emerald, when taken internally, is an elixir for long life, though it is not actually a stone <note>likely referring to a "tincture" or chemical essence extracted from the mineral</note>.

<margin>Water of minerals.</margin>
Water is the mother of minerals; therefore the alchemist <term>spagyrus: a practitioner of "spagyria," the Paracelsian method of separating and recombining substances to create potent medicines</term> produces rubies and other gems from them.
Gold cures or masks the symptoms of leprosy.
Jaundice <note>original: "Icteritia"</note> arises from the "saffron" <note>referring to the yellow-orange color</note> of orpiment <note>original: "auripigmenti"; a yellow arsenic mineral used as a pigment</note>.

<margin>Comfrey, Saffron, and Gold.</margin>
Whatever Salt has consumed, Comfrey <note>original: "consolida"</note> cures; whatever Sulfur has dissolved, Saffron <note>original: "crocus"</note> restores; and whatever Mercury has made too subtle, Gold condenses.

# AND THE MEDICINE OF PARACELSUS.

He says that nothing is perfected by nature simply in its **prime matter** <note>original: "materia prima"; the raw, undifferentiated substance of the universe</note>: rather, it is perfected in the "second" and "third" matter by **Vulcan** <note>The Roman god of fire, used here as a metaphor for the alchemist or the transformative power of heat/chemistry</note>. This is to be understood *relatively* <note>original Greek: "προς τι" (pros ti)</note>, that is, so that things may be adapted for the use of others, because all things are simply perfect in their own being.

->*Explanation of the Mysteries.*<-

<margin>*Man as a microcosm.*</margin>
But let this be the latest addition to the understanding of Paracelsus’s most difficult axioms: lend me your ears and your minds <note>original: "favete iam linguis animisque"; a ritual call for silence and attention</note>. **Man is a microcosm** <note>a "little world" that mirrors the "macrocosm" or the great universe</note>, and he is made so that he may be known from within. For the physician, the **light of nature** <note>original: "lumen naturae"; the innate wisdom or intuition required to understand the natural world without relying solely on ancient books</note> is necessary—that is, the knowledge of how all things established in the greater world arise, grow, change, and perish. Through this, he can penetrate into the inner and hidden nature of man with the sharpness of his mind. And since, according to Aristotle, the Sun (or the Heavens) and Man together beget Man, the Heavens must be understood by the physician. <margin>*The generation of man.*</margin> Furthermore, for the preservation of man, nothing should be considered more excellent than man himself, such as the **balsam of blood** or the **liquid of mummy** <note>original: "mummiae liquore"; in Paracelsian medicine, "mummy" refers to a vital spiritual essence or a medicine derived from the life-force of a body</note>. If these are dried out too much within him, his **sulfur** is set on fire, his **salt** is turned into lime, and the human body perishes. <margin>*The distinction of the Sun.*</margin> Yet a certain invisible sun fosters the fire within man—a concept passed down by philosophers and offered to the **Archaeus** <note>The "internal chemist" or vital force that governs the body's functions</note>. When the Archaeus is nourished and refreshed by that native fire, he performs **Vulcanic chemistry** <note>internal alchemy</note> within himself, by which he separates the pure from the impure. (This is according to **Theophrastus** <note>Paracelsus’s given name</note> in his *Surgery*). He purifies his "gold," partly from the chyme and metallic dregs, and partly from the toxic vapor of **realgar** <note>arsenic disulfide; viewed here as a poisonous mineral byproduct</note>. Thus (as he said regarding **antimony**), the health of the human body [rests] in the highest state of its gold...

<margin>
The cycle of all things.
</margin>
...the mixture of [elements] in Paracelsus is not ridiculous, nor did it spring from some vain imagination of his. For it is according to Plato that, although all things have drawn their origin from the One, there is a certain cycle of all things turning into all others through thickening <note>original: "concretionem"</note> and scattering <note>original: "dissipationem"</note>. Air is born from the extinguishing of fire, and in turn, when thinned, it gives back fire from itself; from two fires mixed together, a single element of air is begotten. Conversely, air divided into small parts is scattered into two bodies of fire; and again, when compressed and condensing into itself, it turns into moisture. Thus, in all things, that which exists beforehand always provides a ready origin for others through its own transformation; and each thing retains within another body a certain anticipated and primary power of its own origin.

<margin>
Paracelsus above regarding air diffused into other elements.
</margin>
However, as he <note>Paracelsus</note> wrote to the Athenians <note>Referring to Paracelsus's *De Philosophia ad Athenienses*, a work on the origins of the world from chaos</note> using things learned from the Greeks, the nature of air and water was extremely mixed; these indeed withdrew during the first distribution of chaos, having been mingled with many other kinds.

<margin>
Melusinas.
Nymphs.
</margin>
Nor did he—to finish explaining these mysteries—establish his Melusinas <note>Melusina: a legendary female spirit of fresh water, often depicted as a mermaid or serpent-woman in alchemical lore</note> and Nymphs of the air and water merely as a certain state or force diffused within them; nor like statues fixed to a base, but as beings which may also go forth into other elements, even if one might call this a kind of "rapture" <note>original: "raptum." This suggests a sudden movement or transport between elemental realms</note>.

Sometimes they are understood literally, yet not in the chapter on the extraction of the quintessence...

40 COMPENDIUM OF PHILOSOPHY

...of the essence, etc., concerning which I will here briefly summarize the opinions of the Philosophers.

<margin>The matter of the Philosopher's Stone.</margin>
Certain individuals have established that the matter for the work of the <term>Philosopher’s Stone<note>The legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and granting eternal life.</note></term> lies in vegetable substances, about which Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, an influential 8th-century polymath and "father of chemistry."</note> wrote. They posit this as possible indeed, but not for themselves: for their life would fail them <note>The process is suggested to be longer than a human lifespan.</note> before they could complete it, etc.

Others choose only a "vegetable liquor" for the dissolution of metallic matter; in this, they rely either on reason or on authority. The chief authority seems to be Raymond Lull <note>A 13th-century philosopher to whom many later alchemical texts were attributed.</note>, from whom this reasoning is also drawn: If all the elements of the Stone were purely mineral, they would not be able to penetrate, transform, or multiply <note>Alchemists believed that a "vegetable" or "growing" principle was needed to make the metal "grow" into gold.</note>.

But Raymond, in his *Epistola Accurtatoria* <note>The "Abridged Letter," a famous alchemical treatise.</note>, says that in the "path of minerals" there is a <term>menstruum<note>From the Latin *menstruus*; in alchemy, this refers to a powerful solvent used to dissolve solids.</note></term>, whose spirits multiply only the <term>tincture<note>The concentrated essence or "soul" of a substance used to transform other materials.</note></term> of the ferment. He specifically distinguishes this from the vegetable type, lest anyone should cite from his *Questionnaire* that a certain menstruum originates from vegetable matter—any more than the "vegetative power" <note>The capacity for growth and reproduction.</note> is planted in "gold-ness" and "silver-ness" <note>original: "aureitate & argenteitate"</note>, as discussed in the first question. For if "vegetative" were understood there as referring to plants, the work would be made of gold, silver, and plants alone; indeed, the <term>Great Work<note>The "Magnum Opus" or final goal of alchemy.</note></term> would be made from "vegetable mercury," which accords with any of the metals. Therefore, this "vegetable" (as the solvent which must be thickened by the substance it dissolved) will be the other part of the Stone's matter.

<margin>The first principle: quicksilver with the metals.</margin>
But in Book 1, Raymond says: "The first principle is quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> along with all its metals." These words sound as though they refer to mineral quicksilver, from which metals draw their origin—lest anyone cite from the chapter concerning the method of extracting mercury from the most pro-

# C O N F E C T I O N S
## O F  P A R A C E L S U S

->*On the tincture of the Sun, that is, of Gold.*<-

Once the tincture of the Sun <note>original: *Solis*. In alchemical symbolism, the Sun represents Gold.</note> has been extracted, its body remains white, but the tincture is pure and is separated from the impure—that is, from its own body. This separation is necessary; the tincture must be clarified or "exalted" <note>An alchemical term for increasing the potency or purity of a substance.</note> in its own grade, which is doubled five times in twice twenty-four [hours]. It does not progress higher than this. Then it can be administered to anyone for the renewal of the blood to its former state, as will be described in the section on administration.

->*The extraction is as follows.*<-

The body [of the gold] must be corrupted <note>To "corrupt" in alchemy means to break down the physical form of a metal, usually through corrosion or dissolution, to release its inner essence.</note> from its metallic nature and its malleability by means of salt water; finally, the residue must be washed with fresh water, and afterwards the tincture is extracted by the spirit of wine <note>original: *spiritum vini*; distilled alcohol, used as a solvent.</note>.

The process of vaporizing a substance so it rises and leaves heavier impurities behind.</note>, which refines the matter, but does not allow itself to be refined beyond the fifth essence <term>Fifth essence: also known as the *quintessence*, the purest and most potent medicinal core of a substance.</term>: that is, to a degree of 240; otherwise, it is burnt by proceeding further.

### The use and administration is as follows.

You shall give one dram <note>original: *dragmam*. A unit of weight, roughly 3.9 grams.</note> of this mixed with one ounce of Venetian treacle <term>Venetian treacle: or *theriaca veneta*, a famous polypharmaceutical compound containing dozens of ingredients, used as a universal antidote.</term> on an empty stomach; at each dose, give one scruple <note>original: *scrupulum*. A small unit of weight, about 1.3 grams.</note>. Afterward, let the patient be covered in bed and sweat: let this be continued for 10 or 12 days.

## THERE IS ALSO IN CORAL

Let its body be ground finely into a powder <note>original: *alcool*. In early chemistry, "alcohol" often referred to an extremely fine, "atomized" powder before the term was narrowed to distilled spirits.</note>, and let its tincture be extracted, just as from gold, by means of the spirit of wine; and let them ascend <note>Vaporize and condense.</note> together sixteen times; afterwards, let them be separated through distillation. ### *The dosage for administration is:*

That one ounce and two drams <note>original: *dragmae*. A unit of weight, roughly 3.9 grams.</note> of it be mixed with ten ounces of chicory water or germander <note>original: *gamandreae*. ### *Tincture of Balsam.*

Take half an ounce of balsam and twenty ounces of spirit of wine <term>Spirit of wine: a high-proof alcohol produced through distillation, often used as a solvent in alchemical tinctures.</term>. Place them together in a pelican <note>original: *pellicanum*. A specialized alchemical vessel with two curved arms that allow the liquid to cycle back into the base, symbolizing the "pelican in her piety" feeding her young.</note> or a double vessel, and let them be circulated in the Sun for a month. Once this is done, it allows itself to be distilled together with the spirit through an alembic <note>original: *alembicum*. A classic distillation apparatus consisting of a boiling flask and a cooling cap with a delivery tube.</note>. This distillation is better in this instance than one through a retort <note>original: *retorta*. A glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck; the text suggests the alembic provides a gentler or more suitable separation here.</note>. In this way, the mixture remains together in a single composition. To this, you shall add another half-ounce of balsam and allow it to be digested <note>original: *digeri*. In early chemistry, "digestion" refers to the application of gentle, steady heat over a long period to encourage chemical bonding.</note> in a closed vessel, so that it may be mixed with the others, and that which comes out of its body may be perfected. For whatever must be graduated <term>Graduate: to refine or concentrate a substance through repeated heat treatment or distillation.</term> must have its substance conclude in a single body.

And when this has been made above the volatile part, let another half-ounce of balsam be added again, which you shall exalt <note>original: *exaltabis*. In alchemy, "exaltation" is the process of raising a substance to a higher level of purity, potency, or spiritual quality.</note> as before, up to two ounces, by adding and graduating. This is the most powerful preparation of balsam, which renews and cures whatever other preparations cannot. For the sake of preservation, it has acquired this virtue from heaven above all other things.

I REPEAT what we briefly touched upon at the beginning of this compendium.

### On the water of salt.

Hassardus <note>Likely referring to an early commentator or editor of Paracelsus's works.</note>, in his section on the "water of salt" <note>original: *aqua salis*</note>, wrote: "Take <note>original: *R.*, the standard abbreviation for *Recipe*</note> powdered salt," although he says later, "powder it." The past tense used is the German word *Geflossen*, which is interpreted as "melted" or "poured" <note>original: *fusum vel alatum*; 'alatum' is likely a printer's error for 'elatum' or 'dilutum'</note>, just as a little later the infinitive *Fliessen* is translated by Hassardus as "to flow" or "to be melted." However, Gerardus <note>Gerhard Dorn (c. 1530–1584), a Belgian philosopher and one of the most important editors of Paracelsus.</note> passed over this in silence.

<margin>Melted salt.</margin> To me, it seems it should read "Take melted salt" <note>original: *sal fusile*</note> due to an error by the German translator. This substance is recommended by all chemists, and perhaps it should be understood as "fossil salt" <term>Fossil salt: Naturally occurring rock salt (halite) mined from the earth rather than evaporated from sea water.</term>, which a certain writer of Pharmacopoeias <note>original: *Antidotarij scriptor*</note> believes to be "salt of gems" <note>original: *sal gemmae*; a very pure form of rock salt.</note>. Our Paracelsus uses this in drawing out the oil from Antimony <note>original: *Stibio*</note>, as we will teach in its own chapter in Book III—unless you prefer common salt made "melted" by human art. However, here he wants it to be pure by nature and explicitly rejects art by name; therefore, he orders it to be liquefied or melted quite often, which is what happens in the common preparation. Hassardus adds *radis* for *radix* [root], that is, he interprets the "blood herb" <note>original: *sanguineam herbam*</note> as Radish <note>original: *Raphanus*</note> or Shepherd's Purse <note>original: *bursa pastoris*</note>, though I do not know on what authority. But you should understand the salt to be pure rock salt, dissolved, strained, and congealed.

### On the spirit of wine.

I wonder at those who wish to be recognized as disciples of Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus Paracelsus.</note>, yet have not noticed that this extraction is highly corrupt. In this method, "circulation" <term>Circulation: A process of continuous distillation and condensation in a closed vessel, intended to refine and "spiritualize" a substance.</term> is the first step, whereas among the masters of the quintessences—John of Rupescissa <note>A 14th-century Franciscan alchemist who wrote extensively on the 'Quintessence' of wine (alcohol).</note> and Raymond Lully <note>A Catalan philosopher and mystic to whom many influential alchemical texts were attributed.</note>—it is always the last. Furthermore, the phlegm <term>Phlegm: In early chemistry, the watery, inactive byproduct of distillation that was thought to "kill" or weaken the active spirit.</term> that kills the spirit is not separated, nor are the dregs in the work of circu-
<meta>The catchword 'landi' indicates the next page begins with the completion of the word 'circulandi' (circulating).</meta>

It transitions from the previous discussion on "water of salt" into the specific technical signs of successful distillation.</meta>

<page-num>51</page-num>

<header>AND THE MEDICINE OF PARACELSUS</header>

...distilling <note>The text begins mid-word, likely completing "distillandi" from the previous page.</note>. He does not declare a sign for when the spirit ceases to rise. It is written that this distillation of the spirit occurs in the cold—unless we understand the "serpentine" <term>Serpentine: A coiled cooling tube, often submerged in water, used to condense vapors back into liquid.</term> instrument to be meant here—whereas such things are usually done with fire. 

For the sign of completion is twofold: namely, in the taste and flavor of the dripping water, if it should become tasteless. And in the visual signs of the alembic <note>A distillation apparatus consisting of a boiling vessel and a cooling cap.</note>, if the water begins (as they say) "to vein," that is, to form streaks <note>original: *venas facere*; this refers to the "tears" or oily streaks seen on the glass as different fractions of a liquid condense.</note>; for the burning follows the sharpness of the taste. 

However, what kind of statement is it to say that what follows is "water of life" <note>original: *aqua vitae*; a term for concentrated alcohol.</note> and not "spirit"? Is not the spirit of wine called "water of life" by everyone? Therefore, it should have been read as "water of wine" or "water of the vine," which at that point is as tasteless as spring water.

Finally, a tincture of gold is said to be drawn out into the spirit of wine, leaving a white earth residue at the bottom of the vessel. Which of the philosophers has not said, along with Geber <note>An influential 8th-century alchemist, often cited as an authority on the nature of metals.</note>, that gold is "homogeneous" <note>Meaning it is uniform throughout and cannot be separated into different components.</note>? Therefore, according to Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman naturalist who wrote on the properties of metals.</note>, it is unconquered by fire, and it possesses a constancy against the juices of salt and vinegar, which are the masters of all other things. 

Therefore, every single part of gold is gold; although Cornelius Agrippa <note>Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa (1486–1535), a famous polymath and occultist.</note> falsely boasts that he extracted a certain "extensive spirit" from the mass. Pantheus <note>Giovanni Agostino Panteo, a 16th-century Venetian priest and alchemist.</note> adds that this spirit will become "intensive" if it is reduced back into its own body—that is, into the "oil of glass" <note>original: *oleum vitri*; likely referring to a concentrated metallic oil or a specific acid.</note>. Thus, it cannot be that a saffron or lemon-colored part is drawn into the spirit while a white part remains; it is even more miraculous to claim that a "metallic water" can be drawn from such a residue. 

I believe, therefore, that these ideas were never drawn from the clear fountains of Paracelsus himself, but were most subtly inserted by those who claim to know the inner secrets of the craft. This is most clearly evident from Hassardus <note>An editor or commentator of Paracelsus's works.</note> himself, who, concerning the three enigmas, second...

...[as he] did: place one after five, nothing (represented by N), then a thousand after five—that is, VINVM <note>original: *VINVM*. > And they call it burning water, and the liquor of life,

However, regarding the dissolution of essences, Raymond <note>original: *Raymundus*; likely referring to Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315), a philosopher to whom many alchemical works were falsely attributed.</note> and Augurello <note>Giovanni Aurelio Augurello (c. 1441–1524), author of the alchemical poem *Chrysopoeia*.</note> do not keep them in the heat for so long, but only until—as that man says—there appears a **quintessence** <term>Quintessence: Literally the "fifth essence," the purest and most concentrated form of a substance, believed by alchemists to be separated from the four physical elements.</term> of the **color of heaven** <note>original: *coloris coeli*; a sky-blue or celestial blue color, often considered a sign of high purity in alchemical preparations.</note>, distinct from the dregs as if by a diametrical line. Yet, in another German codex, "forty days" are read for our **circulation of wine** <term>Circulation: A process of continuous distillation in a closed vessel where the vapor condenses and flows back into the liquid, meant to "exalt" or refine the substance.</term>; and in Book III of *On Long Life*, a two-month period is prescribed for circulating and thus drawing out a certain "fatness" on the surface, which is the **spirit of wine** <note>original: *spiritus vini*; concentrated alcohol.</note>, while the remainder is **phlegm** <term>Phlegm: In early chemistry, the watery, tasteless, and inactive residue left after the "spirit" or "oil" has been distilled off.</term>. In this way, the spirit could be drawn out by circulation alone without the use of chemistry, were it not that in the *Book of Degrees* he distinguishes **water of life** <note>original: *aqua vitae*; distilled alcohol.</note> from **circulated water**; but let us call this one "circulated."

There remains, at the end of this extraction, the **graduation** <term>Graduation: The process of increasing the "degree" or potency of a medicinal spirit, or refining a metal to its highest purity.</term> of that spirit, which both authors write cannot be refined beyond the "fifth essence"—though the German language sounds as if it goes beyond the fifth turn, that is (they say) **2.4.0.** where it should be read as **24**. This is the final degree of the natural perfection of gold—that is, **24 Carats** in the language of goldsmiths and minters; otherwise (they add) it is "burned." Who has ever dared to affirm that gold is burned? I will add that in the administration of medicine, **Venetian theriac** <note>original: *theriacam venetam*; a famous and complex poly-pharmaceutical "cure-all" containing dozens of ingredients, including viper flesh and opium.</note> is prescribed by Gerard <note>Likely Gerard Dorn (c. 1530–1584), a prominent Belgian editor and defender of Paracelsus.</note>, whom I doubt was thinking of **turpentine**; the label on the theriac is ridiculous, and the addition to the author in the *Epitome* is superfluous. From these examples, the reader may guess at the rest of these interpreters' dreams. I shall add here only something regarding the degrees of gold or **Carats**, from a certain inquiry on the plague by an uncertain, yet highly learned author, whoever he was: let us suppose that pure, unadulterated native gold is of one degree...

### *Concerning the philosophical salt.*

<margin>Gold cannot be reduced into a salt.</margin>
### Take of the salt of gold, etc.
Since gold, as I said above, is homogeneous and devoid of all flammable sulfur, it does not seem possible for it to be **calcined** <term>Calcination: The process of heating a substance to high temperatures in the presence of air to reduce it to a powder or "ash," usually the first step in creating a "salt."</term> by fire, and consequently, it cannot be reduced into a salt. This is despite the fact that Bernard of the Garden <note>likely referring to Bernard of Trevisan (1406–1490), a famous alchemist often associated with the "Allegory of the Fountain."</note>, and the inventor of a certain impregnable city, asserts that he knows the method for making this salt; it is rumored that this man is preparing a "serious war" against the chemists <note>This "war" likely refers to a scholarly or polemical attack on the theories of contemporary alchemists.</note>.

<margin>Salt of Antimony.</margin>
Indeed, I have produced a crystalline salt of Antimony <term>Antimony: A metallic element used in the early modern period both in metallurgy and, controversially, as a powerful medicinal purgative.</term> from its red powder. Other types of salts are very easy for me to make, as I have demonstrated by experience to certain most learned and honorable physicians of this city; and I have done so by a triple method: one that is ready at hand, another more subtle, and a third most subtle. I have also heard from the renowned hero of Maligny, the Vidame of Chartres <note>Jean de Ferrières (1520–1586), a French nobleman and diplomat known for his interest in Paracelsian medicine and his military leadership.</note>—who is equally skilled in warfare and occult literature—that Adam von Bodenstein <note>A famous German physician and early champion of Paracelsus's works.</note>, the distinguished physician and disciple of <term>Theophrastus</term> <note>Referring to Paracelsus, whose full name was Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim.</note>, provides excellent remedies for the sick with these salts. But not all the secrets of the art (as he says) are to be prostituted by allurements, except to the sons of [wisdom]— <note>The text breaks off mid-word; "fi-" likely completes to *filiis sapientiae*, or "sons of wisdom," a common alchemical term for initiates.</note>

A doctor must know the power and nature of all things, and learn the method of extracting them, using the example of **Antimony**: from which alone it was discovered by the chemical art that **gold** is rightly purged, and rendered pure and bright, with no dross or foreign <term>scoria</term> <note>original: *scoria*; the dross or slag left over after smelting metal</note> left behind. In which purging, silver and other metals, if they are contained in the mass of gold, are worn away and consumed. This is the exposition of the first proposition of the chapter on Antimony in Book IV, just as gold follows. **Man** is of the same <term>complexion</term> <note>original: *complexionis*; in historical medicine, this refers to the balance of qualities or temperament of a substance or body</note> as gold; therefore, he can be equally purged by Antimony, and the health of both can be raised to the highest degree. Antimony is of a fiery nature, which consumes some things and preserves others. From it is drawn a **purgative medicine** without evacuation through the <term>stool</term> <note>original: *secessum*; the author is claiming this refined medicine heals without the violent diarrhea or vomiting associated with common antimony</note>, to which no other is equal in the shops of the pharmacists. For it pursues and puts to flight all noxious <term>humors</term> <note>the four primary fluids—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile—thought to govern health</note> in the body, and leaves the man healthy and pure. Many in our age have attempted its preparation, yet no one before me has achieved it through use and experiment.

->*The Chemical Preparation of Paracelsus.*<-

<margin>Of Antimony.</margin>
Take, therefore, Antimony; choose that which is best, and reduce it into <term>alcohol</term> <note>original: *alcool*; in this period, this refers to an extremely fine, impalpable powder rather than a liquid</note>, then <term>reverberate</term> <note>original: *reuerbera*; a process of heating a substance in a furnace where the flames are reflected or "reverberated" onto the material</note> it in a closed vessel with fire from above for thirty days. Here **P. Hassard** <note>Pierre Hassard, a 16th-century physician known for translating Paracelsus's works</note> erred, who spoke of a "reverberatory vessel." Thus it is rendered volatile; and first it turns white, then yellowish, and finally it is converted into a transparent dark red color, with fineness and lightness.

Therefore, from that which has been so reverberated, extract the <term>lily</term> <note>original: *lili*; an alchemical term for the "tincture" or the most refined essence of a substance</note> by means of a spirit...

# AND OF PARACELSIAN MEDICINE

The administration of it is as follows: into a vat of fresh wine in September or October—that is, **must** <note>freshly pressed grape juice that contains the skins, seeds, and stems</note>—for every twenty **lot** <note>a historical German unit of weight, roughly equivalent to 14–17 grams; the author notes that Gerard Dorn used this measure simply</note>, half an ounce of the tincture should be added. Patients should drink this wine for three or four weeks in place of their other drinks, and not before other drinks, according to **Gerard Dorn** <note>a 16th-century Belgian philosopher and one of the most important editors and defenders of Paracelsus</note>.

<margin>*Alcohol.*</margin>
Note here that **Alcohol** is an extremely fine powder, as if passed through a very fine sieve or a hair-cloth <note>the word "alcohol" originally referred to "kohl," a fine metallic powder used as eyeliner; in this period, it meant any substance refined to its most subtle, powdered state</note>. <margin>*Alcohol.*</margin>
in the book *On Surgery*, he mentions "Alcohol of wine" <note>original: *Alcohol vini*; this refers to distilled spirit or ethanol, showing the transition of the word's meaning from powder to liquid essence</note>, with a difference in the aspiration <note>referring to the spelling or pronunciation of the "h" in Alcohol</note>.

And as for what is written here concerning a duration of 30 days, I believe it should be read as 3—that is, three, not thirty—due to a common error of scribes when writing numerical notes. For this reason, **Leon Battista Alberti** <note>a famous Italian Renaissance polymath and architect</note>, in his book *On Architecture*, ordered that numbers should be written out in full words. Thus, I find in the book *The Testament* by **Geber** <note>the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the "father of chemistry," though many Latin works attributed to him are now known as "Pseudo-Geber"</note> that the **calcinations** <note>the process of heating a substance to a high temperature to reduce it to powder</note> of metals take 30 days, which in his book *On Investigation* and in the *Sum of Perfection* he established should be completed in only three days.

Likewise, in the dialogue titled *Chrysorrhoas* <note>a work by Leo Suavius published in 1570, defending Paracelsian alchemy</note>, it is said under the persona of Paracelsus: "From this source, the friendships and hatreds of minerals with metals are discovered (which we call **sympathy** <note>original: *Sympathiam*; the hidden natural attraction or 'liking' between certain substances in nature</note> in Greek), such as those of antimony, **mercury** <note>original: *hydragyri*; literally 'water-silver'</note>, and so on." And a little later: "I confess indeed that I have discovered many things regarding the energy and efficacy of both metals and minerals with the help of physics itself." Where, under "minerals" (as noted above), he especially understands antimony, which he teaches here holds the primary place among them.

### AND OF PARACELSIAN MEDICINE

There remains only the new word **Lilig**. **Lilig** must be explained from the German book *On Surgery* by **Theophrastus** <note>Paracelsus</note>; I find it used in no other language, even though I have consulted commentaries in various tongues and men skilled in them. I suspect it was either made up by him in his usual fashion, or rather should be read as *ilech* <note>a Paracelsian term for the "first matter" of a specific mineral</note>, which he used frequently in many books regarding **Tartar** <note>original: *de Tartaro*; deposits formed in the body, which Paracelsus believed caused disease</note>, on **Degrees**, etc. This could have been derived from *hyle* <note>original: *hyle*; the Greek word for "matter," referring to the primordial substance</note>, unless we read **stibium** instead of **lilli**, as *Gerard Dorn* <note>a prominent Belgian editor and defender of Paracelsus</note> reads it. Dorn erroneously adds "saffron-colored" after "yellow" in the process of **calcination** <note>the reduction of a mineral to powder through high heat</note>. For the meaning of *Paracelsus* is clear: the **quintessence** <note>the "fifth essence" or purest medicinal core of a substance</note> of **Antimony** is to be drawn out in this way by **spirit of wine** <note>original: *spiritum vini*; high-proof alcohol or ethanol</note>; this is what *P. Haslardus* <note>Peter Haslard, an English Paracelsian physician</note> has caught the scent of. I shall finally make an end of **Stibium** <note>original: *Stibio*; the Latin name for antimony</note> when I have added some things from *Paracelsus* himself.

**Antimony** can be reduced into a kind of paste through the **water of vitriol** <note>a solution derived from sulfate minerals, often containing sulfuric acid</note>. Therefore, take **Salmiax** <note>original: *Salmiax*; Sal Ammoniac or ammonium chloride, used as a flux in alchemy</note> from it and filter it; then you will find a certain thick liquor that is very useful for **ulcers**.

**Flowers of Antimony** <note>the volatile powder produced by vaporizing and condensing antimony</note> expel the poison of **realgar** <note>an arsenic sulfide mineral, considered highly toxic</note>.
