### AND THE MEDICINE OF PARACELSUS

...two cups, a third flowing spontaneously within the bowels of the earth and already in its own form. Although Marcellus <note>Marcellus Vergilius (1464–1521), a translator of Dioscorides</note>, in his commentary on Dioscorides, adds a fourth—though I know not by what authority—extracted from fragments of marble. Regarding its qualities, I will omit the ridiculous dispute of the physicians of our time, some contending it is cold and moist, while others argue it is hot and dry. For it is certain that it possesses one set of qualities when it is in its natural state, but acquires others if altered by art, such as in its **sublimated** <note>original: *sublimatum*; a substance purified by heating it into a vapor that then solidifies</note> or **precipitated** <note>original: *præcipitatum*; a substance made to settle out of a solution</note> forms; there will be a place for more copious discussion of these later.

<margin>Santes Ardoyni, Galen.</margin>
Meanwhile, I shall state that **Santes Ardoyni** <note>An Italian physician (fl. 1420) who wrote a famous treatise on poisons</note> falsely declared it to be a poison on the authority of **Galen** <note>The most influential Greek physician of the Roman Empire (c. 129–216 AD)</note>. It is well known that Galen, in his book *On Simple Medicines*, confesses that he does not know whether it is a poison when taken internally or applied externally, and that he had not made a trial of it himself. On this subject there exists a witty epigram by **Ausonius** <note>A 4th-century Roman poet</note> concerning a jealous woman who, after giving her husband a toxin, gave him quicksilver to hasten his death, but it instead served as an antidote. But let us proceed to the three preparations of quicksilver of our **Paracelsus**.

<margin>Preparations of quicksilver.</margin>
Mercury has three bodily forms: the first is before it is "born" and is already its own; the second is when it is in the form of a liquid, or **living water**, which the **Spagyrists** <note>alchemical physicians who "separated and recombined" substances to create medicine</note> call "dry" <note>original: *ficcam* (sic), likely *siccam*; mercury was often called "the water that does not wet the hands"</note>; the third is when it is prepared by art and rendered similar to a snowy powder or the **burnt lime** <note>original: *calci*; a powder produced by intense heating</note> of metals. Thus, three remedies are drawn from it: one for ointments for the **Neapolitan disease** <note>original: *morbi Neapolitani*; a common 16th-century name for Syphilis</note>, another for washes, and the last for **fumigations** <note>the medicinal use of vapors or smoke</note>.

### Fumigation

<margin>Fumigation of quicksilver.</margin>
You should know that the power of mercury resides not in its physical body, but in its spirit, which escapes from it like heat from a furnace. Therefore, it may be prepared and administered in many ways.
Take mercury, "kill" it <note>original: *mortifica*; to change the physical state of the metal so it is no longer liquid and flowing</note> with sulfur, just as artificial **cinnabar** <note>mercury sulfide, a bright red mineral</note> is made. Then, **sublimate** <note>heat a substance until it turns to vapor and then cools back into a solid</note> it with an equal weight of **saltpeter** <note>original: *salis nitri*; potassium nitrate</note>. Place this in an instrument whose lower part—the base—is very wide, but whose upper part—the opening—is quite narrow; the vessel should be two palms high. Set it over the fire in such a way that only the lightest smoke rises, intended to be received by the **emunctories** <note>original: *emunctoria*; the organs or parts of the body that carry off waste, such as the lymph nodes or sweat glands</note>, rather than the substance of the metal itself. Now, the word **Ore** <note>original: *Ertz*</note> signifies to the Germans sometimes a metal in the fire, and sometimes a ductile and standard copper. To me, in the first preparation of mercury, it seems to signify the raw mineral earth, a word very close to the Hebrew language, in which *Eres* <note>original: *Eretz*</note> is "earth."
There now remain the mercurial essences for a singular remedy for the **venereal disease** <note>original: *venerei morbi*; a historical reference to syphilis</note>, the names of which follow:
**Vitriolized sulfur** <note>original: *Sulphur vitriolatum*</note> is sulfur made from vitriol that has been heated, in a dose similar to **black hellebore** <note>a medicinal herb often used as a powerful purgative</note>.
**Liquefied vitriol** <note>original: *Vitriolum liquefactum*</note> is vitriol extracted from copper that does not solidify. **Mercurial tallow** <note>original: *Mercurialis seua*</note> is a water made from alum in which Mercury is "born"; I read this as "of ore" as mentioned above.
**Laxa chimolea** <note>an alchemical term for a specific type of salt-based powder extracted from minerals</note> is a powder extracted from the salts of mineral brines.

### COMPENDIUM OF PHILOSOPHY

...drawn out from the metals of gold and silver.
**Precipitated mercury of metals** <note>original: *Mercurius metallorum præcipitatus*</note> is the reduction of metals into their **prime matter** <note>the fundamental, formless substance from which all things are made in alchemical theory</note>; afterwards, the metal itself is cast down and, as it were, dashed upon the ground. You should know, however, that **quicksilver** <note>original: *argentum vivum*; liquid mercury</note> in all its preparation must be refined to such an extent that it becomes, as it were, weary of life and stripped of all its corrosive sharpness. It is reduced into an oil by the spirits of **saltpeter** <note>original: *salis nitri*; potassium nitrate</note>. What is truly marvelous is that a ring made from this mercury—once it has been congealed and turned back into a metal—will heal **gout of the hand** <term>chiragra: a historical term for gout specifically affecting the wrist or hand</term> when worn on the finger. 

Just as in the book of the *Magic of Picatrix* <note>a famous 11th-century Arabic grimoire of astrological and talismanic magic</note>, a mystical censer is cast from it. The true nature of this censer is understood by few, no more than the nature of the **phoenix** (which is born from it), a unique creature according to **Baccius** <note>likely Andrea Bacci, a 16th-century Italian physician and writer</note>. This animal is prepared for six hundred years of the Arabs <note>referring to the legendary lifespan of the phoenix in Arabic or Eastern traditions</note>, and according to **Albertus** <note>likely Albertus Magnus, the medieval scholar often cited in alchemical texts</note>, it pertains to mystical theology. Through this, we may "wipe away the sweat of **Plutarch**" <note>a metaphorical expression likely meaning to clarify or resolve the difficult questions posed by the Greek philosopher Plutarch</note> and defend against the "incredulity of **Pliny**" <note>referring to Pliny the Elder, the Roman naturalist who was often skeptical of certain magical claims</note>.

# An epigram by PIERRE MOREL of
## Rouen, concerning THEOPHRASTUS PARACELSUS
## and LEO SUAVIUS. <note>Leo Suavius was the pseudonym of Jacques Gohory (1520–1576), a French scholar who translated and summarized Paracelsus’s works to make them more accessible.</note>

->J. G. P.<- <note>Likely the initials for *Iacobus Gohorius Parisiensis*—Jacques Gohory of Paris.</note>

Greece, having gazed upon the image of **Theophrastus Paracelsus**, tell me of this attendant of **Nature**; and from the ancient times, crown the initiates of **Labor** <note>original: Ἀθλώης (*Athloēs*); likely referring to the Great Work or alchemical striving</note>. You will find them all joined together in this one man.

Therefore, Greece, keep your mouth muzzled. This man, being a **Hyperborean** <note>literally "one from the far north"; here referring to Paracelsus's Germanic/Swiss origins as a source of northern wisdom</note>, shines with a radiant light for you in place of **Anacharsis** <note>a famous Scythian sage who traveled to Athens in antiquity</note>.

Through his books, you might learn to dig into the hidden depths of the earth, and to ascend the mountains of the heavenly vault. Through his books, you might learn the life-sustaining gifts of nature, so that you may be numbered among the **Long-lived** through his gift of life.

Obeying his command and wise aphorism: **"If you are able to be your own, do not be another's."** <note>original: *Alterius non sit, qui suus esse potest*; this was Paracelsus’s famous personal motto, emphasizing intellectual independence.</note>

But if you are ignorant of the windings of the **labyrinth**, then **Leo Suavius** <note>the Latinized name of Jacques Gohory</note>, acting as a **Theseus** <note>the mythical hero who navigated the Labyrinth of Crete</note>, will keep you from wandering. He has condensed long pages into a brief summary, and is powerful enough to reveal them by the oracles of **Loxias** <note>an epithet for the god Apollo, referring to his role as the god of prophecy and truth</note>.

<column-break/>

# AN EPIGRAM BY GILLIUS PINAVTIUS <note>Gilles Pinot was a 16th-century humanist scholar and poet.</note>
## FROM THE GREEK INTO LATIN
### EPIGRAM.

*Greece, gaze upon nature’s servant,*
*When you look upon the likeness of **Paracelsus**.*
*However many among the Greeks in the ancient age cultivated your **Minerva** <note>The goddess of wisdom; here representing the arts and sciences of antiquity.</note>:*
*This one German man encompasses them all.*
*A second **Anacharsis** <note>A famous Scythian sage who traveled from the "barbarian" north to Athens to seek wisdom; here, Paracelsus is seen as a northern sage returning wisdom to the world.</note> has come forth here from the*
*Hyperborean <note>A mythical land in the far north; a common Renaissance poetic term for the Germanic and Swiss regions.</note> shores:*
*Who compensates you for the wealth of the Greeks with his own genius.*
*From his writings, you are able to search the very bowels of the earth,*
*And you can climb the temples of the high Heavens.*
*And thus, you may marry heavenly gifts to this earth,*
*So that you might count out long days of life.*
*He unfolds the windings of the **Labyrinth**, like a second **Theseus** <note>The hero who navigated the Labyrinth of Crete; here, Paracelsus is the guide through the "labyrinthine" secrets of nature.</note>:*
*Sweet in his eloquence, a **Lion** in heart and spirit. <note>original: *Suauis... Leo*; a clever wordplay on the name of the editor, Leo Suavius.</note>*
*In this very matter, he has lent an ear to the saying of **Theophrastus**:*
*“**Let no man belong to another, who is able to be his own.**” <note>original: *Alterius ne sis, qui tuus esse potes*; Paracelsus’s famous motto emphasizing intellectual independence.</note>*
*Suavius has condensed his long work into a narrow space,*
*This **Lion**, powerful enough to reveal the oracles of **Phoebus** <note>Apollo, the god of medicine, light, and prophecy.</note>.*

<summary>A commendatory poem by Gilles Pinot praising Paracelsus as a "Northern Sage" surpassing the ancients, and celebrating Leo Suavius (Jacques Gohory) for condensing Paracelsus's vast writings into a more accessible form.</summary>

# VALENTINVS DE RETIIS
## ON THE WORKS OF PARACEL-
->*To the Reader.*<-

THEOPHRASTUS Paracelsus, of noble Swedish <note>original: *Suedigena*. While Paracelsus was Swiss, early biographers often confused his origins with Swabia or, as seen here, Sweden.</note> lineage, was born among the Hermits of Switzerland <note>A reference to Einsiedeln, Switzerland, which grew around a Benedictine hermitage.</note>. Called "the Great Paracelsus" by the Athenians <note>A rhetorical flourish suggesting that even the centers of classical learning would have honored him.</note>, he wrote 230 books on Philosophy, published 40 on the science of medicine, 12 on the Republic <note>statecraft or political science</note>, 7 on mathematics, and he compiled three works together into a single volume called the *Theophrastia*. Furthermore, he composed 66 books on occult and abstruse matters. The first work is called the *Archidoxes* <note>term: *Archidoxis* (The Arch-Doctrines); one of Paracelsus's most famous works concerning the preparation of chemical medicines.</note>, in which he explains the extractions and separations of virtues from the infirm <note>referring to the extraction of active medicinal "virtues" from crude or "weak" matter</note>. The second is called the *Parasarchum*, in which he treats the highest good in eternity; the third is called *Carboantes*, in which he explains transmutations in form and being. Gellius Zemeus <note>A contemporary humanist scholar.</note> wrote concerning this German philosopher Theophrastus to Passeshallus Ceveus: "There now exists among the Germans a young man to whom the world bears no equal, who has written so excellently on Philosophy, Medicine, and Mathematics, as well as on the justice of the Republic, that I believe there is either a miraculous influence in his birth, a greater grace of the Holy Spirit, or an immense presence of spirits <note>original: *dæmonum*. In this context, it could refer to "demons" or the classical Greek "daemons"—supernatural entities that provide inspiration.</note>. For it is beyond human capacity to scrutinize what he himself holds in low esteem <note>or perhaps: "it is inhuman to investigate what he has mastered."</note>; at the very least, I do not remember having read anyone more learned." Therefore, you, Reader, receive the writings of Theophrastus with a sincere mind, and do not fear to prefer these new things to the old—for they deserve it.

->*Farewell.*<-

# LEO SUAVIUS REGARDING THE CATALOGUE of Paracelsus’s works <note>Leo Suavius was the pseudonym of Jacques Gohory (1520–1576), a French physician and scholar who was instrumental in defending and organizing Paracelsus’s chaotic literary legacy for a more academic audience.</note>.

Lest it be beyond belief that so many books were written by Paracelsus, consider that most learned man, Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BCE) was an ancient Roman scholar and writer known for his staggering output across nearly every field of knowledge; very little of his work survives today.</note>—who was described by Terentianus <note>Terentianus Maurus, a Latin grammarian. The phrase "undecunque Varro" suggests Varro was a man of universal learning, complete from every side.</note> as being universal—who was called by his fellow Romans the most erudite of all citizens, beyond any risk of envy. He wrote four hundred and ninety books (according to Saint Augustine in *The City of God*), though he disregarded the refinement of his words; Cicero briefly touched upon these works in his *Academics*.

Gaius Plinius Secundus <note>Better known as Pliny the Elder (23–79 CE), the author of the famous *Natural History*.</note>, according to the testimony of his nephew Pliny <note>Pliny the Younger, whose letters provide much of what we know about his uncle’s disciplined writing habits.</note>, wrote one book on the throwing of the javelin from horseback, and two books on the life of Pomponius Secundus. He also wrote twenty books on the *Wars of Germany*, and a work titled *The Students* in three books—which were divided into six volumes because of their great size. Furthermore, he wrote eight books *On Doubtful Speech*, thirty-one books of *Histories* continuing from the end of the works of Aufidius Bassus, and thirty-seven books of *Natural History*. This last is a vast and complex work, as varied as nature itself.

->I. G. P.<- <note>These initials likely stand for *Iacobus Gohorius Parisiensis*, the Latin form of the author’s real name, Jacques Gohory of Paris.</note>
->*NATURE AS LEADER*<- <note>original: *NATVRA DVCE*</note>
->*INDUSTRY AS COMPANION*<- <note>original: *COMITE INDVSTRIA*</note>

## PARACELSUS OF HOHEN-
### heim, Doctor of both Medicine and Philosophy, on

### Chapter I.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring elaborate scrolling foliage, floral patterns, and a stylized mask or face centered at the bottom of the frame.</image-desc>
<margin>Immortal life.</margin>
<margin>Mortal life.</margin>
BEFORE I begin to philosophize regarding *Long Life* in the presence of you, my most watchful disciples, I judge it will be to your benefit if I first and thoroughly describe what life is: and especially indeed that which is **immortal** <note>Paracelsus often refers to a "sidereal" or spiritual body that exists alongside the physical one</note>, which surely many others in their writing have hitherto left entirely dismissed and untouched—I think plainly out of ignorance, or because it was not sufficiently understood by them. Hence it has happened that, until this time, they have wished to provide for the other kind alone—namely, the **mortal**—with great dispute <note>original: *magna disputatione*; Paracelsus is likely critiquing the academic physicians of his day who focused only on the physical humors</note>,

<meta>This page continues the introduction to Chapter I of Paracelsus’s "On Long Life." Having just introduced the concept of mortal and immortal lives on the previous page, he now shifts to a detailed anatomical and philosophical breakdown of the physical body and the nature of death.</meta>

# PHILIP THEOPHRASTUS PARACELSUS.

Now, however, so that both of these <note>Referring to the "mortal" and "immortal" lives mentioned on the previous page</note> may be more clearly distinguished, I believe I must certainly speak from the beginning regarding the **physical body**, the general practice <term>praxis: here referring to the practical study or medical management</term> of which body is conducted in this manner.

<margin>General practice of the physical body.</margin>
In the beginning, its parts—so many and so varied—are considered: the marrow, bones, cartilages, ligaments, nerves, flesh, and limbs; finally, whatever constitutes the principal organs—namely, the heart, liver, brain, bladder, spleen, and so on. Furthermore, one must consider whatever constitutes the external members, such as the muscles, the upper arms, and other parts of that kind which encompass the **Physical life**. But before we arrive at those matters, we shall indicate in a few words what death is, and what sickness is.

<margin>What death is.</margin>
Death is the **dissolution** <note>original: *dissolutio*; Paracelsus views death not as an end of existence, but as the "untying" or breaking apart of components that were joined at birth</note> of life, both of the mortal and also of the immortal, which the day of birth joins and couples together. For every union of mortal things—especially those that are diverse—brings dissolution along with it. Just as dissolution follows every union of natural things and of those things which are beyond nature, so too is dissolution the companion of life that has been joined. From this source and origin comes this evil: the generation of disease, which continuously...

<meta>catchword: inflicts/brings (infer-)</meta>

<summary>Paracelsus begins his anatomical survey of the physical body and defines death as the inevitable "dissolution" or separation of the mortal and immortal elements joined at birth.</summary>

DE VITA LONGA LIB. I.
<header>ON LONG LIFE, BOOK I.</header>

...death follows. From these points, it will be easy to conclude what life is—both the mortal and the immortal—and by what means each should be preserved. However, we shall explain these matters quite extensively further on, where we will treat the **Physical body**.

---

## SUMMARY of Chapter II

He suggests that physicians work in vain when they focus on medicines made from thick and dreggy substances <note>original: *crassaru & feculentarum*; Paracelsus is criticizing traditional herbal or mineral medicines that have not been "purified" through alchemical distillation</note>; rather, ethereal medicines are to be sought. The body is threefold: physical, celestial, and another added from the outside—namely, the **ferment** <term>ferment: in alchemy, a substance (like yeast in bread) that has the power to transform and "leaven" the whole body into a higher state</term>. By this, Raymund <note>original: *Raymund.*; referring to Raymond Lull, a 13th-century philosopher and alchemist highly influential in the development of "long life" theories</note> says that what has fallen away from its balanced temperament <term>temperament: the specific mixture of qualities or "humors" that maintains health</term> is first strengthened. For there is a second body, which must not be violently dissolved as the first one is. The perishable body is a created thing, but the celestial body is life.

---

### Chapter II.

In the beginning, it is necessary that we have a thorough understanding of the entire system and nature of both the **Physical body** and **Physical life**. Yet, neither the body nor the life of the body should be considered on their own in this section; for nothing can be drawn from the mortal which might produce long life. Indeed, long life exists outside the body and is preserved by the body; furthermore,

<summary>Paracelsus introduces a threefold division of the human body (physical, celestial, and external ferment) and argues that true longevity cannot be found in the mortal physical frame alone, but requires "ethereal" medicines.</summary>

<keywords>threefold body, celestial body, ferment, Raymond Lull, alchemy, ethereal medicine, temperament, physical life</keywords>

--- Page 90 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion from Chapter II, following the statement that physicians must understand the system of both the physical body and physical life. It completes the thought that neither life nor the body should be viewed in isolation, as their separation leads to death.</meta>

-> PH. THEOPHRASTUS PARACELSUS <-

...neither through the intervention of the body should the dissolution of both lives arise. For wherever immortality is not joined to mortality, there dissolution <note>original: *dissolutio*; refers to the breaking apart of the components that hold a living being together</note> cannot fully exist. On this matter, the Hippocratic Muse <note>original: *hippocratica Musa*; referring to the traditional medical teachings and inspiration of Hippocrates</note> labored greatly—namely, by what means she might preserve the body as if with a balsam <term>balsam: in Paracelsian medicine, an internal life-preserving essence that prevents decay</term>, so that it might not expose itself to the cause of death, being unmindful that in life, death does not exist. For death is nothing else but a certain dissolution; when this happens, then finally the body dies. Hippocrates directed all his findings toward this goal, deciding to take that little body into his hands—subject as it is to death—and preserve it with a mortal remedy. Yet, in that body there was never any life that flowed from the fountain of life: since the body is a created thing <term>creature: from the Latin *creatura*, meaning a physical, created object or vessel rather than the vital spirit itself</term>, but it is not life itself. 

<margin>Otherwise accepted.</margin> 

You might say that the Hippocratic Muse should not be entirely relegated to mortality. So be it; yet you will find a much easier path to health. For God granted nothing to Hippocrates beyond those things which belong to created objects. 

But let us return to our purpose. To this body, God joined something else—namely, a celestial element—which exists as the life within the body. This is the task, this is the toil <note>original: *Hoc opus hic labor est*; a famous quote from Virgil’s *Aeneid* regarding the difficulty of a great undertaking</note>, to ensure that [it does not...]

Spagyric medicine involves the alchemical process of separating a substance into its components, purifying them, and recombining them.</note>, so that he may properly learn the extraction of mysteries. ## *Chapter IX.*

### ON ULCERS.

<margin>*Mortification*</margin>
In the beginning, whatever exists in the form of discharges or humors, if it breaks out at an **emunctory** <note>original: *emunctoriū*; an organ or biological gateway, like a lymph node or pore, through which the body excretes waste</note>, it is brought under the same method of healing according to this principle: First **mortify** <note>original: *mortifica*; in this context, to neutralize or kill off the diseased or corrupt tissue</note>, then **cleanse** <note>original: *mundifica*</note>, and finally **strengthen** <note>original: *consolida*; to heal the wound and encourage the formation of new, solid flesh</note>. Regarding mortification, the matter stands thus: Take the **alkali** <note>original: *alcali*</note> that comes from **realgar** <note>original: *realgare*; a naturally occurring arsenic sulfide mineral used in alchemy and early medicine</note>; with this, mortify whatever in the body is corrupt and defective.

<margin>*Gum*</margin>
Once the area is mortified by the **Estphara** <note>a technical Paracelsian term likely related to *eschara*, a dry scab or slough produced by a burn or corrosive substance</note>, release the **gum** <note>original: *gummi*; referring to the sticky or resinous discharge from the sore</note>; once it is freed, restore it to its original health <margin>*Mumia*</margin> by means of **Mumia** <note>original: *Mumia*; in Paracelsian medicine, this refers to a vital "balsam" or life-force inherent in the body, or a medicinal preparation made from preserved remains believed to contain that force</note>. Although there are certain ulcers that do not require mortification at all, there are nevertheless others, such as **Esthiomenos** <note>original: *Estiomena*; from the Greek for "eating," referring to gangrenous or "eating" sores that spread rapidly</note>, which require mortification more urgently. Therefore, whatever their nature, they are left to the judgment of the surgeon. There are, moreover, countless other recipes of physicians; however, because they have deceived people more than once, and because those who devised such things perished by their own inventions, I do not see why you should use them. This is what I have to say regarding ulcers.

### Chapter X.

## ON WOUNDS.

<margin>A threefold method of healing wounds.</margin>
There is a threefold method for healing wounds: **Natural**, such as that of **balsam** <note>original: *balsami*; in Paracelsian thought, this often refers to an internal life-force or "mumia" that naturally heals the body</note>; **Specific**, such as that of ***brassidellia*** <note>original: *brassidellia*; a term used by Paracelsus for specific plants, likely water-pepper or persicaria, believed to have specialized healing properties</note>; and **Characteristic**, such as that of ***magoreo*** <note>original: *magoreo*; a technical Paracelsian term referring to "magnetic" or spiritual influences that affect the body's health</note>. But before we descend to those details, we will first point out things that will seem like a miracle to those who are unskilled in these matters: namely, that neither the type of wound nor its location needs to be strictly observed—a point which the ancient physicians discussed with very lengthy arguments. They debated, for instance, whether or not wounds of the brain, the intestines, or the bladder could be healed; and they did so for this reason: because we see that wounds—whether caused by a stabbing or by some other means—inflicted where life cannot reside, nevertheless result in death. Therefore, we shall say nothing at all about lethal wounds for the time being, since they manifest themselves by their own nature. Furthermore, this is the first caution: that the **surgeon** <note>original: *chirurgicus*</note> must not take a wound that is treatable and make it incurable or even fatal. This, therefore

### Chapter I.

After speaking about the particular secret remedies <note>original: *arcanis*; Paracelsus used this term to describe the hidden, potent spiritual essences within natural substances that perform the work of healing</note> which restore a body worn down by disease to its former health, we shall begin from where the previous discussion ended. Furthermore, the sum of the whole matter consists in this (since everything said in this book about the **elixir** <note>an alchemical preparation intended to prolong life or transform base metals</note> is to be applied to long life): that the whole of nature be reduced into a **spagyric** <note>the alchemical process of separating a substance into its components and recombining them in a purified form</note> mixture or balanced state, which is nothing other than the essential goodness of nature, containing nothing corruptible or harmful within it. Although this same goodness of nature is perceived in various different ways in the **tincture** <note>original: *tinctura*; a potent spiritual or medicinal extract capable of "dyeing" or transforming a body</note> according to the prescriptions of nature—such as that which exists in the **philosopher’s stone** <note>original: *lapide philosophorum*; the legendary substance supposed to grant immortality and turn lead to gold</note>; or in **Antimony** according to the "nature of the crow" <note>original: *corvi naturam*; a reference to the "black stage" or *nigredo*, the initial phase of alchemical transformation</note>; or in **sulphur** according to the effect of the moonwort plant; and so on in other things. However, in all of these, there is one and the same balanced state, which lies hidden among the metals in the form of **mercury**. (I speak of the Mercury that is present in all metals). Among gems, it is found under crystal; among stones, under the *zelotus* <note>an obscure or technical term for a specific mineral or "zealous" stone in Paracelsian mineralogy</note>; among liquids, under amber; among herbs, under valerian; among roots, under masterwort; among bitters, under **vitriol** <note>a salt of metallic acids, often iron or copper sulfate, central to alchemical experiments</note>; among flints, under Antimony. Furthermore, just as mercury is present in every single metal, so too is Antimony...

Instead, we wish them to search more diligently, so they may eventually deem these things beautiful and useful, and be bound to admit it openly.

# ON LONG LIFE, BOOK II.
## THE PREPARATION OF GOLD

...we shall make mention of it. If you understand the reason for this one, you cannot help but know the others which are separated from the body. Regarding the rest which are not separated from the body, we shall not forget them below, where the treatment of wine will be undertaken.

<margin>*Gold with its whole substance.*</margin>
The practice regarding the **elixir of gold** is as follows: dissolve pure gold <note>original: *obrizum*; ancient term for gold refined by fire</note> together with the whole substance of the gold in a corrosive agent, and let it remain there until it becomes one with the corrosive. Nor should your mind shrink from this method of treatment. For as long as gold is gold, the corrosive provides its power, and without the corrosive it is "dead"; therefore, we affirm that the quintessence of gold without the corrosive agent is useless.

<margin>*The power of the corrosive.*</margin>
Then this dissolved mixture must be removed through **putrefaction** <note>original: *putrefactionem*; in alchemy, the process of breaking down a substance through gentle heat to release its spiritual essence</note> or **incineration**, even if the corrosive clings quite tenaciously. If the power of gold is so great that it preserves the [human] body and renders it free from all illness, nor allows it to be corrupted, how much more so will it protect itself—and this without any infection. For it corrects and mends whatever is not pure.

Therefore, the corrosive used with gold should by no means be called a "corrosive," because the power of the **arcanum** <note>original: *arcani*; the "secret" or vital healing core of a substance that acts directly on the human spirit</note> overcomes every poison.

<margin>*Realgar.*</margin>
For all **Realgar** <note>original: *Realgar*; a red arsenic mineral, here used as a symbolic term for all harsh, poisonous, or corrosive substances</note> "dies" in the elixir of gold, and in the tincture... <note>The text cuts off here, continuing the word "tinctura" on the next page.</note>

<summary>Paracelsus explains the preparation of the Elixir of Gold, arguing that a corrosive agent is necessary to "activate" the gold's quintessence, as the gold's own inner power (arcanum) is strong enough to neutralize any poison.</summary>

### Chapter VI.
## ON ANTIMONY

Furthermore, there are those who were preserved for a time—and even in secret—throughout a long life; because there is no explanation for this other than what they attributed to the **Iliastes**, I believe they should be passed over in this section.

For to you, as a most learned physician, a book of medicine is rightfully offered. Indeed, when Jean Fernel <note>Jean Fernel (1497–1558) was a legendary French physician who revolutionized the study of physiology and served as the physician to King Henry II.</note>—that most learned man and your predecessor as Royal Chief Physician—was on his deathbed and was asked whom among the order of royal physicians he considered worthy of his own rank and place, he judged you the most worthy successor by his own decree, just as Socrates was judged by the oracle of Apollo. # LEO SUAVIUS (JACQUES GOHORY OF PARIS)

## TO THE READER.

Just the day before yesterday, reader, several books by Theophrastus Paracelsus were brought to me. It seemed right to list them here for you, just as I did with as many as possible in the preface to my *Compendium* <note>Gohory refers to his earlier work, "The Compendium of the Philosophy and Medicine of Paracelsus" (1567), where he attempted to organize and explain the chaotic Paracelsian corpus.</note>.

**Many treatises of the *Great Philosophy*, namely:**
*   On the True Influence of Things.
*   On the Discovery of the Arts.
*   On the Time for Labor and Rest.
*   On Both Kinds of Fortune <note>original: "De vtraq; fortuna" — referring to both good and bad luck or prosperity and adversity.</note>.
*   On Blood Beyond Death.
*   On those Affected by the Moon.
*   On the Generation of Fools.
*   On Nymphs, Pygmies, and Salamandris <term>Salamandris: elemental spirits of fire, according to Paracelsian elemental theory.</term>.
*   On Animals Born from Sodomy <note>In the context of 16th-century alchemy, this often refers to "monstrous" or unnatural births and hybrid creatures rather than strictly the moral act.</note>.
*   A Work on the Astronomy of the World.
*   On Meteorology <note>original: "De Metheoris" — this refers to "meteors" in the Aristotelian sense, covering all atmospheric phenomena including rain, wind, and lightning.</note>.
*   Four Books of the *Paramyrum* <term>Paramyrum: one of Paracelsus’s major medical works, which seeks to establish the causes of diseases beyond the traditional four humors.</term>.
*   On the Womb.
*   The *Paragranum* <term>Paragranum: literally "beyond the grain," a foundational text where Paracelsus outlines the four pillars of medicine: Philosophy, Astronomy, Alchemy, and Virtue.</term>.

**Also another volume, containing several treatises:**
*   On Physiognomy <note>The practice of assessing a person's character or personality from their outer appearance, especially the face.</note>.
*   On Turpentine.
*   On Both Types of Hellebore <note>Referring to Black and White Hellebore, powerful plants used in ancient and Renaissance medicine as purgatives.</note>.
*   On the Prolapse of the Womb.
*   On Guaiac Wood <note>original: "ligno Gaiaco" — a medicinal wood imported from the Americas, famously used at the time as a treatment for syphilis.</note>.
*   Commentaries on Several Aphorisms of Hippocrates.

### J. G. P. <note>J. G. P. stands for Jacobus Gohorius Parisiensis, the Latin name for Jacques Gohory of Paris.</note> On his own Scholia <note>original: "In sua Scholia." Scholia are explanatory comments or annotations intended to clarify a difficult text.</note>.

<margin>On the two editions of the book *On Long Life*.</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'Q' decorated with foliate scrollwork.</image-desc>
Since Adam von Bodenstein <note>Bodenstein was one of the earliest and most prolific editors of Paracelsus’s manuscripts, though he was often criticized by contemporary scholars for his editorial style.</note> adorned this little book by Theophrastus Paracelsus *On Long Life* with two prefaces, both of them extremely long, the reader will perhaps wonder why I have ordered them to be omitted in this edition, and why I have substituted this preface of ours in their place as if they were dead and gone. He attached the first to the book published in the year 1560, which was indeed "pure and simple" <note>original: "puro puto" — a Latin idiom meaning unadulterated or nothing but the thing itself.</note>, which we have already discussed in our *Compendium*. Adam (a man otherwise not unskilled in fine literature) consumed that entire preface in common debates over Aristotelian philosophy, without interjecting any explanation at all of either the meanings or the most difficult words of Paracelsus. It should be a source of shame hereafter to delay the reader from reading Theophrastus himself with such wordy nonsense; you pave no path to his concepts, you explain nothing of the obscurity, by which at last some fruit might be gathered from such great loquacity. ### ON HIS OWN SCHOLIA.

Aristotle’s matter, form, and privation <note>original: "materia, forma, priuatio" — the three principles of Aristotelian physics used to explain change in nature.</note> are not the same: it is apparent that these are not the first principles of nature, but rather the dreams of a subtle mind. For this reason, these concepts are often called into question by countless other philosophers (as is evident from Diogenes Laertius <note>A 3rd-century biographer of Greek philosophers whose work was a standard reference in the Renaissance.</note>); to say nothing of the fact that they ought to be rejected as being contrary to Christian wisdom regarding the eternity of things. 

He adds—what is also clear from the writings of our Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim, known as Paracelsus.</note>, like that axiom of principles—that the Elements are not simple bodies, but rather "matrices" <note>original: "matrices." In Paracelsian thought, a matrix is a "womb" or nurturing environment in which things are formed.</note> born from the three first principles <note>Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury—the "Tria Prima" of Paracelsian alchemy.</note>. These matters are indeed quite clear, yet they do not open any path toward uncovering the mind of Paracelsus; although (as he himself frequently warned) in understanding these things, one should not so much apply eyes to reading as hands to the actual work <note>A hallmark of the "Spagyric" or alchemical tradition: true knowledge comes through laboratory experimentation, not just theory.</note>. 

<margin>Paracelsus, in his book *On Degrees*, concerning the knowledge of the terms of the art.</margin>
He says that the knowledge of <term>spagyric</term> <note>Spagyric refers to Paracelsian alchemy, which focuses on separating and recombining the components of substances to create medicines.</note> terms must be fished out from the work itself, not from what is written. 

However, into these four books *On Long Life*, he <note>Referring to Adam von Bodenstein.</note> inserted a certain fourth book that is somewhat fraudulent, while the true and legitimate fourth book was forced into the fifth position by a kind of violence, unjustly cast out from its rightful place. 

<margin>Concerning a certain fraudulent fourth book *On Long Life*.</margin>
In the remaining books, he made almost ridiculous changes to certain words or syllables just so the work would be more marketable, making it seem to the buyer like a new and expanded edition (for the book fairs in Germany today are large and profitable). I am surprised that Adam the Physician <note>Adam von Bodenstein, a prominent but often criticized early editor of Paracelsus.</note> was not ashamed to push forward this fourth book, which is overflowing with empty trifles; it neither coheres logically with the rest of the work, nor does it reflect the subtlety of Paracelsus’s thoughts or the weight of his style. I wonder, I say, that for the sake of profit or some small glory he so favored the printer’s deception—the printer who, in the manner of peddlers selling stolen goods...

->### ON HIS OWN SCHOLIA <note>Scholia are explanatory notes or commentaries on a text.</note><-

...[the editor] twists [the meaning] into a sense other than what you, being devoid of that mind and thought, might suppose. I shall not omit what we touched upon in our *Compendium on the Accident according to Paracelsus*: <margin>The Paracelsian Accident.</margin> namely, that it is not to be understood according to the Peripatetic <note>original: "peripatetica disciplina" — referring to the school of Aristotle, which emphasized physical observation and categories.</note> school, but rather the Platonic or Academic one. In that school, every form that exists in matter seems to approach the nature of an **accident** <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that does not belong to the essence of a thing (like the color of a shirt), as opposed to its "substance."</note> rather than a true substance; and such a thing is better said to be "becoming" than "being." **Arnaldus de Villanova** <note>A famous 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note> likewise explains in his paraphrase of the *Rosary* that the **tincture** is an accident that comes to decaying matter, from which the **spagyric** <note>A term coined by Paracelsus for alchemical preparation, usually involving the separation and recombination of plant or mineral constituents.</note> form results. 

However, reader, in these mystical books, certain things can be published without penalty to provide a "scent" of the secret matter—<margin>Mysteries to be hidden.</margin> as if to be excited by friction or a certain heat—although it is a sin to openly reveal the truly secret teachings. This is why the Sphinx was once placed by the Egyptians before the doors of their temples: to remind us that mysteries must be kept hidden. This is why the Hebrews said that iron (referring to doors and locks) is a symbol of the wise, and why the Greeks imagined **Pallas** <note>Athena, the goddess of wisdom.</note> to be armed. <margin>Why Pallas is armed.</margin> **Dionysius the Areopagite** also judged that mysteries should be covered in writing but revealed by the living voice. For the same reason, the commentators of the Chaldean **Zoroaster**, like the man himself, speak in riddles. <margin>Plato.</margin> The truly divine **Plato** wrote to **Dion** about the supreme substances under the cover of a riddle. Thus **Pythagoras**, when dying, entrusted only a few writings to his daughter **Dama**. Likewise, those among the more recent philosophers who scented this hidden wisdom—**Al-Kindi** the Arab, the Englishman **Roger Bacon**, and **William of Paris**—wrote only for the "sons of doctrine" <note>A traditional term for initiated students of alchemy and hermetic philosophy.</note>. <margin>Al-Kindi, Roger Bacon, William of Paris.</margin> But many, in the manner of **Hercules**, as **Plutarch** says, burst into sa—

You hope that by this you might falsely write upon his remains—or rather, “you think,” as you meant to say. Tell me, I pray, Weyer: with what face do you accuse that Trithemius, whom your own host and teacher praises so greatly that he seeks the entire reputation of his own work from that man’s judgment and testimony?

<margin>Cornelius Agrippa’s testimony concerning Trithemius</margin>

The old saying can be aptly used here: *The disciple is not above the master.* Hear how much Agrippa values Trithemius; in his preface he says: “I confess, I began to write these books as a very young man, yet with the hope of eventually publishing them more corrected and expanded; and for that reason I first offered them to be corrected by Johannes Trithemius, a man most industrious in hidden matters <note>original: "arcanarum rerum," referring to the study of secrets or occult sciences</note>.” He says the same in his dedicatory epistle: “Never into this...”

### IN HIS COMMENTARIES.

I have dared thus far to descend into the arena of restoring Magic, but after the conversation we shared regarding these matters, your excellent skill and learning, and your ardent exhortation, added boldness and spirit to me. I now submit these books <note>Agrippa is referring to his *Three Books of Occult Philosophy*, the foundational text of Western esotericism</note> to your examination—you who possess the fullest expertise in these things—to be corrected, appraised, and judged. Thus, if anything has been written in them by me which could tend toward an insult to nature, an offense to the heavenly beings <note>original: "coelitum," referring to the angels or the divine host</note>, or an injury to religion, you may condemn the error. But if the scandals of impiety are cleared and purged, you may defend the tradition of truth. And thus you might wish to deal with these books of ours and with magic itself, so that nothing that could be beneficial be hidden, nor anything approved that could do nothing but harm. By this means, at last, these books, approved by your examination, might be worthy to go forth into the public one day under happy auspices, and not fear to undergo the judgment of posterity. Farewell, and be indulgent toward these bold undertakings.

I have transcribed these things at greater length, reader, so that you might hear Agrippa’s judgment of Trithemius, and so that the name of "magic"—which will soon be used by our Paracelsus and is still harsh to our ears—might be softened for you by the usage of others. Regarding this, we shall also hear Marsilio Ficino <note>A celebrated priest and philosopher of the Italian Renaissance who sought to reconcile Neoplatonic magic with Christianity</note> in his own place. But so that we may pierce that Bovillus <note>Charles de Bovelles, who had accused Trithemius of sorcery</note> as if with final weapons, receive Trithemius’s response to Agrippa, which silently grazes him while offering advice.

<margin>Trithemius’s advice to Agrippa regarding the caution of secrets.</margin>

### ON CHAPTER II.

<margin>
*Privation.*
*Qualities: the two keys.*
</margin>
Here he treats of the two bodies, which we briefly touched upon in the *Compendium* as existing in a single man. Regarding these, how beautifully Adam von Bodenstein <note>Adam von Bodenstein (1528–1577) was a Swiss physician and one of the most important early editors and promoters of Paracelsus’s works</note> speaks at the end of his second preface to the *Five Books on Long Life*. "Farewell," he says, "with your two bodies and one spirit." You see here that the physical body is also called "mortal," and another "immortal" or "celestial" body is joined to it. The union of these brings life, and their dissolution brings death. Moreover, dissolution cannot occur without a preceding union, just as they say that "privation presupposes habit" <note>A principle in Scholastic logic meaning you cannot be "deprived" of something (like sight) unless you are the kind of being that normally possesses it (the "habit" or state of being)</note>. But regarding the earlier discussion about the principles of things in our preface, remember that for Aristotle, "privation" is only an intellectual principle—a way of thinking about change—not a physical reality. This is similar to the qualities of the elements: Paracelsus established only two in his book *On Degrees*, namely the hot and the moist; the remaining two, the cold and the dry, are considered to be a state of "privation" rather than real, active qualities. However, a distinction that is not sufficiently clear regarding both bodies produces some obscurity in this chapter.

### SCHOLIA.

For the body indeed dies—that is to say, the mortal, physical, or perishable body. Yet this body is to be preserved through the intervention of that other body, namely the celestial one <margin>With which.</margin> <note>original: "quo." The author clarifies that "with which" (quo) should be read instead of "which" (quod) to show the celestial body is the means of preservation</note>, which God joined to it. Through the intervention of this celestial body from the outside, the physical body grows strong; from it comes the **renewal** <margin>Renewal.</margin> <note>original: "instauratio." Gohory notes that "restauratio" (restoration) is a "barbarous" or linguistically improper term compared to the more classical "instauratio"</note> of the other body. This physical body is like wood, and the celestial body is like fire.

In this matter, he [Paracelsus] believes that Hippocrates erred, along with the rest of the medical sect, because they labored over mortal remedies to preserve this physical body. From these, they wrongly sought remedies for a long life—such as from <term>balsam</term> <note>original: "balsamo." In Paracelsian medicine, the "internal balsam" is a vital preservative fluid within the body; Gohory warns not to confuse the physical plant resin with this spiritual principle</note>—namely from physical creatures or bodies in which the fountain of life does not reside. Instead, it resides in that celestial body which lies beneath, in which a long life flourishes. 

Paracelsus himself said in Book 4, Chapter 1, that the theoretical reasoning for a long life is treated in this first book, just as the practice of a healthy and sound life is treated in Books 2 and 3 (specifically, the part of medicine concerned with curing diseases). However, he claims that Hippocrates neither touched upon nor fully understood the true **preservative** art. Therefore, his [Paracelsus’s] primary aim is to discuss a long life that goes beyond nature, and to teach here those things which have been untouched and ignored by ancient physicians until now. For this reason, he gave the title "On Long Life" to the entire work, even if he discusses a healthy life only in passing <note>original: "per transfennam." A Latin idiom meaning "through a lattice-window," signifying a brief or indirect glance at a subject</note>. 

Here he uses the term **little body** <note>original: "corpusculum"</note> out of contempt for the mortal and perishable body. As for the "celestial" body, consider whether you might more readily accept the description from **Plato** regarding the **spirit**, which he established as the medium between the mortal body and the immortal soul...

# LEO SUAVIUS

<margin>On the metallic spirit</margin> [a link] of both is necessary, being of a certain middle nature, about which the poet Augurellus <note>Giovanni Aurelio Augurello (1441–1524) was an Italian humanist and poet famous for his alchemical poem "Chrysopoeia."</note> skillfully writes:

> Between these two a healing spirit comes, which you would call neither 
> body nor soul, but that which, always participating in both, 
> brings these two extremes back into one.

<margin>Marsilio Ficino.</margin> Regarding this (and you should refer these things to minerals along with him), Marsilio Ficino <note>The famous Florentine philosopher (1433–1499) who revived Neoplatonism and wrote extensively on the "spirit of the world" (*spiritus mundi*) as a bridge between soul and matter.</note> writes: "There is also a spirit in metals and stones, but it lies hidden, oppressed by the heavy mass of matter; if this spirit is rightly separated and preserved in secret as a <term>seminal virtue</term> <note>The inherent power within a substance to generate its own kind, similar to a seed.</note>, and if it is then applied to matter of its own kind, it will be able to generate its like: <margin>Elixir.</margin> which the Arabs call the **Elixir**." To this I shall add a <margin>Zoroaster.</margin> mystery from the 17th aphorism of Zoroaster <note>Renaissance scholars often cited the "Chaldean Oracles" or other mystical texts attributed to the ancient Persian sage Zoroaster.</note>: that through the triple garment of linen, cloth, and skins, a triple domicile or dwelling-place of the soul is understood—the celestial, the spiritual, and the earthly. However, such parabolic interpretations should not be despised by those who perhaps do not understand them at first glance. In the summary of the *Heptaplus* <note>Pico’s 1489 work "Heptaplus" is a mystical seven-fold interpretation of the Book of Genesis.</note> by Pico [della Mirandola], the author draws an argument from St. Paul: *He who eats should not despise him who does not eat, and he who does not eat should not judge him who eats.* <note>A reference to Romans 14:3, used here to suggest tolerance between those who understand deep mysteries and those who do not.</note> It is better to bathe these mystical things in words than to submerge them entirely. But if the earlier philosophers have harvested the greater crops, they have left for me, as a poor man, the <term>gleanings</term> <note>original: "spicilegium." A common scholarly metaphor for gathering the small bits of information left behind by great predecessors.</note>.

### COMMENTARIES

...while the deficiency of the body. This restoration must occur repeatedly because of the decay that happens daily. **Restoration** is the recovery of what has been lost in the perishable body, specifically from another body—namely, the celestial one. This pertains to the practice of conservation. The common crowd of physicians has wrongly tried to apply the well-known <margin>Balsam.</margin> balsam—whether the Judean, natural, or artificial variety—manufactured by some without knowledge. We have written much regarding these in our compendium. The nature of such a balsam only prevents corruption by filling a vacuum; it does not supply the true material of restoration. Therefore, another balsam must be sought from the <margin>Spagyric Balsam.</margin> **Spagyrics** <note>Spagyric medicine is a branch of alchemy that involves the "separation" and "recombination" of natural elements to create more potent, purified remedies.</note> for legitimate conservation. 

The other practice belongs to the common physician: namely, the curing of diseases (which are manifold), so that he may remove the corruption that has come upon it, and fortify (or "mummify") the body affected by disease. I read <margin>otherwise "they may fortify."</margin> this from the fabricated word **mumia** <note>original: "mumia." In Paracelsian medicine, *mumia* refers to the inherent vital force or "balsam" of the living body, though it was often confused with the medicinal use of ground Egyptian mummies.</note> (concerning which, see Book 2). Indeed, the preservative part fortifies against corruption so that it does not occur, while these specific remedies remove and drive it away. Their use relates to a short life, just as the Spagyric balsam relates to a long life. Regarding these specific remedies, there is an abundance in all the books of the physicians. 

Long life consists in the **spirit of life**. For the body committed to the care of the physician is mortal, not a celestial body. (I read this not as "insofar as" and "death," but like **Leonine** <note>Referring to "Leonine leprosy," a form of the disease that causes the skin of the face to thicken and wrinkle, resembling a lion's head.</note>—not a lioness—that is, a man polluted by this species of leprosy, just as **tympanites** <note>A condition where the abdomen is stretched tight with gas, sounding like a drum (tympanum) when tapped.</note> is mentioned shortly after, etc.) 

I will speak in passing about <margin>On Ophthalmia.</margin> **ophthalmia** <note>A general term for severe inflammation of the eye.</note>. Since there are various species of it, it does not seem to be correctly distinguished by our colleagues, who describe the "nail" <note>original: "unguem," referring to a pterygium, a fleshy growth on the eye that can look like a fingernail.</note>...

...life is to be preserved in its own way: namely, the essence by those things which are beyond nature, and the nature by natural things. There are two parts to this composite being: specifically, man through seed and God. Adam received a "long life" <note>original: "vitam longam." In Paracelsian terms, this refers to a vital, semi-immortal balsam that sustains the body beyond its natural limits.</note> from that which is beyond nature, not from creation—that is, from the human generation that proceeds from seed. To this pertains the knowledge of predestination. 

An example of the distinction between the long (or celestial) life and the physical (or natural) life appears in one who sleeps: in such a person, only the life of nature—or the vegetative life <note>The basic biological functions shared with plants, such as growth and digestion.</note>—is active; the other life, namely the animal life <note>The "anima" or soul-life responsible for movement, sensation, and consciousness.</note>, is lulled to sleep and, as if dead, does not perform its duties. The same is true for one whose throat has just been cut with a blade <note>original: "ferro," literally "iron." This is a common philosophical example of the moment where the body's physical mechanisms fail but the vital essence has not yet fully departed.</note>. He concluded that through this "long life" or animal virtue, man is restored—which in Christian language I understand as "to be resurrected"—although some philosophers, such as **Anaxagoras** <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher who proposed that "mind" (Nous) was the initiating force of the cosmos.</note>, reached this level of knowledge. <margin>*Anaxagoras on the resurrection.*</margin> For **Paracelsus** <note>The controversial Swiss physician and alchemist (1493–1541) whom this text critiques and explains.</note> delights in the novelty of his words, which can cast darkness upon the reader. 

<margin>*The logic of the microcosm.*</margin> This noble human composite, therefore, is truly called a **microcosm** <note>The "little world"; the ancient idea that the human body contains all the elements and structures of the entire universe.</note>. Because the discussion here concerns a dual life, it does not fully embrace the mind and reason, which constitute the third and principal part of man—although wisdom lies hidden alongside life beneath the supernatural seed. Since there are three worlds—the intellectual, the celestial, and the elemental—the angelic intellect is situated in man’s brain as if in a citadel; in the heart is the source of celestial heat; and in the genital organs are generation and corruption. Thus, according to the same Anaxagoras, the three worlds are one: because what is in one...

<margin>Dionysius the Areopagite.</margin>
...is in another, but in a different form. Thus, according to **Dionysius the Areopagite** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius (c. 5th–6th century), a Christian philosopher who blended Neoplatonism with theology.</note>, a superior power possesses those things which belong to an inferior power in an excellent and eminent manner <note>original: "excellenter & eminenter." This is a philosophical principle suggesting that a higher level of reality contains all the virtues of the lower level, but in a more perfect form.</note>.

<margin>The mystical structure of the tabernacle.</margin>
The structure of the Tabernacle of Solomon’s Temple encompasses these three worlds with the greatest mystery: the open part, being as it were **sublunary** <note>The realm "below the moon," which in ancient cosmology was the Earthly sphere of change and decay.</note>, is common to both men and beasts; the **Holy Place**, shining with gold and seven lampstands, represents the seven planets of the heavens; and in the **Holy of Holies**, the winged Cherubim represented the Angelic world. Certain thinkers have wished to adapt these mysteries even to the terrestrial and mineral work <note>That is, the "Great Work" of alchemy.</note>: specifically, the first and lower part to raw materials; the second to the elements or waters <note>original: "lymphis," literally "clear waters," often used in alchemy to refer to purified liquids or spirits.</note>; and the third to the **Fifth Essence** <note>original: "V. essentiæ." The Quintessence, the purest and most potent substance that transcends the four physical elements.</note>, following the order of the principles of **Ramon Llull** <note>A 13th-century Majorcan polymath and mystic whose works were foundational to later Western alchemy and logic.</note>.

<margin>Sacred things are not to be profaned.</margin>

> *But those who have prophesied the arrival of the divine offspring*
> *To human shores—that incomprehensible and unspeakable gift—*
> *Did not think these matters to be small. That prophetic mouth,*
> *Sounding forth such great mysteries...*
> *Yet we have dared these things, persuaded by none of our own, etc.*

Finally, I shall conclude: this **celestial body** is correctly said by **Paracelsus** to be joined by God, along with its life, to the physical body. Hence **Plotinus** <note>The founder of Neoplatonism (c. 204–270 AD), who taught that the soul originates from a divine "One."</note> judged that every soul is from a divine principle. The use of the name "body" for this celestial matter is quite far from common doctrine—unless you understand "spirit" in the sense of **Plato** as something sensible, consisting of a subtle elementary composition, just as **Apuleius** <note>A Roman philosopher (c. 124–170 AD) who wrote on the nature of "daemons" as intermediate beings with bodies of air.</note> established that the bodies of daemons were aerial.

### SCHOLIA <note>Scholia are explanatory notes or commentaries on a primary text—in this case, the works of Paracelsus.</note> ON CHAPTER V.

<margin>Twofold seed: natural and supernatural.</margin>
This fifth chapter concerns the twofold **seed**, natural and supernatural. No one doubts that the natural seed is **hereditary** <note>original: "hæreditariũ." In early modern medicine, this refers to traits passed down through the physical "humors" or "balsam" of the parents.</note>, but it is a marvel that even in that body which is beyond nature, there is a certain hereditary seed. And if two people of the same **complexion** <term>complexion: In Galenic and Paracelsian medicine, this refers to the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) that determines a person’s temperament and health.</term>, that is a man and a woman, are joined: nevertheless, the supernatural seed is by no means truly joined (lest you ever read otherwise).

<margin>Twofold marriage: divine and human.</margin>
Therefore, marriage is twofold: one human, the other divine; that is, what man has joined or what God has joined. For this reason, there is an old and well-worn proverb in common speech, that **true marriages are made in heaven before they are made on earth.** <note>original: "vera connubia in cœlo priusquàm in terra fieri."</note>

Lest anyone easily recoil from this **paradox** <note>A statement that seems contradictory but may be true; here referring to the idea of a "supernatural" heredity.</note>, let him consider within himself that God found **David** to be a servant **after his own heart** <note>original: "secundum cor suum"; a reference to 1 Samuel 13:14.</note>, and from **St. Paul**, that the **judgments of God are an abyss, incomprehensible** <note>original: "abissum esse, incomprehensibilia iudicia Dei"; referencing Romans 11:33.</note>, which it is not permitted for man to call into dispute. I truly testify here and everywhere that I have no intention to affirm anything which, in the judgment of learned and pious men, will seem contrary to our sacred religion, and I freely submit all things to their censure.

But to return to the matter: although **Paracelsus** treats primarily of those things which are always beyond nature—as he does here concerning divine marriage—yet he treats in passing even of natural things. This is because (according to **Aristotle**) the **science of opposites is the same** <note>original: "disciplina est contrariorum." This Aristotelian principle suggests that to understand one thing, one must also understand its opposite.</note>, and indeed they shine more clearly when compared to one another. Wherefore, concerning human seed, he holds these views: that there is absolutely no pure complexion in man...

<margin>Concerning corrupted human seed according to Roger Bacon. Concerning the name Tetragrammaton.</margin>
...[the theory of complexions] passed down by physicians, such as the melancholic, the choleric, etc. Instead, he suggests that today there are various constitutions of the physical body mixed among themselves, arising from a contrary seed that was once confused. Read, therefore, that in the beginning, no one was purely "sanguine" nor "choleric." Regarding this human seed, which has been corrupted <note>original: "adulterato." There remains here a brief explanation of the name of God, the **Tetragrammaton** <term>Tetragrammaton: From the Greek for "four letters," referring to the sacred four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH.</term>: a name with which today’s dull and foolish magic is bloated. For everyone initiated in the basics of the Greek language realizes that the name consists of four letters, which is hinted at but not expressed: just as the Hebrews similarly used the name **Adonai** <note>original: "adonay." To avoid pronouncing the sacred four-letter name, Jewish tradition substitutes it with "Adonai," meaning "Lord."</note> to refer to it. But those "fine" summoners—a filthy herd—write that name in their magic circles as if it were some divine power. Many, led by a veneration of this name, have investigated it in the **Sibyls** <note>Ancient prophetesses whose oracles were often interpreted by Christians as foretelling the coming of Christ.</note> and other ancient monuments (which we touched upon long ago in a little book on mysteries), and now we shall briefly address it due to the varied and spotted treatment by **Cardano** <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), a famous Italian polymath and physician known for his works on medicine and the occult.</note>. Giovanni Pantheo of Venice, in his enigmatic book *Voarchadumia*, interprets it as **Jehovah**, which **Giovanni Pico** <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a Renaissance philosopher who integrated Kabbalah into Christian thought.</note> considers to be the name of the future Messiah:

<margin>Yod He Vav He.</margin>
Pantheo twists this toward his **Alchemy** <note>original: "Chymiam." At this time, alchemy and chemistry were treated as the same discipline.</note>; whether he does it violence or not, I leave to the judgment of the wise. For there are four letters: a word used in the divine books which signifies **Him who is**, or who exists, whereas other things are not truly in existence, being in perpetual motion and flux, tending continuously from their very birth toward their end.

<header>NOTES.</header>

Thus we, as a youthful pastime, applied the Greek word *arsenikon* <note>original: "ἀρσενικὸν." In Greek, this word means "masculine" or "potent," but it is also the root for the mineral "arsenic," which held great importance in alchemy.</note> to the Greek Sibylline verses <note>The Sibylline Oracles are a collection of Greek oracular utterances. One famous riddle in Book 1 describes a divine name through its letter counts and numerical values.</note> concerning the divine name: in
<margin>Arsenikon.</margin> which all things seemed to fit beautifully; namely, it has nine letters and four syllables; the first three syllables consist of two letters each, and the remaining syllable consists of the rest—that is, three letters. > Indeed, whatever exists beyond nature is like a treasure of nature committed to God: a fact which is obvious among those skilled in the **Spagyric art** <note>term: "Spagyric," a word coined by Paracelsus, referring to the alchemical process of separating and then recombining the components of a substance to purify it</note>.

> **Chemistry** <note>original: "Chymia"</note> is loved by many and is chaste: she has many familiar handmaidens who guard their mistress with perpetual vigilance, and place themselves in her stead, so that she may be kept forever untouched by the commerce of so many troublesome lovers. Vanity, fraud, deceit, sophistication, greed, falsehood, lying confidence, folly, poverty, despair, flight, proscription, and beggary are the attendants of Chemistry. While they pretend to be the beloved mistress, they keep her unviolated, and they willingly prostitute themselves to her wealthy, avaricious, greedy, and foolish suitors. Thus says Trithemius.

> Now I shall finish, once I have given warning about the **Treasure of Life** which he said was committed to God: many will treat these words in a chemical sense, guessing...

# A COMPARISON OF MARSILIO
## Ficino’s *On Long Life*, with Paracelsus.

<margin>Twofold Magic.</margin>
First, I establish that in order to explain the Magic and Kabbalah <note>A Jewish mystical tradition that Renaissance scholars like Ficino and Paracelsus adapted into Christian philosophy.</note> of Paracelsus, we must recognize that the ignorance of our century stems from a disbelief in the greatest things—specifically those which depend upon magic. For magic is twofold: the first is vain and superstitious, rooted in the worship of evil demons <note>original: "cacodæmonum"</note> and the fabrication of monstrous portents; the second is true and salvific, marrying heaven to earth and reconciling the favor of the higher realms to the lowest materials. Many are alienated from faith in this true magic because they are ignorant of the universal golden chain of the world described by Homer <note>original: "cathenam orbis vniuersi auream ab Homero descriptã"; the *Catena Aurea* or "Golden Chain of Being" connecting all levels of existence.</note>.
<margin>Homer’s Golden Chain. Platonic Rings.</margin>
Recognize here the symbol of metallic matter, and the Platonic rings <note>In Plato’s *Ion*, Socrates uses the image of magnetized iron rings to explain divine inspiration.</note> hanging from the living power of the Craftsman like iron rings hanging from a Herculean stone <note>original: "lapide Herculeo"; the lodestone or magnet.</note>. Those who deny this take away the life and soul of the world, the heavens, and the stars, through which celestial influences are poured into these lower things.

<margin>Ficino’s Apology regarding Magic.</margin>
Ficino writes skillfully of these matters in his *Apology*: yet, unless the priest himself <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) was an ordained priest, and his writings on magic often required careful navigation of Church doctrine.</note> had wrongly twisted the sacred words of the Gospel to support this opinion, he would not have pretended to merely narrate—rather than approve—the magic he now teaches and confirms. For lest he should seem to slide into superstition, he falls into a manifest error when he prefers the concoctions of medicines over the carvings of stones and metals. 
<margin>On the carvings of stones. Constellated medicines.</margin>
He claims the latter are carved in a mere moment, yet they require time for melting, time for shaping under the hammer, and a long time for the actual engraving. But he rightly places beyond any doubt those ointments and medicines <note>original: "pharmaca"</note> breathed upon by the favor of the stars, with their powers...

<margin>The coals of heaven: Mars and Jupiter.</margin>
...is clearly established in the sacred exorcisms of spirits. The "astronomasters" <note>A derogatory term for pseudo-astronomers or those who practice astrology poorly.</note> used to seek help from the "coals of heaven" of Mars or Jupiter—that is, from the stars themselves, which they call celestial bodies and which are natural in essence. (Indeed, the comparison to a glowing coal fits Mars wonderfully due to the star's reddish brilliance.) Yet, those physical bodies have power only over mortal things; as every theological academy confirms in the debate over predestination, they cannot influence the human celestial body, which is invisible, whereas the stars themselves are visible.

Therefore, we must conclude that the subject of miraculous works is our **supernatural body**, and the effective force or power behind them is **supernatural influence**. Johannes Pico della Mirandola <note>A famous Italian Renaissance philosopher known for his "Oration on the Dignity of Man."</note> interprets this—as does Trithemius <note>A German abbot and polymath known for his work on cryptography and magic.</note>—as the "moving intelligence" of the celestial spheres, which the author here also calls the "second influence."

<margin>Johannes Reuchlin.</margin>
However, he seems to accuse Pico of ignorance, or perhaps Johannes Reuchlin in his books *On the Kabbalah* and *On the Miraculous Word*, despite the fact that they drew many of these ideas from Hebrew sources.

<margin>On Images.</margin>
<margin>Marsilio Ficino.</margin>
Furthermore, he paves the way for achieving a long life by means of **images** and **Gamaheas** <note>Talismanic stones or natural minerals believed to contain celestial signatures or "images" created by the stars.</note>. Marsilio Ficino <note>The influential head of the Platonic Academy in Florence.</note> wrote eloquently and extensively on these, drawing from Platonic teaching in his book *On Obtaining Life from the Heavens* <note>original: "De vita coelitus haurienda"</note>. This is the third book in his series, following the first, *On a Healthy Life*, and the second, *On a Long Life*. It appears that Ficino treated the very same subject matter as Paracelsus. Therefore, for the sake of explanation and confirmation, let us briefly compare a few of Ficino's principles with these **Paracelsian** <note>original: "Theophrasticis," referring to Theophrastus von Hohenheim, known as Paracelsus.</note> ones.

# A COMPARISON OF MARSILIO
## Ficino’s *On Long Life*, compared with Paracelsus.

<margin>Twofold Magic.</margin>
I first establish that, in order for us to explain the Magic and Kabbalah of Paracelsus, we must realize the ignorance of our current age stems from a disbelief in the greatest of things—specifically those that depend upon magic. Since magic is twofold—namely, a vain and superstitious kind rooted in the worship of <term>cacodemons<note>From the Greek "kakodaimon," meaning an evil spirit or demon.</note></term>, which produces monstrous things, and a true and healthful kind which marries heaven to earth and wins the favor of the higher powers for the lowest materials—many people remain estranged from belief in it. This is because they are ignorant of the <margin>Homer’s Golden Chain</margin> **golden chain** of the entire universe described by Homer <note>A famous Neoplatonic metaphor based on the *Iliad*, representing the interconnected hierarchy of being that links God to the physical world.</note>. Recognize, meanwhile, the symbol of metallic matter, and the <margin>Platonic Rings.</margin> **Platonic rings** <note>A reference to Plato’s *Ion*, where he compares divine inspiration to a magnet—the "Herculean stone"—which transmits its power through a series of iron rings.</note> hanging from the living power of the Creator just like iron rings hang from a **Herculean stone** <note>An ancient term for a magnet or lodestone.</note>. Such ignorant people strip the life and soul away from the world, the heavens, and the stars, through which celestial influences are poured into these lower realms.

<margin>Ficino’s Apology for Magic.</margin>
Regarding these matters, Ficino writes skillfully in his *Apology*: "unless the priest himself were to wrongly distort the sacred words of the Gospel toward this opinion, and unless he were to pretend he was merely recounting, not approving, the magic he now teaches and confirms." For lest he should seem to fall into superstition, he falls into a manifest error <margin>On the carvings of stones.</margin> while he prefers the concoctions of medicines over the engravings of stones and metals, because (as he says) the latter are engraved in a single moment—yet these actually require a time for melting, a time for malleability under the hammer, and then a long time for the engraving itself. <margin>Constellated medicines.</margin> However, he rightly and beyond doubt values ointments and <term>constellated medicines<note>original: "pharmaca constellata," medicines prepared or gathered when specific stars or planets are in a favorable alignment.</note></term> inspired by celestial favor, through the powers...

As for Marsilio Ficino’s hesitation and doubt regarding the importance of engraving <note>This refers to the practice of carving specific symbols or "sigils" into stones or metals at astrologically significant times.</note>, it is easily refuted by the action of stellar rays and the sudden penetration of light. Say this, then: Marsilio placed faith in images and Sigils, but—as is very easy to gather from his various writings—he hid it out of fear of religion <note>Ficino was a priest and often had to defend his interest in "natural magic" against accusations of heresy or demon-worship from the Church.</note>, while meanwhile he wrongly restrained or held in suspense the faith of many others in these most difficult matters.

However, their writings show that they only tasted the surface of such great wisdom; no miraculous works or deeds of theirs testify that they penetrated to their innermost mind <note>Suavius is critiquing the famous Renaissance Humanists for being merely "bookish" scholars of magic rather than practical wonder-workers like Paracelsus.</note>. Nevertheless, they left behind a great admiration of themselves in others who have not tasted those ancient monuments.
