### ON THE CABALA. <note>The author uses "Cabala" to refer to the Jewish mystical tradition, which during the Renaissance was heavily adapted by Christian scholars like Pico della Mirandola to explore "divine science."</note>

<margin>Cabala.</margin>
To me, one form of the Cabala is universal, encompassing the works of the entire universe; the other is particular, which aims at the principles of the individual. <note>original: "indiuidui rationes collimat."</note> Properly speaking, the Cabala is to the Hebrews a successive tradition of mysteries passed down from Moses (who received them from God) to others.
<margin>The art of combination. The revolution of the alphabet.</margin>
Nevertheless, the "art of combination," or the "revolution of the alphabet," or a method of proceeding in the sciences—likewise that part of magic dealing with the virtues of the higher powers above the moon—is also called "Cabala" by the Hebrews by a general name. <note>The "art of combination" refers to *Gematria* or *Temurah*, where the letters of the Hebrew alphabet are rearranged or assigned numerical values to find hidden meanings.</note>
<margin>The twofold Talmud.</margin>
Furthermore, the Cabalistic books are the Jerusalem Talmud and the Babylonian Talmud. <note>The author here conflates the Talmud (legal and narrative tradition) with the Cabala (mystical tradition), a common blurring of lines in Renaissance Christian Hermeticism.</note> Those things which proceed from these Cabalistic books are called oracles, as seen in the writings of Elias the Hebrew. <note>Likely referring to Elia Levita (1469–1549), a Hebrew teacher to Christian humanists who wrote on the Hebrew language and tradition.</note> According to the Chaldeans, the duration of the world will be as many thousands of years as there were days in the creation of the world, namely:

->Two thousand of nature<-
->Two thousand of law<-
->Two thousand of grace,<-
<note>This refers to the "House of Elias" prophecy found in the Talmud, which divides the 6,000-year lifespan of the world into three eras: the Era of Chaos (Nature), the Era of Torah (Law), and the Era of the Messiah (Grace).</note>

<margin>Ezra. Against Pico. The art of memory.</margin>
Regarding which Giovanni Pico <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a seminal figure of the Italian Renaissance who integrated Kabbalah into his *900 Theses*.</note> says: "If there is any human conjecture concerning the final times, we can understand through the most secret way of the Cabala that the consummation of the age will occur 514 years and 25 days from now." <note>Pico's calculation, based on his reading of mystical texts in the late 15th century, pointed toward the year 2000 as a significant eschatological date.</note> Some, however, say in passing against Pico: Since the prophet Ezra <note>Ezra the Scribe; according to the apocryphal book 2 Esdras, he was inspired to rewrite the scriptures after the originals were destroyed during the Babylonian Captivity.</note> restored the books of Moses—which had been burned by the Chaldeans (who were also called Babylonians)—using his memory as an archetype, how shall we suppose that the individual letters and syllables remained the same and in the same order as a foundation for the Cabala...

...[quater]nary projection from the <term>Spagyric</term> <note>From the Greek words meaning "to separate" and "to combine"; a term coined by Paracelsus for alchemical medicine.</note> axiom. With these things agree what the same Trithemius wrote concerning the <term>quaternary</term> <note>The number four.</note>, though they may seem to disagree. Pythagoras of Samos warned his disciples not to forget the quaternary, in which the first perfection of counting is contained. For we count thus: 1, 2, 3, 4: stay your mind, for you have 10. <note>The Pythagorean "Tetractys": 1+2+3+4 = 10.</note> For the <term>denary</term> <note>The number ten.</note> is the head of perfection. What is 11, but the denary and unity? What is 20? Twice ten. What is 30? Thrice ten. What is 40? You have four times ten, and you have by no means departed from the quaternary. And what is 100, if not ten times ten? Profound mysteries lie hidden in these things, manifest to few. Out of love for brevity, we pass over many in silence who, helping nature through art, applied wisdom to secrets; and what seemed impossible to many ignorant people, they brought forth into easy use through sagacious study. A cultivated mind is capable of great things, and he who clings to God becomes higher than the world in understanding.

<margin>Paracelsus on Kabbalistic magic.</margin>
There remains in this sixth chapter of Paracelsus: "The whole of <term>Kabbalistic magic</term> <note>Renaissance scholars used the term "Cabalistica" to refer to a blend of Jewish mysticism and Hermetic magic used to understand the hidden structures of the universe.</note> includes this within itself: to make manifest that the body which is according to nature is sustained and administered (by that, I add) which exists beyond nature and is implanted in us like an image; so that it may render diverse and far-distant senses—for instance, the Eastern and Western—equal, and make unknown thoughts known even when one is absent."

<margin>Trithemius on the mysteries of Steganography.</margin>
He adds that these things are deservedly difficult to know, which were openly handed down by <term>Trithemius</term> <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a Benedictine abbot and polymath who taught Paracelsus.</note>, the teacher of our Theophrastus <note>Paracelsus’s real name was Theophrastus von Hohenheim.</note>, in his books on <term>Steganography</term> <note>A work ostensibly about secret writing (cryptography) that many believed contained a system of spirit or angel magic.</note>; of which he himself says: *the kernel lies hidden beneath the bark.* <note>original: "latet sub corticè nuclei." This means the true meaning is hidden under the literal surface of the text.</note>

Our *Steganography* <note>Trithemius’s famous work on "hidden writing," which used the names of spirits as a cryptographic code; it was often accused of being a work of black magic.</note> is rightly buried, so that it might not be revealed to unworthy babblers. It was, after all, a worthwhile task to ensure that the work of *Polygraphia* <note>Trithemius's later, more technical work on cryptography, which used complex tables and substitutions rather than the "angelic" masks of the Steganographia.</note> should not prejudice the other, but that the proper right of each should be maintained inviolate. 

<margin>
The distinction between Steganography and Polygraphy.
</margin>

Take this example of the distinction from his own mouth: concerning his *Steganography* as distinguished from *Polygraphy*, and its silent explanation, found in the key to Book II of *Polygraphia*. In *Steganography*, it is not that a single word represents a single letter; rather, each word represents another entire word that fits the secret mystery. We shall provide an example of a "veiled sentiment of the heart" <note>A phrase used by Trithemius to describe the hidden meaning within a coded text.</note> according to the limits of *Steganography* in two ways. For that work teaches how to hide a secret within nearly infinite narratives, not just the one or two prescribed here.

->Example.<-

"Melancius, Tiberius, John, and Peter, servants of the Count of Asoto, have conspired for your death, and on the fourth day after the feast of Saint Lawrence <note>August 10th. The "fourth day after" would be August 14th.</note> at night, they will surround your house; therefore, consider what you should do." <note>original: "Conspirauerunt in necem tuam Melancius, Tyberius, Ioannes & Petrus famuli Comitis de Asoto, & IIII. die post Laurentii de nocte circum vallabunt domum tuā, proinde quid agas."</note> This example is cloaked by *Steganography* in this way: 

"I pray you, my dearest friend, that you would lend me ten florins by the bearer of these presents, because they are very necessary to me for the construction of a certain building; I shall faithfully repay them to you." <note>original: "Oro te amicè charissimè vt mutuò mihi transmittas decem florenos cum latore pręsentium, quia sunt mihi valdè necessari i pro constructione cuiusdam ædificii, eos tibi fideliter restituam."</note>

Let us place the same message under a different narrative:

> Lord Jesus Christ, son of the living God, who willed to become man for us, to suffer and to die, have mercy on me, an unworthy sinner, now and in the terrible hour of my death. <note>original: "Domine Iesu Christe fili dei viui, qui homo fieri pro nobis, pati & mori voluisti, miserere mei peccatoris indigni, nunc & in terribili hora mortis meæ."</note>

### ON CHAPTER VII.

In this chapter, Paracelsus <note>Theophrastus Paracelsus (1493–1541), the Swiss physician and alchemist whose work this text explores.</note> demonstrates that within the science of magic there lies a path to the long life possessed by Adam and by Methuselah <note>A biblical patriarch said to have lived 969 years.</note>: these two preserved the spirit of the highest life. He laments, however, that this science has perished. Yet it is handed down in the very extensive *Book of Raziel* <note>original: "libro Razielis"; the *Sefer Raziel HaMalakh*, a medieval grimoire of practical Kabbalah supposedly revealed to Adam by the angel Raziel.</note>, which has not yet been lost—provided it is genuine. Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), the Benedictine abbot and occultist.</note> relies only upon its foundations in the second book of his *Steganographia*, as does a certain "Solomon the Hebrew"—not that most wise king, as some believe, any more than the Democritus of Abdera <note>Ancient Greek philosopher; many early alchemical texts were falsely attributed to him.</note> named by Hermolaus <note>Hermolaus Barbarus (1454–1493), a Venetian scholar.</note> is the true author of chemistry. Nor is it more likely to be the noble Athenian Plato, whose enigmatic papers are read with an Arabic paraphrase; nor the secrets of Aristotle the Stagyrite <note>Aristotle was born in Stagira; Suavius refers to the *Secretum Secretorum*, a popular medieval book of "secrets" attributed to Aristotle.</note> which are found addressed to Alexander. Indeed, Bacon <note>original: "Bacho"; likely referring to Roger Bacon (c. 1214–1292), the English philosopher and friar.</note> judges that those men were ignorant of these mysteries. But I, for my part, willingly except the divine Plato, using the words of Cicero: I see that Plato overflows with the most fertile fables, which seem to me to agree perfectly with the ancient mysteries. Thus, Bacon seems to act carelessly <note>original: "Oscitanter"; literally "yawningly" or "negligently."</note> in citing Aristotle as the author of that art, which he elsewhere plainly takes away and denies to him. Likewise, our Paracelsus here denies that Moses used magic to attain his long life, even though the Holy Bible <margin>Justinus and Cornelius Tacitus on Moses.</margin> testifies that he was instructed in all the learning of the Egyptians; and Cornelius Tacitus <note>A Roman historian who discussed the origins of the Jews in his *Histories*.</note>, the writer of Roman history, proclaims him a most wise mage. The Hebrews, however, say that before Moses...

<meta>Continuing from page 201, Leo Suavius (Jacques Gohory) concludes his introduction to Artephius by listing the eight specific areas of secret knowledge that enabled the legendary figure to live for a thousand years. This page transitions from the general defense of Artephius to a detailed breakdown of his magical and alchemical curriculum.</meta>

<page-num>202</page-num>
<header>LEO SUAVIUS</header>

...through these arts he attained a life of a thousand years; they are worthy of eternal monuments. 

First, he teaches the characters <note>original: "characteres"; referring here to magical signs or sigils believed to harness planetary power</note> of the planets, of rings, and of seals.

Second, what the movements of birds signify.

Third, how to interpret the voices of birds and animals, and how to cast lots <note>original: "sortes proiicere"; a method of divination using objects thrown to determine the divine will</note>.

Fourth, he teaches the virtues of herbs.

Fifth, the philosophers' stone <note>the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and granting immortality</note>.

Sixth, he teaches how to know the past, present, and future through three vessels <note>likely referring to "hydromancy" or scrying using water-filled containers</note>.

...if it croaks; for a silent bird shows none of these things. If it should begin to fly from a high place to a lower one and then comes to rest, it indicates not the *time* but the *person*. If it rests in front of you, your enemies will soon be reconciled to you. If it flies descending over you, your authority will be over your enemies. If it rests on high, then they will be raised up against you. If it establishes itself there, you will be in their power. If it does not rest, consider the place of its descent; for if it is before you, it is good for you, but if it is opposite you, it is good for your enemies. If, after these things are done, it sits on the right side, it rejoices over a deceived companion, and it means nothing to you. Similarly, if it sits on the left, it signifies the imminent death of whoever is with you. If you are alone, the bird announces death to itself. Take care, however, that it does not do these things for the sake of food or because it was driven away by someone; for in that case, nothing is shown.

<margin>Casting Lots.</margin>
Next, he takes two square stones in the shape of dice. Into one of them, he places a bit of emerald <note>original: "smaragdi"; highly valued in alchemy for its association with Mercury and clarity</note>, root of mugwort <note>original: "artemisiæ"; a herb often used for protection and visions</note>, and mandrake <note>original: "mandragoræ"; a root famous for its humanoid shape and magical potency</note>. He called this the "first stone" <note>original: "calculum"; literally a pebble, used here for a die or game piece</note>.

On the second stone, he marked the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6, just like on dice, but he used numerals instead of dots. He likewise marked that same character <note>the X sign mentioned previously</note> on it and called it the "second stone." Then he said: "Consider your thought and your journey, as well as the quality of the bird, ensuring that it does not croak or chatter because of anyone [else]..."

**The Third** way is for the lot of the stones to be interpreted, as follows:

# THE WORKS OF LEO SUAVIUS.

<margin>The Experiment of Bellerophon.</margin> **The Fourth Experiment**, that of Bellerophon. If you fill a silver vessel with water and look into it by the light of a candle, while catching the rays of the moon with a polished knife so that the light reflects from the knife into the water, he says that you will see the image of whoever you desire. Note also that in the three vessels described in the illustration, a shining knife is positioned because, in that operation, it is necessary for the rays of the sun or moon to fall upon a sword—which you should hold in your right hand—and reflect from it into the vessel into which you wish to look.

**Observe secondly**, that you must wait for the light of the stars to pass through small openings <note>original: "foramina," likely apertures in a wall or screen used to isolate specific light rays</note>. This is necessary because the light will not fall upon all three vessels at the same time; you must arrange the three vessels according to the position of the circles in the region of the Sun, Moon, or stars, at their midpoint or their quarter-phase.

**Observe thirdly**, that candles should be placed in front of the vessel toward the wooden support—each candle before its own vessel, between the wood and the vessel. Specifically, place the first and second candles between the first and second vessels, and the third candle between the second and third vessels. For this ritual, he defines the "first vessel" as the one into which the rays of the sun, moon, or stars that cast a shadow first enter—such as **Lucifer** <term>the Morning Star, or the planet Venus</term> and the **Pleiades** <term>a well-known star cluster in the constellation Taurus</term>.

**Observe fourthly**, that a **poplar wand** <note>original: "populea virga"</note> is used to mark the circle and to indicate the arrangement of the vessels. This wand is placed at the foot of the vessels upon the disc in such a way that the debarked side <note>the side where the bark has been stripped away</note> faces toward the wine.

**Fifthly and lastly**, observe that the **root of a gourd** <note>original: "cucurbite"</note> is placed upon the disc; it adds ease and speed to the operation because of its natural properties.

**The Fifth Experiment** is to cut the root of a **nettle** <note>original: "vrticæ"</note>, pulverize it, and place it in a bronze vessel

**The Experiment of Bellerophon.** The fourth part: if you fill a silver vessel <note>original: "vas argenteum"</note> with water and look into it by the light of a candle, amidst the rays of the shining moon, using a polished knife from which the light reflects into the water, he says that you will see the figure of whomever you wish. And note that in the three vessels described in the figure <note>this refers to a diagram or illustration appearing elsewhere in the manuscript</note>, a shining knife is positioned because, in that operation, it is necessary that the rays of the sun or moon fall upon the sword which you hold in your right hand, and reflect from it into the vessel into which you wish to look. 

Observe secondly, that you should wait for the light of the stars through apertures <note>likely holes in a window shutter or roof designed to isolate specific celestial beams</note>; and this is because the light will not fall upon all three vessels at once. You shall arrange the three vessels turned according to the position of the circles <note>astrological houses or orbits</note> in the region of the Sun or Moon or stars, whether in their half or quarter phase. 

Observe thirdly, that the candles are placed before the vessel toward the wood—each one before its own vessel, between the wood and the vessel: the first and second between the first and second vessel, and the third between the second and third vessel. And he calls the "first vessel" for now that one into which the rays of the sun, moon, or stars that cast a shadow first enter—such as **Lucifer** <term>the Morning Star, the planet Venus</term> and the **Pleiades** <term>a prominent star cluster in the constellation Taurus</term>. 

Observe fourthly, that the poplar rod <note>original: "populea virga"</note> is that by which the circle is marked, and which indicates the vessels within vessels, and which is placed at the foot of the vessels upon the disk, so that the peeled part <note>the part of the branch with the bark removed</note> faces toward the wine. 

Fifth and finally, observe that the root of the gourd <term>likely a plant from the Cucurbitaceae family, such as bryony, used in folk magic for its rapid growth</term> is placed upon the disk; it adds ease and speed to the result on account of its natural properties.

### On Numerical Cabala.

Therefore, let the Cabalistic <note>Here referring to Kabbalah, the Jewish mystical tradition, though viewed through a Renaissance Christian lens.</note> instruction follow the magical one, which seems to be another school of magic attributed to Moses by Pliny; its foundations were laid only in the preceding chapter: namely, that it consists in the power of numbers. Among these, the triad <note>The number three.</note> and the decade <note>The number ten.</note> are formal <note>Possessing the essential form or spirit.</note>, while the others are material. Let us hear the mysteries of the ancients regarding the triad: <margin>Proclus on the mystical triad.</margin> Proclus <note>A Greek Neoplatonist philosopher (412–485 AD) who heavily influenced later mystical thought.</note> says of the dual-natured Trinity: Jupiter is substantializing <note>original: *substātificatiuus*; making things exist in substance.</note>, Neptune is life-giving, and Pluto is converting <note>leading the soul back to its divine source.</note>. Note here that "leaders" <note>original: *duces*</note> are named <margin>Leo Suavius</margin> in *Steganography* <note>A famous work by Johannes Trithemius involving angel magic and cryptography.</note> after the prince spirits.

The third Trinity of the supermundane gods is called Apollo, and the power of "conversion" is assigned to him. A guarding and preserving trinity accompanies the Trinity of Proserpine at her side.

Just as the first trinity after unity <note>The "One" or the source of all being.</note> is to measure all things intelligibly and in the form of limits <note>original: *finiformiter* (perhaps *finitiformiter*)</note>, so the second trinity is all things vitally, truly, and in the form of infinity <note>original: *infinitiformiter*</note>; the third is all things according to the property of the mixture and in the form of beauty <note>original: *pulchriformiter*</note>.

The first trinity only remains (or does it flow? <note>A pun in Latin between *manet* (remains) and *manat* (flows).</note>); the second remains and proceeds forward; the third, after its procession, "converts" <note>Returns toward the source.</note>. The "containing property" belongs to the middle order of the second trinity, which in the *Phaedrus* <note>A dialogue by Plato.</note> is called the "celestial circumference." <margin>Leo Suavius</margin> Note concerning this containing faculty: see Arnaldus <note>Arnald of Villanova, a famous medieval physician and alchemist.</note> in his *Philosophical Paraphrase*, and Jo. de Gravia in the chapter of the *Rosary* <note>Likely the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a foundational alchemical text.</note> concerning the rule of dissolution.

The second trinity of the intellectual week— <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence at the end of the page.</note>

### ON CHAPTER VIII.

<margin>Magic of life. Magic of the intellect.</margin>
In this eighth chapter, Paracelsus <note>The famous Swiss physician and occultist (1493–1541).</note> discusses the multiple kinds of magic—namely, the true magic of the biblical Magi and of the imitating Archeus <note>original: *Archei (seu Archelai)*. In the Paracelsian system, the Archeus is the "inner alchemist" or vital force that directs the functions of life.</note>, and the false magic. True magic is of two kinds: one of long life, the other of the intellect beyond nature—that is, which regards our supernatural body.

<margin>St. Augustine</margin>
moon, Saint Augustine testifies in his
work *On the Christian Struggle* <note>original: "de Agone Christiano." A treatise written by Augustine of Hippo around 396-397 AD focusing on the spiritual warfare of Christians against the devil.</note>, saying thus: **Demons do not dwell in the heavens where the sun and stars are, but they all move within the sub-lunar region.** <note>original: "Dæmones non habitant in cœlo ubi sol & stellæ sunt, sed omnes sub regione lunari versantur."</note>
Moved by this, as I believe, Apuleius said that demons were **fiery** animals, because Aristotle confirmed that in burning furnaces certain small animals were often seen flying about, fitted with little wings <note>Aristotle mentions "fire-born" creatures (*pyrigenoi*) in his *History of Animals* (V.19), which Renaissance scholars often linked to the concept of salamanders or fiery demons.</note>, which spend their whole life in fire, since they are born with the fire and are extinguished with it, and vanishing, they return to the place from which they came: there is no fellowship <note>original: "confortia," meaning association or companionship.</note> between them and sorcerers <note>original: "maleficis." This term refers to practitioners of harmful magic.</note>, because as they dwell in fire on account of their **subtlety** <note>In early modern science, "subtlety" refers to a refined, non-dense state of matter, as opposed to "crass" or heavy matter.</note>, they cannot put on a thick or aerial body.
<margin>The 2nd kind.</margin>
The **second kind** is called **aerial**, which wanders in the air near us and dwells there. These indeed can descend to the lower parts and, having taken on bodies from the thicker air, sometimes appear visible to men. With God’s permission, they often disturb the air, stir up thunder and storms, and all together they conspire for the destruction of the human race: like men, they are moved by the affections of the passions: they are touched especially by **pride** and **envy**, and by continuous disturbances; and they are neither clothed in a solid body, nor do they stay in one place. Nor...

...they do not all have one single form, but many, and they change these quite often, according to the variety of passions <note>or "afflictions of the soul"</note> with which they either appear when summoned by the spells of witches <note>original: "maleficarum carminibus." But I do not know whether an object is produced in the air from a real consistency, or whether indeed the restricted motion of the eyes represents false images—not without damage to the sense of sight, though slight; nevertheless, I have made a trial of the aforementioned experiment.
<margin>Third Genus</margin>
Truly, we call the third genus "terrestrial" demons, whom we do not doubt in the least have fallen from heaven to earth because of their sins.

### SCHOLIA. 221

Concerning these matters, that most holy prelate and martyr of Christ, Ignatius, <note>Ignatius of Antioch (c. 35–107 AD), an early Christian writer and bishop who was martyred in Rome.</note> formerly called Theophorus <note>original: "Theophorus," a Greek name meaning "God-bearer."</note>, writes thus in a certain epistle to the Ephesians:
> "Nothing is better than to possess peace, in which every weapon of both aerial and terrestrial spirits is brought to nothing." <note>original: "Nihil melius est quàm pacem habere..." This quote emphasizes spiritual peace as a shield against demonic influence.</note>

Among these demons, some dwell in the forests and groves where they set snares for hunters; others live in the open fields and cause travelers to wander astray at night; several stay in hidden places and caverns; and the rest, less furious and disturbed than the others, delight in staying with humans in the dark. They are led not by one single impulse but by various ones, for some are less depraved than others, although all are full of evil disturbances. Out of these, some enjoy terrifying people with mere illusions; others desire to draw their listeners into admiration of them through predictions of the future; several, however, labor with the greatest effort to terrify, harm, or kill men who are already disturbed by irrational fury or raging with melancholy <note>In the 16th century, "melancholia" was understood as an excess of "black bile," a physical condition that made one spiritually vulnerable to despair and demonic manipulation.</note>—something we know through experience has often happened.

<margin>Chrysostom</margin>
Hence Saint John Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Church Father known for his "golden-mouthed" eloquence.</note>, in the third book of *On Providence* addressed to the monk Stagyrius <note>Stagyrius was a friend of Chrysostom who suffered from what was described as demonic possession or severe depression; Chrysostom wrote this treatise to console him.</note>, says:
> "The magnitude of sorrow <note>original: "moeroris." This refers to deep, paralyzing grief or despondency.</note> is more powerful for causing harm than any diabolical action, because the demon overcomes whomever he overcomes through sorrow. If you take that away, no one can be harmed by a demon in any way."

This kind of demon, however, is rarely an intimate of sorcerers <note>original: "maleficis," those who practice harmful magic.</note>, because of the inconstancy of their impulses and their levity, with which they enjoy terrifying many...

...rather than be subject to the command of one insignificant woman. <note>original: "mulierculæ." The author uses this diminutive term to emphasize the perceived indignity a spirit feels when commanded by a practitioner of low status.</note> Nevertheless, they sometimes linger—as they promise—for the frenzied in glass, in crystal, or in a mirror; stirred by incantations, they give answers to women, and if someone who is traveling toward them has spoken ill of them on the road, they announce it. This kind of sorceress <note>original: "maleficarum"</note> sometimes differs from the others: for while those others make a person sick through harmful magic <term>maleficium | a Latin term for "wrongdoing," specifically referring to harmful sorcery or "black" magic</term>, these women promise to cure them. <margin>The Fourth Kind.</margin>
The fourth kind of demons is called "aquatic," because they immerse themselves in moisture and live around lakes and rivers. They are full of anger, restless in crowds, and fraudulent; they stir up storms at sea, sinking ships into the deep and taking the lives of many in the waters. Whenever these demons assume a visible body, they appear more frequently in the female sex and are more rarely seen in the male. This is because they dwell in damp places and follow a more refined way of existence; <note>In Renaissance elemental theory, water was considered a "finer" or "purer" element than earth, leading to the belief that its inhabitants possessed more graceful forms.</note> they cannot easily assume the coarse appearance <note>original: "vile schema"</note> common to other spirits. For this reason, the ancients long ago named the water nymphs "Naiads" and "Nereids" in the female sex, not the male. Our own people, however, call them "water-women"—that is, *wasserfrauwen* <note>original German: "wasserfrauwen." Suavius is linking classical mythology to local Germanic folklore.</note>—in the common tongue. On the other hand, those who dwell in drier and somewhat arid places transform themselves into visible men whenever they appear physically to humans. They also take on the forms of various beasts, according to the different passions by which they are moved.

Holy angels, however, because they never vary in their disposition, always appear uniformly in male form. <note>original: "forma virili." <margin>The Fifth Kind.</margin>
The fifth kind is called "subterranean," which dwells in caves, caverns, and the remote hollows of mountains. These demons are the worst in their disposition; they especially attack those who dig wells or mine for metals, as well as those who seek treasures hidden in the earth, being most ready for the destruction of the human race. They cause chasms in the earth, stir up flame-breathing winds, <note>original: "flammiuomos," literally "flame-vomiting."</note> and shake the foundations of buildings. Sometimes the ringing of bells <term>Nolarum | a term for small bells, traditionally said to be named after the city of Nola in Campania, where bell-founding was perfected</term> is heard among them, and they occasionally lie, claiming to be the spirits of the dead. They seek nothing more than the fear and awe of men. From this, we have discovered that they have sometimes led certain simpler people into their mountain hiding places, showing marvelous sights to those who watch in wonder; they pretend to be friends of the living, acting as if the dwellings of the blessed were located there. <header>COMMENTARY ON BOOK II OF THEOPHRASTUS PARACELSUS'S *ON THE LONG LIFE* BY LEO SUAVIUS (J. G. P.)</header>

->*Commentary on the Preface of Paracelsus.*<-

<margin>
Concerning gout
not hindering 
a long life.
</margin>
Although Paracelsus says here that he will treat in particular in Book II what he treated in general in Book I of *On the Long Life*: this is not to be understood as referring to the entire subject matter of Book I—which is only completed in Book IV, as he himself states in its preface—but rather to the specific remedies and types of diseases which he briefly touched upon in Chapter III of Book I. These, indeed, he said pertained to a short life, not a long one. For a long life persists unharmed even with the torment of the limbs, as is clear especially in the case of **gout** <term>gout: historically known as "podagra," a painful inflammatory arthritis often thought in the Renaissance to be a "safe" disease because it affected the joints rather than the vital organs</term>. Those afflicted by it are said to live a long life, either because this disease does not affect the vital parts contained within the "casket of the chest" (as the common people say), or because nature—or the **Archaeus** <term>Archaeus: in Paracelsian medicine, the internal "alchemist" or vital force that governs the body's functions and separates nourishment from waste</term>, according to Paracelsus—diverts all the filth of the body there as if into a cesspool. Now, therefore, what our **Theophrastus** <note>Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim, better known as Paracelsus (1493–1541).</note> touched upon in passing in Book I concerning particular diseases, he will complete in this Book II.

*It is necessary, however, that you far prefer an intact and healthy life.*

Understand that, in truth, a healthy life is to be preferred as the foundation of a long life: although he said that diseases contrary to a healthy life do not hinder a long life. But this [pertains to the diseases] of particular

<summary>In this commentary, Leo Suavius explains that Paracelsus distinguishes between a "long life" and a "healthy life," noting that chronic conditions like gout can actually coincide with longevity because they bypass vital organs. He introduces the concept of the Archaeus as the body's internal regulator that manages waste and disease.</summary>

<header>COMMENTARY</header>

...you will understand it as concerning diseases of the limbs; but you will establish that the art of a life beyond nature is much more excellent than that which was diligently and subtly written by the ancient doctors for a healthy and whole life, as even **Roger Bacon** <note>original: "Rogerius Bacho"; an English Franciscan philosopher and scientist (c. 1219–1292) who wrote on the prolongation of life through alchemy.</note> confesses. For this purpose, he employs the power of the **arcanum**, and then the **balsam**.

<margin>For a whole life, Arcanum and Balsam.</margin>

->*Balsam preserves the body firm; the arcanum restores the sick body from corruption.*<-

He explains the **arcanum** <term>arcanum: a "secret" or "mystery"; in Paracelsian medicine, a powerful, concentrated substance that contains the formative power of a natural thing</term> in his book *On Degrees*, when all the species useful for curing a disease are enclosed as if in secrets. Therefore, by reason of a particular disease, this method of healing is called "singular"; but by another reason—that is, the reason of all the things included in the remedy—it can deservedly be called "universal." Here all species are concluded under one genus. But there is a more common arcanum that embraces all genera, such as **Cheiri** and **Saphiricus Anthos** <term>Saphiricus Anthos: literally "Sapphire Flower," an alchemical preparation believed to have the celestial properties of the sapphire</term>: concerning which he says he has treated copiously in the book titled *The Parisian Archidoxes*. In this matter, he praises the tincture of the **philosopher's stone** which, just like fire (according to **Lull** <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316), a Majorcan philosopher to whom many later alchemical works were attributed.</note>), seizes upon the metal; so similarly it works in the humors, namely by drawing away the **dross** <note>original: "scorias"; the waste matter or slag left after metal has been smelted.</note> and leaving the subject pure.

<margin>Cheiri. Saphiricus Anthos.</margin>

However, he explains **Cheiri** <term>Cheiri: an alchemical term often referring to a quintessence of gold or certain plants like the wallflower, symbolic of a "healing hand."</term> and **Anthos** as being **potable gold** <note>original: "aurum potabile"; a legendary liquid medicine made from gold, believed to be a universal cure-all.</note> or the **Fifth Essence** <term>Fifth Essence: or Quintessence, the purest, celestial element that remains after the four worldly elements (earth, air, fire, water) have been removed.</term>; using an unheard-of word, just as the rivals of **Arnald** <note>Arnald of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note>—that is, Lull and others—have handed down under the name **Lunaria**. **Cheiri**, therefore, is the power of the arcanum. Moreover, **Lunaria**, according to **Marsilio Ficino** <note>Italian priest and influential humanist philosopher (1433–1499) who sought to reconcile Neoplatonism with Christianity.</note>, is a herb handed down by Mercury with blue leaves and...

*Far, I read, of a long life:* <note>original: "Longe, Lego, longæ, scilicet vitæ"</note> namely, because health is the foundation of a long life, which, if that foundation is destroyed, must necessarily collapse.

*The power of the arcanum:* It is taken internally, while that of the **balsam** is applied to external parts.

*To be kept firm:* This can be understood as the perfect body which the **Spagyrics** <term>Spagyrics: alchemists who follow the Paracelsian method of "separating and recombining" (from the Greek "spao" and "ageiro") to create medicines.</term> order to be treated and dissolved while preserving its essential form.

*The medical canon:* He uses these words because the Spagyrics call their work "medicine," and they call the rules of the work "masteries" <note>original: "magisteria"</note> or "operations of preparations," such as **calcination**, **solution**, and so forth.

<margin>Trevisanus <br/> Jo. Valentianus.</margin> *They are gathered together:* They say the **Great Work** <note>original: "Opus magnum"; the alchemical process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note> is called "universal" and converts all things without distinction; from this, the argument is that all things are present within it, according to **Trevisanus** <note>Bernard of Treviso (1406–1490), an Italian alchemist.</note> and **Joannes Valentianus** <note>Jean de Valence, an alchemical author often cited in the 16th century.</note>.

<margin>Iamblichus.</margin> *Something common:* I find no better interpretation than that from **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote on theurgy and Egyptian mysteries.</note> regarding the threefold distinction of Hermetic speech: namely, **solar**, **lunar**, and **universal**. For the solar contains many particulars, and the lunar likewise contains many. Then there is one general solar, and likewise a general lunar; however, the "common" or universal contains both the solar and lunar together, just as a red vine is grafted onto a white one.

*Archidoxes:* This is a book by Paracelsus among many...

...matters to others (of whom I have written a catalog) to whom he refers the reader in all difficult matters.

**Sickness:** The impurity of a thing to be administered or displayed, which must be removed through preparation. <note>Suavius defines illness here not just as a human condition, but as an "impurity" within a substance that a chemist must "cure" before it can be used as medicine.</note>

**Cheiri, Saphyricum, and Anthos:** These are well-known terms of the **Spagyric** <term>Spagyric: The alchemical art of separating and recombining substances to create potent medicines.</term> enigma <note>original: "ænigmatis Spagyrici"</note> used to represent the essence of silver and **potable gold** <note>Gold in a drinkable, liquid form, believed to be a universal cure.</note>. Thus, *Anthos* refers to the white flower of rosemary, and *Cheiri* to the yellow violet.

**That [phrase], "I read it":** Namely the method, or both medicines—that is, the medical and surgical arts.

**Of this matter:** That is, of the Spagyric or chemical operation.

### Dispute concerning Cheiri and Lunaria.

But a fuller dispute must be entered into here regarding **Cheiri** and **Lunaria**. For *Cheiri* is an Arabic word, just as *leucoion* <note>original: "leucoion"</note> is a Greek word: both express the "violet" of the Latins, which however is correctly called <gloss>ios</gloss> <note>original: "ios," the Greek root for violet.</note> in general by the Greeks. 

<margin>The Leucoion <br/> (White Violet)</margin> It seems absurd among the writers of Herbals that the *leucoion*, which properly signifies only "white," is transferred promiscuously to blue, white, purple, and yellow colors; this is something that **Matthiolus** <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, a famous 16th-century physician and botanist who commented on Dioscorides.</note> suspected in his commentary on **Dioscorides** <note>A 1st-century Greek physician whose "De Materia Medica" was the primary botanical text for centuries.</note>. I have heard from skilled physicians that the yellow flower which is often found on walls in our region is properly called *Cheiri* by the apothecaries: this would especially agree with the enigma of Paracelsus. However, I believe that *leucoion* is used thus generally by Dioscorides for every "greater violet": for the small ones which the French call "March violets"...

...a certain herb or plant by the name of **Lunaria** <term>Lunaria: Known as "Moonwort," this plant was prized by alchemists because its moon-shaped seed pods suggested a connection to the moon and silver.</term>, or otherwise called **Borissa**, whose root is a metallic earth; its stem is reddish, four-cornered, and tinged with blackness. I shall conclude: Paracelsus played with fictitious names after the manner of the ancient **Spagyrists** <term>Spagyrist: A term for an alchemist who focused on the separation and recombination of natural elements for medicinal purposes.</term>, who freely used the "rose" because of its double color, white and red. ### On Chapter I.
## CONCERNING GOUT.

For the cure of gout <note>original: "podagra," specifically gout of the foot</note>, three things are required.

1 **Purging**, which is done with the "coralline secret" <note>original: "arcano corallino," a Paracelsian preparation likely involving mercury</note> or that which is made from the essence of gold: this elicits a flow <note>a medicinal discharge of humors</note> on the fifth or seventh day. If, however, residues remain, or the patient becomes too weak to bear such a great repetition of this purging—by which words he seems to suggest that this kind of purging is violent.

2 **Opening** should be made in the center through the "alkali of spirits": from which a swelling will arise, in which it breaks out in a discharge. Regarding the **eschar** <note>original: "Aeschparæ," likely a variation of "eschara," the dead tissue or scab following a caustic burn</note>, whatever has become embedded in the center (I read *insenuit* <note>meaning "grown old within"</note> instead of *inseruit* <note>meaning "inserted"</note>).

<margin>Eschar.</margin>
> The **eschar** <note>original: "Aeschpara"</note> seems to be the callus produced by a "potential cautery" <term>Potential Cautery: A chemical substance used to burn or sear the skin, as opposed to a "fire" or "actual" cautery.</term> from Chapter III, Book I of *On Degrees*, concerning those things that cause scarring—that is, those making an eschar, which are things that scrape away corrosive flesh. But in Chapter VI he writes: Whatever stings sharply in corrosion and casts into an eschar to cause putrefaction occupies the "third degree" of intensity. Such things include **colcothar** <term>Colcothar: A reddish-brown iron oxide residue left after the distillation of vitriol.</term>, arsenic, ammonium salt, borax, orpiment <note>original: "auripigmentum," a yellow arsenic sulfide</note>, and other alkalis of that kind.

3 **Strengthening** (once the flow has ceased) with a poultice of **Mummy** <term>Mummy: In Paracelsian medicine, "Mumia" refers to a medicine prepared from preserved flesh or a specific spiritual essence believed to have great healing and "magnetic" power.</term>: But if it has not hardened (I read *induruit* instead of *indurauit*), it can be cured with Mummy alone—namely, treated with alkali—and by anointing the limbs with the liquor of Mummy.

By **alkali-infused** <note>original: "Alcaligatam"</note>, I understand **mummy** <note>original: "Mumiam," a medicinal substance derived from human remains</note> joined with the **alkali of spirits**: among which one may also add **sublimated mercury** <term>Sublimated Mercury: Also known as corrosive sublimate, a chemical compound of mercury and chlorine used in alchemical medicine.</term>.

<margin>Mummy.</margin> Now, **mummy** is a concoction made from the fluids of a human corpse, mixed with the liquid aromatics with which it is preserved in the tombs of the Egyptians. However, the legitimate version is rarely found among us; rather, we have only the adulterated kind, as **Mattioli** <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, a famous 16th-century physician and botanist</note> rightly reasons in his commentary on **Dioscorides** <note>The ancient Greek author of "De Materia Medica"</note>. **Noël Ramart**, a royal physician, extracted another kind of "mummy" by the force and power of **scammony** <note>a harsh medicinal root used as a purgative</note> from a living and healthy body. Others say it is formed from human bodies in the sandy places of **Arabia**, where they are buried in the sand and dried out by the sun.

<header>SCHOLIA.</header>

...is composed of both male and female seed, that is, with sulfur, and is therefore congealed. And in the *Lesser Rosary* <note>original: "Rosario minore," likely referring to the *Rosarium philosophorum*, a famous 16th-century alchemical treatise</note>, "coagulated Mercury is the matter of the philosophers," etc.

<margin>Nicolas Flamel.</margin>
Nicolas Flamel indeed—whose monuments of the art still exist in great number in Paris <note>original: "Lutetiæ"</note>—also left a written record stating that no natural congealing of metal can be reduced back into unstable and flowing **quicksilver** <term>Quicksilver: Another name for mercury (argentum vivum), prized by alchemists for its liquid state and ability to dissolve other metals.</term>. He claimed that all who dare to assert such a thing are impostors. 

However, Ramon Lull <note>a 13th-century Majorcan philosopher and reputed alchemist</note> admits in the third book of his work *On the Fifth Essence* <note>original: "de v. essentia"</note> that plant matter can be reduced with great labor into a certain type of quicksilver. Augurellus <note>Giovanni Aurelio Augurello, author of the alchemical poem *Chrysopoeia*</note> says that slag is converted into true silver by the Euganean <note>referring to the Euganean Hills near Padua, Italy</note>; without which, I have heard from those who claim to practice this very thing, they attempt nothing of the sort. This leads to a suspicion that this substance emanates from the rot of such plant matter rather than from metal. 

You will say, however, that there is frequent mention of such things among the chemists, as is also mentioned here. True; but their teachers interpret this as being about a different **first matter** <term>First Matter: Also known as "materia prima," the primordial, formless substance from which all things are made in alchemical theory.</term>, which exists in a form like a dissolved sprout, not like running quicksilver. Concerning this, that tombstone saying should be understood:

> *Begone, you worst of thieves, with your Mercury,*
> *The one wearing the traveler's hat and bearing the herald's staff.*
<note>original: "Ite pessumi fures cum vostro Mercurio Petasato, caduceato." This quote warns against literal or "vulgar" mercury, invoking the classical image of the god Mercury with his winged hat (petasos) and staff (caduceus).</note>

<margin>Extraction. Fiction.</margin>
But some of these "wise men" <note>original: "sophorum," often used ironically to describe those who claim secret knowledge they do not possess</note> claim the fixation of that Mercury of Saturn <note>Mercury associated with or derived from lead</note>, while others claim its extraction, and they have not yet agreed upon their shared symbols. From these theories, they promise mountains of gold to others; yet they themselves—in the words of Plautus <note>a Roman comic playwright</note>—crawl along, parched with hunger. Regarding that sense of the "sprout," the Greek chemists call it...

...they call quicksilver itself the "Seminal Discharge of the Dragon" <note>original: "Apospermatismum draconis"</note>; quicksilver derived from gold, they call the "Disk of the Sun"; and quicksilver from tin, "Dragon’s Gall" <note>original: "Fel draconis"</note> (lest anyone mistakenly interpret the "oil of gall" mentioned in the final chapter of Geber’s <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century father of chemistry</note> work *On Waters and Oils* in any other way). Moreover, quicksilver that has already been thickened and bound by cold they call "Gypsum" <note>original: "Gypson"</note>; and the scales of raw copper that spontaneously fly off in the furnace, they call "Seed of Venus" <note>original: "Semen veneris"</note>.

<margin>Vulcan’s Clay.</margin>
<margin>Horizon.</margin>
<margin>Potable Gold.</margin>
<margin>Description of the golden liquor</margin>
They also call a mixture of barley flour with egg white "Vulcan’s Clay" <term>Vulcan’s Clay: Also known as "Lute," this was a sealing paste used by alchemists to protect glass vessels from breaking in high heat.</term>. Aristotle, following the Pythagoreans, also refers to the Moon as "celestial earth" and "terrestrial heaven"; the poet Lucan calls Mercury the "arbiter." From this comes the discussion of the **Horizon**—a term in which you will recognize the higher allegory mentioned before concerning the East and the Dawn. Paracelsus, however, insists that the **Horizon** be distinguished from **Potable Gold** <term>Potable Gold: A legendary medicinal "gold liquor" (aurum poculentum) believed to cure all diseases and grant longevity.</term>, because one is more thoroughly "cooked" and tempered by fire than the other. For Hermolaus <note>Hermolaus Barbaro, a 15th-century Venetian scholar known for his translations of Aristotle and Dioscorides</note> suspects that **Potable Gold** is that precious liquor described in a certain epitaph, which almost all the books of the Arabs mention, though none have ever explained it clearly. The masters of chemistry explain it—or rather, they entangle and wrap it in riddles in their usual way—so that in this age, no one can display this singular gift of the art. Thus, I wonder at Marsilio Ficino <note>A famous 15th-century Italian priest and philosopher who led the revival of Platonism</note>, the interpreter of Platonic mysteries: while he preaches so many benefits of the golden liquor, why does he describe it in his *Antidote against the Plague* <note>original: "Antidoto epidemie"</note> only according to the opinion of Gentile <note>Gentile da Foligno, a prominent 14th-century physician</note> and not from his own experience? Namely, through the calcination <term>Calcination: The process of heating a substance to high temperatures in the air to change its physical or chemical state, often reducing it to powder.</term> of mercury, then its solution in bugloss water <note>a plant-based medicinal water</note>, using these words: *It can perhaps happen that gold may be led back to a form...*

->In Chapter II.<-

### ON THE DROP.

For all species of the **Drop** <term>The Drop: Known in Latin as "Gutta," this historical term usually refers to Gout, but could encompass various conditions where "bad humors" were thought to drop into the joints or organs.</term>, a general care for the power of nature is required.

The Drop, however (regarding quantity), contains no more than one **scruple** <note>A small unit of weight used by apothecaries, roughly 1.3 grams</note> within itself; **Apoplexy** <term>Apoplexy: A historical term for a stroke or sudden loss of consciousness caused by a blockage or hemorrhage.</term> does not quite ascend to one scruple: therefore.

<margin>Apoplexy.</margin>
Strengthening remedies <note>original: "Confortatiua"</note> must be prepared which expel "nature" (I read this as "matter"), namely **secrets** <term>Secrets: Translated from "arcana," these were Paracelsian remedies believed to contain the concentrated "inner essence" or medicinal power of a substance.</term>, and which conquer by their own nature. Therefore, in the book *On Degrees* <note>original: "lib. de Grad."</note> he says: "Degrees of strengthening are required for the drop." Apoplexy occurs when the drop suffocates the channels in the lung.

For contractions, therefore, there is a double secret: the vitriol-based remedy and the **Mercury of gold**, or the **horizon**, which they falsely call "drinkable gold" <note>original: "aurum poculentum"</note>.

<margin>The miracle of Peony, according to Galen.</margin>
Regarding the peony, there is a remarkable story in the works of Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD) was the most influential physician of the Roman Empire; his theories dominated European medicine for over a thousand years.</note>, wherein a peony root hung around the neck would keep an epileptic upright; but when it was removed, the patient would immediately fall.

### *From surgery, a twofold method of healing is sought.*

The first method is for preparing a "falling" emunctorium <term>Emunctorium: Historically, a part of the body where waste is expelled; here it likely refers to an artificial opening or "issue" created to drain the "peccant humors" thought to cause seizures.</term>, as follows:
Open the skull with suitable instruments; then, with a gold and silver tube placed in its spot, restore the consolidated matter to its former good life. <note>original: "lego impoſitâ conſolidatum"; Suavius is suggesting a textual correction here, implying the tube helps the area heal or "consolidate" correctly.</note>

The second method: dissolve a limb or the upper part of a limb—for instance <note>original: "puto (lego, vt puta)"; Suavius corrects the text to clarify he is giving an example.</note> the ligaments and arteries in the surrounding area—and do this with a narcotic corrosive all the way to the bones, then consolidate it again. Some judge that this corrosive is produced imperceptibly from oil of vitriol <term>Oil of Vitriol: Concentrated sulfuric acid, a powerful chemical agent used by alchemists for both metal transmutation and radical medicine.</term> extracted in the chemical manner.

Now, to return to the physical <note>meaning "natural" or medicinal</note> reasoning: Take oil of vitriol, corrected and "aurified" <note>ennobled with gold</note>, either tempered by its phlegm <note>the watery byproduct of distillation</note> in a circular fashion, or (I read: "not by") but take the red or green oil under which the *colcothar* <term>Colcothar: The reddish-brown residue (iron oxide) remaining after the distillation of vitriol; it was highly valued in alchemical medicine.</term> lies hidden. Either one frees the patient from the disease.

Also, let the memorial part <note>The back of the head, where memory was thought to reside.</note> be anointed with a balsam made from ivy <note>original: "lego, hæderis"</note>, and let this be done after the paroxysm <note>the seizure or fit</note>.

Furthermore, let the back of the head be anointed with balsam of *Helenium* <note>Elecampane, a plant historically used in respiratory and neurological complaints.</note> during the most violent seizure. *Helenium* is a well-known herb. Likewise, use the secret remedy <term>Arcanum: In Paracelsian medicine, the "arcanum" is the concentrated, celestial essence of a substance that performs the actual healing.</term> of blood and of certain organs.

->On Chapter 5: Concerning Fevers.<-

Three things are required:
1. Purgation by means of *diaceltatesson* <term>Diaceltatesson: A complex Paracelsian purgative composed of various botanical and mineral ingredients, designed to "drive out" the cause of a disease.</term> so that every fever residing in the "sinning matter" <note>original: "materia peccante." In Renaissance medicine, this refers to the morbid or corrupt substance (humors) believed to be the root cause of an illness.</note> may be expelled; especially if the disease is still spreading and being dispersed through the limbs.
2. A specific cure is performed through the *oppopyron* <term>Oppopyron: A term likely derived from the Greek for "through fire," referring to a medicament prepared or refined by intense heat.</term> of laudanum: to expel the fever along with its spreading.
3. Causal bloodletting <note>original: "minutio causalis," a targeted form of phlebotomy intended to remove the specific cause of a malady rather than just reducing blood volume.</note>, whether from the *salvatella* <note>The salvatella is a vein located on the back of the hand, between the ring and little finger.</note>, or the *cephalica* <note>The cephalic vein is a large vein in the arm, traditionally bled to treat disorders of the head.</note>, or that which draws out the sinning matter in the blood through the spinal column: and that (I read this as "and also") from between the skin and the flesh, that is, the humors exuding from the veins toward the flesh, etc.
Regarding the dosage, however, one must observe what has spread and what has not: that is, to what extent.
Concerning those things which contribute to the *arcanum* <term>Arcanum: In Paracelsian thought, the "secret" or "inner essence" of a substance that contains its true healing power.</term> of fevers: the same is discussed more extensively in the final book, Chapter 2, *On Degrees*.
Regarding laudanum, I will only say here that a book was written by envious rivals against Paracelsus, to which they gave the title *Holy Laudanum* <margin>Holy Laudanum.</margin>: in which they accused his new method in the healing art, relying solely on the foundation of the authority of the ancients <note>Referring to the traditional followers of Galen and Avicenna, who opposed Paracelsus's chemical medicine.</note>, whose slanders he easily evaded. Furthermore, laudanum was among the primary *arcana* of Paracelsus.
I will, however, add here the description of laudanum, mentioned by Paracelsus in so many and such great places, the use of which Adam von Bodenstein <note>A 16th-century physician and one of the most important early editors and promoters of Paracelsus's works.</note> describes in desperate illnesses.
<margin>False composition of Laudanum.</margin>Take 1 ounce of leaf gold <note>original: "Orizei foliati." This is likely a variation of "Aurizeus" or "Aurum foliatum." In Paracelsian recipes, gold leaf was a common ingredient in high-level elixirs.</note>.
Of un-pierced pearls, half an ounce.

### On Chapter 10: Regarding wounds.

<margin>Cato, *On Agriculture*.</margin>
Note that this grave philosopher <note>original: "grauem hunc philosophum." Referring to Cato the Elder, known for his stern morality.</note> did not shrink from the symbols found in hanging inscriptions <note>original: "scriptis pendulis." Likely referring to amulets or phylacteries worn around the neck.</note>, nor from blessings consisting of words uttered by the mouth. Examples include the common old wives' formula for "raising the chest" <note>original: "erectione pectoris." A folk remedy for respiratory distress or perhaps a sagging chest.</note>, and Cato’s strange, unknowable words for dislocations, and so on. In his book on *Surgery*, however, [Paracelsus] approves of constellations, stones, and words, while rejecting certain conjurations and ceremonial arrangements of figures.

->SCHOLIA.<-

<margin>Characteristics.</margin>
Regarding the magical <term>Magoreo: A term derived from the Greek *magos*, referring to the "characteristic" or symbolic branch of magic used in healing.</term> characteristic method of curing wounds—since the *Archidoxa* <note>One of Paracelsus's major works on the hidden forces of nature.</note> in which he treated these matters are not extant—we shall discuss a few points from the writings of the ancients.
These methods were approved by Marcellus Empiricus <note>A 5th-century medical writer who recorded many folk remedies.</note>, the "new" Dioscorides, Alexander Trallianus, Cato, and Constantine in the *Geoponica* <note>A 10th-century collection of agricultural lore.</note>. The editor of Celsus adds Pliny to this list, but falsely, for Pliny was a perpetual enemy of all "magical vanity." Most witty is the method of Quintus Serenus Sammonicus against semitertian fever <note>original: "hemitriteum." A specific type of malarial fever.</note>:
Using the written word *Abracadabra* <note>A famous ancient magical formula, first recorded by Sammonicus.</note>, drawn so that it tapers into a cone down to the final letter, and thus hung around the neck. Al-Kindi and Porphyry also approve of figures and characters.
<margin>Homer on stopping blood.</margin>
To stop the flow of blood (which Paracelsus discusses here), Homer describes a song used by the sons of Autolycus for the wounded Ulysses. Others express these words as:
*Chũrat, cara, sarite, confirma, consana, imaholite.* <note>These are "voces magicae," or nonsense words intended to have power through their sound rather than their literal meaning.</note>
<margin>In the catching of fish.</margin>
That same Constantine even used the names *Iao Sabaoth* <note>original: "Iao Sabãoth." Hebrew for "Lord of Hosts," often used as a word of power in Gnostic and magical papyri.</note> for the catching of fish.

<margin>Against the bite of a rabid dog.</margin>
Against the bite of a rabid dog, these words are written upon bread: *Irioni, Rhiriori: estlera, Rhuder, fere*; it is then eaten. Or, on pieces of an apple: *Hax, pax, max, God, adimax.* <note>These are "charactery" or magic squares of words where the sound and rhythm were believed to hold curative power, often mixing corrupted Latin, Hebrew, or nonsensical syllables.</note>

<margin>
Against scrofula.
A clever cure for scrofula.
</margin>
Against scrofula <term>Strumas: Swellings of the lymph nodes, typically associated with the disease known as the "King's Evil" or scrofula.</term>, the ancients believed that mullein <note>original: "verbascum." A common medicinal plant with fuzzy leaves.</note> crushed with its own root, sprinkled with wine, wrapped in a leaf, heated in hot ashes, and applied to the swellings would drive them away. This was especially effective if a fasting virgin performed the act and, touching the site with the palm of her hand, said: "Apollo denies that the plague can grow, which a naked virgin binds" <note>original: "Negat Apollo pestem posse crescere, quam nuda virgo restringat." This formula invokes the god of healing and the ritual purity of a virgin.</note>; it was also thought that one should spit three times during the process.

For epilepsy, mentioned above, the verse is:
"Caspar brings myrrh, Melchior incense, Balthasar gold." <note>The names of the Three Magi were frequently used as a protective charm against the "falling sickness" (epilepsy).</note>

<margin>To discover a theft.</margin>
To discover a theft, after the prescribed prayers, one says: *Dies, nues, reschet, benedoefet, douuina, euitemaus*; then the names of the suspects are pronounced during the turning of a sieve <term>Coscinomancy: An ancient form of divination where a sieve is balanced on shears or a cord; it was believed the sieve would shake or turn when the name of the guilty party was spoken.</term>.

<margin>Against toothache.</margin>
Against the pain of teeth, these words are quite effective: *Galbes, galbat, galdes, galda*. This ridiculous inscription is also attached: "Scrapers and toothed sickles, heal the toothache thoroughly." <note>original: "Strigiles falcesq́; dentatæ dentium dolorem persanate." A humorous or symbolic appeal to tools that possess "teeth" to fix human teeth.</note> Well known is Cato’s chant for dislocated limbs: *danata, daries*, etc. It is also a wonder what they place on the beak of a chick: *Gibel, Got, gabet*; then they pierce the head straight through the middle with a very sharp stylus, and the chick leaps away and lives, especially in the summer. There remains what Weyer <note>Johann Weyer (1515–1588), a physician who famously argued against the persecution of witches but was often a harsh critic of Paracelsus's "superstitions."</note> wrote to insult Paracelsus: that his followers clear a house disturbed by spirits <note>original: "lemuribus." Ghosts or restless spirits of the dead.</note> by hanging virgin parchment containing sacred words in the four corners.

<margin>
Concerning unknown words.
Against Giovanni Pico.
</margin>
Then he adds, mocking the physicians: "If they establish the principles of their art in the same way they have concocted this cure, there is no reason for us to fear that ancient medicine will be overturned." <note>original: "Si eodem modo suæ artis statuũt principia quo hanc conminenti sunt curationem, nõ est quod veterem medicinam euersum iri metuamũs."</note> Now let us consider what is said by the Chaldeans <note>The "Chaldeans" were often cited by Renaissance writers as the ancient masters of astrology and magic.</note>: that characters and figures possess more power than any material quality possibly could. But regarding those unknown voices of the charms mentioned above, Giovanni Pico <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a famous Italian Renaissance philosopher who sought to reconcile Platonism, Aristotelianism, and the Hebrew Kabbalah.</note> seems to hold a most distorted view, thinking that non-signifying words have more power in magic than signifying ones, because any word has power in magic insofar as it is formed by the voice of God. He also thinks that none are effective unless they are Hebrew or derived closely from it. For the most certain reasoning is that words which signify nothing are of no moment or weight; however, I will admit that "barbarous" words <note>original: "barbara quidem verba." In magic, these are called 'voces magicae'—strings of syllables that have no dictionary meaning but were believed to hold divine power.</note> must not be changed by us. For this reason, Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a Benedictine abbot and famous scholar of cryptography and magic.</note> orders in his *Steganographia*—after an oath has been demanded from the disciple—that the master explain to him the formulas of conjurations, which seem to be composed of words that are entirely "barbarous" or rather, signify nothing.

->*Concerning true magic, charms, and characters, against the slanders of Weyer and others.*<-
<note>Johann Weyer (Wierus) was a 16th-century physician who, in his work "De praestigiis daemonum," argued that those accused of witchcraft were often mentally ill, thereby criticizing the magical traditions Suavius is defending.</note>

Do you deny these characteristics, Weyer? Are you (O miserable man!) to be compared in any way with such great men of old? To name only the most recent philosophers here: Apion the Grammarian, Julian Caesar <note>The Emperor Julian "the Apostate," known for his interest in Neoplatonic theurgy.</note>, Artephius <note>A legendary medieval alchemical author.</note>, Roger Bacon <note>The 13th-century English friar and scientist often associated with early experimental magic.</note>, Pietro d’Abano the "Conciliator" <note>A famous 13th-century physician and astrologer who sought to reconcile philosophy and medicine.</note>, Albertus Magnus <note>One of the most influential medieval scholars, legendary for his knowledge of the natural world and occult properties.</note>, Arnold of Villanova, Anselm of Parma, and the *Picatrix* <note>The "Picatrix" is a famous medieval handbook of talismanic and astral magic, originally written in Arabic.</note>...

# SCHOLIA.

...the Spaniard <note>Likely referring to Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note>, and Cecco d’Ascoli <note>Francesco degli Stabili (c. 1269–1327), known as Cecco d’Ascoli, an Italian polymath and physician who was eventually executed for his controversial astrological views.</note> the Florentine: there is none among them who does not far surpass you in fame and learning. Indeed, I truly love you as an honest physician; I honor you as a Christian man who shrinks from infamous magic; and I proclaim you a diligent collector or "gleaner" of all antiquity. May God the Best and Greatest be my witness—or rather my judge, as they say—that I am led by no envy against you, nor by any slander; on the contrary, I embrace your labor and your late-night studies, just as I would gladly embrace you in person. 

I suspect that out of fear of slander, you—a man in my judgment learned, neither lazy nor dull—have undertaken a truly rash war against all antiquity. Thus Marsilio Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) was a central figure of the Italian Renaissance who translated Plato and sought to reconcile Hermetic magic with Christianity.</note>, both priest and physician, wrote many mystical things fruitlessly, regarding which he later suspended his assertions in both religion and medicine. But I, good sirs, excuse you; or rather, I weep for the misery of an ignorant age along with Catullus.

<margin>Catullus.</margin>
> *O foolish and witless age.* <note>original: "O seclum insipiens & infacetum." A quote from the Roman poet Catullus (Poem 43), lamenting a lack of taste or discernment in his time.</note>

If a <term>syllogism</term> <note>A form of logical reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two premises.</note> is to be drawn from testimony according to the rules of logic, would these great men not be preferred over you, whom you follow at a great distance? Come to your senses at last, good man, and apply judgment to these mysteries with me: Let us together condemn whatever is foreign to the true and holy religion of God—soothsayers, augurs, along with...

->LEO SUAVIUS<-

...from Moses: let us not reject those things which are brought forth from holy angels, those from the observations of divine names (about which Dionysius <note>original: "Dionysius." Referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian and philosopher whose works on celestial hierarchies and divine names were highly influential in Renaissance mysticism.</note> wrote so excellently), and those which are drawn from certain practical use. It shames me to bring forward Girolamo Cardano <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576) was a famous Italian polymath, physician, and astrologer. Suavius is pointing out his opponent's hypocrisy in using Cardano as a source.</note> as a witness—whom you use as a supporter in certain matters—who praises the charms of Cato, and who foolishly condemns Artephius <note>A legendary medieval figure to whom various alchemical and occult texts were attributed.</note> and Johannes Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516) was a Benedictine abbot and polymath. His works on "steganography" were often mistaken for demonic magic by his contemporaries.</note>. I judge you to be better and more prudent than him: where, then, does this opinion regarding the abstruse arts—hitherto unknown to you—hurry you off sideways, so that it is necessary for you to support your position against even the wisest of men with the testimonies of the most foolish and inept?

You even condemn histories confirmed by antiquity, yet you approve of new ones that support your opinion, such as those of Olaus <note>Likely Olaus Magnus (1490–1557), a Swedish historian whose descriptions of Northern European folk magic were viewed as "barbaric" by Southern European humanists.</note> and other "barbarian" writers. I do not wish to pursue every detail with a flood of words, nor do I take delight in emptiness; I examine the things themselves, and I am entirely focused on them. Now you praise your Agrippa <note>Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa (1486–1535), author of the foundational occult text *Three Books of Occult Philosophy*. He later wrote a "retraction" of human learning, which Suavius's opponent is likely using to dismiss magic.</note>; now, persuaded by the words of another, you say he sprinkled his books with nonsense. What inconsistency is this, what wavering? According to the old proverb, **a liar must have a good memory.** <note>original: "mendacem memorem esse." A Latin proverb from Quintilian, suggesting that those who don't tell the consistent truth will eventually trip over their own contradictions.</note> If you were standing before a tribunal, your own testimony would be inconsistent; what credit, then, do you hope to extract for your words from a prudent reader? If distinguished theologians and excellent physicians act against you, do you not fear the judgment of the wise?

Do not reject Lactantius, nor Aulus Gellius <note>Second-century Roman author of the *Attic Nights*, a collection of notes on grammar, history, and philosophy.</note> concerning Tarquin, nor Roman antiquity—drawn from Cicero—regarding the Sibylline <term>Sibylline books: A collection of oracular utterances, purchased by the last king of Rome, which were consulted by the Roman Senate in times of crisis.</term> books in all the greatest matters...

Therefore, three vowels with three consonants would make three syllables, each consisting of only two letters. As for the remainder, the eighth, will it not necessarily consist of six letters to complete the number nine? If in three [syllables], what prevents the "u" from being doubled in them? If you do not deny this in a divine name, you will be criticized for omitting it in the counting. However, pardon must be granted to mysteries of this kind, unless you can offer something better.

# LEO SUAVIUS.

...[he] will [pur]ge <note>The catchword from the previous page was "gabat," suggesting a word like "purgabat" (was purging), though this page begins with "bit," a future tense suffix. For some of the Angels remained in their original condition, while others violated it and assumed a body. Therefore, **Georgius Pictorius** <note>Georgius Pictorius (c. 1500–1569), a physician and writer on magic and "sublunary" (earthly) matters.</note> says in his *On Sublunary Matters* that witches <term>lamias</term> <note>Originally monstrous females from Greek myth, often used in this period to refer to witches or night-demons.</note> are entered by them and give birth. **Josephus**, **Lactantius**, **Tertullian**, the Christian philosopher **Athenagoras**, and **Justin [Martyr]** [concur]. Truly, the philosophers **Pythagoras**, **Plato** in his *Cratylus*, **Xenocrates**, **Chrysippus**, and **Plutarch** record that the *Nephitim* <note>original: "Nephitim"; refers to the Nephilim or "giants" mentioned in Genesis 6:4.</note>—that is, the sons of God coupled with the daughters of men—gave birth to giants. Following the authority of such great men, I understand this to refer to good spirits <term>eudæmonibus</term>.

Now indeed I shall add from the Chaldean Kabbalists: God, having heard the prayer of **Adam**, immediately gave him the seven *semyphoras* <note>A Latinization of the Hebrew "Shem HaMephorash," meaning the "Explicit Name" of God, often divided into various names or syllables for magical use.</note> which **Solomon** found in the Ark of the Covenant. The first of these is called (according to the prophets) *semiph. yana*; with the fourth [syllable?], He formed him for help in times of necessity.

<margin>Otherwise *Schemhaphoras*.</margin>

With the second *semyphora*, which is *Yoferaye*, he was able to speak with angels, and they brought letters <note>In this context, "literas" likely refers to magical characters or celestial scripts.</note> to him. With the third, he was able to speak with demons and the dead, and sought counsel from them, to which they responded adequately; and this is *Adonai* <note>A Hebrew title for God meaning "My Lord."</note>. With the fourth—that is, with the seven names, namely *languinem* <note>Possibly a corrupted transcription of a divine name.</note> etc.—he bound and loosed animals and spirits. With the fifth—that is, *hyaba* etc.—a woman...

The transformation of Arcadians into wolves upon crossing a swamp—mentioned by Pliny—is called a true transformation by Pomponazzi <note>Pietro Pomponazzi (1462–1525), an influential Italian philosopher who sought naturalistic explanations for the supernatural.</note>, as Paracelsus does in Book 1 above.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Pomponazzi is a great philosopher, but not a very good Christian. By calling all legislators "sons of God," he grants them the unique privilege of Christ. By attaching angels to the celestial spheres <note>The idea that angels are merely the "movers" or souls of the planets.</note>, he seems to deny their specific duty and mission from God to humanity, such as to the Virgin Mother of God, and so on.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;His principal views, however, are found in the introduction to the *Metaphysics* <note>Referring to Aristotle’s work on the nature of reality.</note>, which contains the most hidden secrets of the wise men or magi. In the Persian language, "Magus" is interpreted as "wise man." Knowledge grows through additions, as stated in the first book of the *Metaphysics* and at the end of the second.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Aristotle attributes a certain harmful nature to the nuthatch <note>original: "Sittae"; a small bird</note> in Book 9, Chapter 2. It is noted as the "grey woodpecker" in Gessner’s *History of Birds* <note>Conrad Gessner was a 16th-century Swiss naturalist famous for his encyclopedic zoological works.</note>.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Aristotle's fame does not perish entirely.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Neither unclean spirits nor good spirits—other than those who move the celestial bodies—were admitted by the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy.</note>.

<margin>From Plato.</margin>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Plato used to say that necessity obeys the divine power as a superior nature. He both removed all slanders against philosophy and revealed everything to his listeners as if they were the secrets of nature—that is, he wrote one thing, but understood another, and explained the true meaning only to his disciples.
