[Aristotle] posits God as the first motive of the will; however, he posits that the principle of reason is not reason itself, but something better. <note>Aristotle suggests that the source of rational thought must itself be a higher, divine principle.</note>

The will is moved immediately by God and by the <term>intelligences</term> <note>In the cosmology of the time, 'intelligences' were non-physical beings—often equated with angels—who were thought to guide the movement of the celestial spheres.</note>. Nature acts directed by God and the intelligences, which regulate all these human affairs.

If the soul did not exist in itself before it was in the body, it would not naturally exist without the body.

<margin>Pomponazzi admits.</margin>
The eclipse of Christ <note>The miraculous darkness reported during the Crucifixion.</note> could only have been produced by God alone, because according to the nature described by Aristotle, the heavens cannot rest, nor can an intelligence increase or decrease its own motion.

God is most pure <term>act</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, God is described as 'pure act' (*actus purus*), meaning He is absolute reality without any unfulfilled potential or change.</note>.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>

### *Addition from other books of Theophrastus Paracelsus on Insanity or Frenzy.*

A small German book by Paracelsus on insanity fell into my hands, which has been translated into Latin for me. So that this volume on the treatment of diseases—both medical and surgical—lacks nothing, I will also summarize it in a few words. Speculations collected in the head (called "myrmidons") <note>original: "myrmidones." Paracelsus used this term to describe frantic, ant-like mental activities or invasive thoughts that swarm the mind.</note> are contrary to one another; from some of these a struggle arises, and from others, a frantic dance.

Because the loss of reason in these patients is greater than their pain, they do not feel their own suffering.

An ulcer does not truly make a person insane or furious, but it originates from the same cause as <term>rabies</term> <note>Here used in the broader sense of "madness" or "rage."</note>.

Seven types of mania flow from the element of fire. The boiling of water is the insanity itself, caused by fire; therefore, the fire must be removed so that the boiling ceases.

The cause [of madness] should be attributed to celestial influence <note>The influence of the stars and planets.</note> rather than to the <term>melancholic humor</term> <note>One of the four "humors" of traditional medicine; an excess of black bile was thought to cause depression or madness.</note>.

Wolf’s grains <note>original: "Lupi grana." For just as wine deprives a person of reason, so also these foodstuffs affect them with this disease, which are very [numerous]...

## ON COLIC.

->The causes of colic in man are winds,<-
->just as they are in the <term>greater world</term>.<- <note>The "greater world" or Macrocosm refers to the universe. Paracelsus believed that internal bodily ailments like gas and cramps (colic) were internal "weather patterns" caused by the same forces that create wind in the atmosphere.</note>

There are four types corresponding to the four terminal winds:
* **Colic** related to <term>Eurus</term> <note>The East Wind.</note>:
    * hot
    * dry.
* **Twisting of the <term>cecum</term>** <note>original: "monoculi." Literally the "one-eyed" intestine, referring to the cecum or the beginning of the large bowel.</note> related to <term>Zephyrus</term> <note>The West Wind.</note>:
    * moist
    * cold.
* **Twisting of the navel** related to <term>Auster</term> <note>The South Wind.</note>:
    * moist
    * hot.
* **Affliction of the back** related to <term>Boreas</term> <note>The North Wind.</note>:
    * cold
    * dry.

The cure is derived from:
* <term>Segterna</term> <note>A Paracelsian term likely referring to a specific herbal preparation, possibly Tansy or a related bitter herb used to break "internal winds."</note>
* <term>Sibeta</term> <note>Civet, a musk-like substance obtained from the civet cat, used in historical medicine for its warming and aromatic properties.</note>
* <term>Reinfal</term> <note>Commonly identified as Tansy (*Tanacetum vulgare*), a herb used to treat intestinal parasites and digestive distress.</note>
* **Opium**.

Namely, the first mode of application:
* In the place where the pain is located, such as with **Sibeta**.
* In the opposite cavity, such as with **Opium**.

## ON PHILIP THEOPHRASTUS PARACELSUS
### Book III of *On Long Life*
### Commentaries.

->*On Chapter III, regarding Gold.*<-

No one is ignorant of the fact that gold is the most excellent matter of the terrestrial element (unless, perhaps, you except gemstones); about which the greatest poet <note>Referring to the Roman poet Virgil.</note> cleverly wrote:

<margin>Aristophanes</margin>
Nevertheless, the Golden Age was named after it, during which time all was happiness in the world. <margin>*Against Ficino regarding stones and metals.*</margin>

<margin>*Electrum.*</margin>
Beyond gold and silver, he rejects the remaining metals in this instance; yet elsewhere (forgetting his own rules), he instructs to fashion an image of a virgin out of tin, and in another place, the archetypal form of the world out of bronze. 

I wonder also that in the same book *On Long Life*, regarding a small stone marked with points like certain stars—such as I wear around my neck, called the **Syrtites** stone by Pliny—even if it seems to be a species of *Asteria* <note>A "star-stone" or sapphire/ruby that displays a star-like light effect (asterism).</note>, Ficino says it has the figure of a celestial dragon. 

<margin>*The Syrtites stone*</margin>
For stars do not bear the scaly appearance attributed to a dragon, nor does a stone which he asserts to be round reflect the bodily form of a dragon, since even the celestial dragon <note>Referring to the constellation *Draco*.</note> entangles both Bears <note>The constellations Ursa Major and Ursa Minor.</note> with its winding coils.

Lest anyone truly think this treatment of gold is useless because it appears so thoroughly "cooked" <note>in alchemical terms, "coctum" or "cooked" means a substance has reached its highest state of natural perfection</note> by nature that it cannot be "made raw" <note>original: "incrudari"; the process of making a substance chemically active or digestible again</note>: let us hear Arnaldus <note>Arnaldus de Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a celebrated physician and alchemist</note> in the sixty-eighth chapter of his *Mirror of Medicinal Introductions* concerning milk and seed. For he says that milk is so "cooked" in the breasts that its watery nature is abundantly retained in the substance of the milk in such a measure that, passing into the stomach of the infant and reaching further into its liver, it undergoes transformations that separate the wateriness. Thus it emerges unharmed, and through a wonderful circulation of nature, it happens that the blood—which previously nourished the infant in the womb through the umbilical cord—passing through the organs of milk and being wonderfully "made raw" <note>original: "incrudatus"</note> by their action, is poured into the stomach of the newborn. Finally, being altered and proceeding to the chamber of the liver, it returns to itself <note>meaning it turns back into blood to nourish the child</note>. In this way, he most clearly reveals the whole mastery of alchemy to the "children of truth" <note>a traditional term for sincere seekers of alchemical knowledge</note>, and furthermore rebukes those students of presumption who claim absolutely that what is "cooked" cannot be "made raw."

<margin>Leo Suavius <note>The pen name of Jacques Gohory (1520–1576), a French physician and alchemist known for his commentaries on Paracelsus.</note></margin>

<margin>Against Pliny</margin>
Pliny falsely believed that gold was surpassed by lead in weight, as is proven by the daily experience of goldsmiths in making gold rings, where the mold is first cast in lead. <note>In antiquity and the Renaissance, lead was often thought to be heavier than gold due to its density in hand, but gold is significantly denser.</note> [He also thought gold yielded to lead] in the ease of the material: this must be understood either in terms of melting (in which case we should read "fusibility," yet even straw catches fire more quickly than it takes to melt lead) or in terms of ductility under the hammer—yet no metal is spread more widely or divided into more parts than gold. It should shame Hermolaus Barbarus <note>Hermolaus Barbarus (1454–1493) was an Italian humanist scholar famous for his 'Castigationes Plinianae', a massive work correcting errors in Pliny’s encyclopedia.</note> and the other interpreters of Pliny that, in this history of the natural world, they devoted their labor almost exclusively to the explanation of words rather than the nature of things.

### On Chapter 9, Concerning the Spirit of Wine.

<margin>
Marsilio Ficino on burning water.
</margin>
Enormous errors have flowed forth regarding the spirit of wine <term>spirit of wine: An early term for distilled alcohol (ethanol), which was seen as a powerful solvent and "life essence."</term>, celebrated so much by Jean de Roquetaillade <note>original: *Ioanne Rupescissa*—a 14th-century Franciscan alchemist who pioneered the medicinal use of distilled spirits.</note> and then by Ramon Llull, his ape-like imitator. "Take," he says, "red or white wine." Only Paracelsus clearly demonstrates that one should not drain whole vats in this business of philosophizing. Regarding the "fatness" <note>likely referring to the oily residue or the "essential oil" thought to be contained within the wine.</note> which he says rises, note that it rises just as air rises into its own sphere. For Marsilio Ficino rightly judged that "burning water" <note>original: *aqua ardens*—the Latin term for alcohol because of its ability to catch fire.</note>, which is ignited by fire, is of an airy nature, not a fiery one as the common crowd of physicians believes; for air is the nourishment of fire. However, Augurellus elegantly refutes the error of using wine for the dissolution of metals, explaining the enigma of Ramon Llull.

<margin>In response to Adrianus Turnebus on the differences of wine.</margin>

The dispute is as follows: he seems to compare “vat wine” <term>vat wine: *vinum doliare*, wine stored in large storage jars called *dolia*.</term> not ineptly with “drawn-off wine” <term>drawn-off wine: *vinum diffusum*, wine that has been transferred from large storage vats into smaller jars or bottles.</term>, but it can nonetheless be said—in distinction to “hanging wine” <term>hanging wine: *vinum pendens*, a legal and agricultural term for a grape crop still on the vine, often sold before harvest.</term> (as may be observed in Cato’s *On Agriculture*, according to the subject matter at hand)—that it is certain that “vat wine” signifies nothing other than wine stored in large jars. Thus, Turnebus should not rashly rebuke the interpreters of the law. Indeed, the force of the word relates to the jar (*dolium*) and, depending on the occasion, refers now to “hanging wine,” and now to wine already “drawn off” from the jars. He rightly followed Lambinus, 
<margin>Dionysius Lambinus. Horace.</margin>
that most learned man and commentator on Horace.

->### COMMENTARIES.<-

Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, or Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), author of the *Natural History*.</note> says of this: At the rising of the Dog Star <note>original: *Sub canis ortum*. The rising of the star Sirius in summer, traditionally associated with "dog days" and the spoiling of food.</note>, certain wines change, and later return to their former state. However, this change in wine is for the worse—specifically into a certain sourness—so that we might also call "changed" what the Jurist <note>The "Jurist" likely refers to a specific authority in Roman Law, such as Ulpian or Gaius, often cited in the *Digest*.</note> has termed "acid wine." Regarding the Jurist’s opinion, a dispute once arose between me and the Bishop of Montpellier <note>original: *præfule Montispefulani*. Montpellier was a major center for both medicine and law.</note>, who was then a guest of my father. He did not fully grasp the intent of the law, which decrees that a sale should be rescinded if vinegar is delivered under the name of wine sold, and that the buyer is not bound to accept it. The reasoning for this is plausible: that the **essence** <note>original: *ουσίαν* (*ousia*)</note> of wine and vinegar is not the same.

<margin>*Pliny on vinegar.*</margin>
For this reason, Pliny called vinegar the "viciousness of wine," <note>original: *nequitiam vini*—referring to wine that has "gone bad" or lost its virtue.</note> without which a more refined life could not be led. However, "acid wine" cannot be returned <term>returned: *redhiberi*, a legal term (redhibition) referring to the right of a buyer to return a defective product and cancel the sale.</term> because it is still wine, even if the flavor has changed slightly. We could express these two terms in our French language as *vinegar* and *sour-wine*, just as in the law of the forests the same distinction is made between "lying wood" and "standing wood," or *dead wood* and *worthless wood*. <note>original: *bois mort* (fallen/dead wood) and *mort bois* (scrub or non-timber wood of little value).</note>

<margin>*The experiment of distillation.*</margin>
I will add an undeniable experiment of my own concerning the power and nature of wine, which is not entirely extinguished in "acid wine." From such wine, I extracted a subtle liquor through distillation (which the common people call **burning water**, or **water of life**) <note>original: *aquã ardentem, seu aquam vitæ*—referring to concentrated ethanol or brandy.</note>, whereas not even a single drop of it can be drawn from vinegar. For this reason, Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a polymath and theologian who wrote extensively on alchemy and natural philosophy.</note> called vinegar "dead wine." On this point, another question remains for me with him and the Distinguished Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity.</note>. For if the power of wine were utterly dead in vinegar, from where would that sharpness and dissolving power <note>original: *vis dissolutrix*—the solvent properties of acetic acid.</note> arise, which contains a fiery faculty? Albertus says this is in vinegar...

But I, based on the opinion of the ancient physicians brought forward by Galen in his book *On Simples* <note>original: *De Simplicibus*. Galen (129–c. 216 AD) was the foundational authority on medicine for the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note> (though he himself did not approve of it), believe it proceeds from a corruption by which wine is converted into vinegar, and its entire **fifth essence** <note>Also known as the quintessence; the purest, most potent part of a substance beyond the four physical elements.</note> has evaporated. This is seen in edible birds and fish: if they are stored longer than is proper, they acquire a sharpness harmful to the tongue and palate. Therefore, wine that is "changed" or "sour" will be understood according to the dialecticians <note>Logicians who follow the Aristotelian method.</note> in the category of **quality**, not of the **substance** itself, which receives the name of "alteration" from them. They understand this to refer to some **quicksilver of the philosophers** <note>Philosophical mercury, a symbolic substance in alchemy, not literal liquid metal.</note>: which is "white" for the white work, and "red" for the red stone <note>The "white work" and "red stone" refer to stages in creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note>. ### SCHOLIA <note>Latin for "scholarly notes" or "commentaries."</note>

*Greece admires the Elysian fields.* <margin>Virgil</margin> <note>original: *Elyfios miratur Græcia campos.* A quotation from the Roman poet Virgil regarding the dwelling place of the blessed in the afterlife.</note>
It is as if the **Elixir** <margin>The Elixir?</margin> should be named for the happiness of life which it promises; whereas the **Elysian** fields are rather named <gloss>from the dissolution</gloss> <note>original Greek: *ἀπὸ τῆς λύσεως* (apo tēs lyseōs). The author is drawing a linguistic connection between the Greek word for "release" or "dissolution" (death) and the alchemist's "Elixir."</note>, that is, from the dissolution of the body, through which people migrate into the pleasant assemblies of the pious. Against this very dissolution, Paracelsus <note>The famous Swiss-German physician and alchemist (1493–1541) who argued that chemistry should be used to create medicines.</note> prepares the remedy of the **Elixir** in his first book.

<margin>Gennesaret.</margin>
Thus, Grammarians judge it ridiculous in the word **Gennesaret** and similar terms to seek a Greek etymology—as if it meant "generating a breeze"—for a Hebrew word. Rather, if we derive **Elixir** from the Greeks, let us understand it as coming from the "solution" <note>Here referring to the chemical process of dissolving a solid into a liquid to extract its essence.</note> of things, specifically those that are most temperate and in a way incorruptible. If we take **Elixir** from the
<margin>Nonius Marcellus.</margin>
Latins (for whom *lixa* means water), let us accept **elixum** as "boiled in water," coming from the boiling or decoction of those substances—namely **potable gold**, **liquid pearls**, and so on. These are reduced to a liquid and offered to a person for their restoration and refreshment. From these is made a so-called **Electuary** <note>A medicinal paste or syrup, often used as a vehicle for potent drugs.</note>, which serves as a fortifying mineral source of all virtues.

For the dilemma of that man <margin>Cardan's Dilemma.</margin> <note>Referring to Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), a prominent Italian physician and mathematician whose theories Suavius frequently disputes.</note> is crippled and futile: he argues that such a drink is useless if the matter is not "corrupted" <note>In this context, "corrupted" means broken down or digested by the body.</note> because it would not be conquered by the stomach; and yet, he claims whatever has been corrupted is harmful. Whichever side of his dilemma I choose, it does not work against me. There is a "third thing" which he himself does not notice: a certain "corruption" that takes place while the **essential form** is preserved. The books of the
<margin>Spagyrists.</margin>
**Spagyrists** <note>Alchemists who practiced the "spagyric" art—the separation and recombination of natural substances to create purer medicines.</note> are full of this concept. Therefore, if your logic held, Cardano, no food would be useful to man, because it must necessarily be "corrupted" to be turned into nourishment. Indeed, the **Elixir** which he prescribes from the circulation of **burning water** <note>original: *aquae ardentis*. An early term for distilled alcohol or ethanol, used here as a solvent or base for medicines.</note>...

<margin>Concerning the odor of the Cardanic Ether.</margin>
...concocted. <note>Continuing from the previous page, completing the Latin word *concoctae* or *elixatae*.</note> Regarding the Ether, following Jean de Roquetaillade <note>John of Rupescissa (c. 1310–1366), a Franciscan alchemist who pioneered the concept of the *Quinta Essentia* as a medicine.</note> and Lull <note>Ramon Lull (c. 1232–1316), a philosopher to whom many alchemical works were later attributed.</note> ignorantly, he <note>Referring to Girolamo Cardano, whom Suavius is critiquing.</note> wishes it to be understood in its simplest sense, whereas those authors infuse other substances specific to various diseases into that **Fifth Essence** <term>Quinta essentia: the "fifth element" or pure spirit extracted from matter, believed to hold universal healing powers.</term> of theirs, in which the powers themselves shed their bodily form. "The taste of the ether is somewhat sharp—he meant to say 'sub-acid,' as he often does elsewhere—and somewhat sweet; its color is like clear water, but the odor, unless I have forgotten (which is surprising), is almost like violets." And elsewhere: "The true **Elixir** is the color of wine, with an odor that is indeed sharp and powerful."

<margin>The mysteries of Bacchus.</margin>
However, I am not permitted to pursue the madness of that man any longer here, lest I exceed the limits of this short commentary. Therefore, I shall make an end here by way of the "trietheric" <note>Referring to three levels of the celestial or chemical spirit.</note> mysteries of **Bacchus**, which are not poetic, as you might expect, but philosophical.

<margin>Zoroaster.</margin>
On the 11th aphorism of Zoroaster <note>The legendary ancient Persian prophet, considered by Renaissance thinkers to be a primary source of ancient mystical wisdom.</note> concerning the double intoxication of Bacchus and Silenus <note>In mythology, the elderly, wise tutor of Bacchus; here used as an allegory for different states of spiritual or chemical "drunkenness."</note>; that is, from the **Kabbalah** <note>The Jewish mystical tradition, which Renaissance alchemists often linked to Greek and Persian philosophy.</note> concerning the "double wine."
Also: He who approaches Apollo <note>The god of light and order, often representing the Sun or the completion of the alchemical work.</note> will mediate the work through the **Trietheric Bacchus** and will complete it through the **ineffable name** <note>A reference to the Tetragrammaton, the sacred four-letter name of God in Hebrew, often used in ritual magic and alchemy.</note>.
No one shall be intoxicated by any Bacchus who has not first been joined to his own Muse. He who has perfectly returned into the soul will have made his own form equal to the primary form.
He who attempts the work of this conclusion will approach the "third Jupiter" <note>Likely referring to a specific planetary or elemental stage of the alchemical process.</note> as one living, not merely as one giving life.

## On Chapter III regarding Gold, and Chapter IV regarding Pearls, treated together.

<margin>
Roger Bacon.

I understand "pearls" allegorically to mean the **stone of the moon** <note>original: *lapide lunae*. In alchemical symbolism, the Moon represents Silver, while the Sun represents Gold.</note> (just as Roger Bacon called the "union" <note>original: *unionem*; a large, single pearl, often used as a metaphor for a unique alchemical substance.</note> in his book *On the Marvellous Power of Art and Nature*, and Arnaldus de Villa Nova in that short work which begins, *The most glorious pearl*). The reason for this interpretation is that after the chapter on gold, there ought to follow the chapter on silver, for nothing is more closely related to gold than silver, according to Geber <note>An 8th-century Islamic polymath, known in the West as Geber, considered the father of chemistry.</note> in the chapter on cupellation <term>cineritio: the process of refining precious metals by heating them in a "cupel" or dish made of bone-ash.</term>.

*When its elements are brought back into a balanced temperament, the **Fifth Essence** truly exists without the loss of its forms.*

It remains for us to understand whether he means it is reduced *along with* gold, as Arnaldus says in the *Great Rosary*, or if it is reduced in the *same way* as gold—that is, prepared by a similar method—as Raymond <note>Ramon Lull (c. 1232–1316).</note> says in *Natural Magic*.

*Without loss.* This is how the **Spagyrists** <term>spagyri: alchemists who practiced the "spagyric" art of separating, purifying, and recombining materials to create potent medicines.</term> speak of their ferment, which is not brought so far by the mastery <note>original: *magisterium*; the technical process or "great work" of the alchemist.</note> that it falls away from its balanced temperament; therefore he adds:

*Furthermore, if according to the prescription,*

<margin>Arnaldus.</margin>
That is, if you wish to transmute pearls into the **Fifth Essence**—which is the **white sulfur of nature** <note>A technical term for the fixed, solar principle within silver.</note>—according to the logic of the Fifth Essence (the word "gold" is missing here) and according to the rules of the art: proceed, and change nothing except the "principle," that is, the dissolving liquid. For the substance that is the first material in preparing the Fifth Essence of the **Sun** <note>Gold.</note> ought to be the last material applied in preparing the Fifth Essence of the **Moon** <note>Silver.</note>. For I believe, based on Arnaldus’s paraphrase of the *Rosary*, regarding calcined water...

[...calcin]ative <note>The text begins mid-word, continuing *calcinativam* from the previous page.</note> power of the sun is stronger than the calcinative water of the moon, which is later applied to the moon to bring about its dissolution. [I] give in the *Codicil of Corrosion*: because the **menstruum** <term>menstruum: a specialized solvent used in alchemy to dissolve solids into their primary essence.</term> which you now receive is broken down <note>original: "confractum". That is, it preserves [the body] joined to itself and renders it free from all sickness, nor allows it to be corrupted—that is, so that it is no longer subject to the **sulfurous infections** that infect and corrupt metals. # S C H O L I A .

[It] will be the common **spagyric practice** <term>spagyric: alchemical methods involving the separation of a substance into its elemental parts and then recombining them in a purified state.</term>, that is, the joining of the spirit with its own body, with which it cannot help but agree harmoniously, being as one with itself. Lastly, you will observe concerning the **elixir** <term>elixir: the perfected substance capable of transmuting metals and curing diseases.</term>: to whatever the elixir is applied, it transmutes it in such a way that it remains fixed hereafter, in a manner no different than itself.

This is the **final projection** <term>projection: the final step in the alchemical process, where a small amount of the Elixir is cast upon a base metal to transmute it into gold or silver.</term> by which the metal being transmuted becomes **fixed** <note>In alchemy, "fixed" substances are stable and resistant to heat, unlike "volatile" substances that evaporate or change under fire.</note> just like the substance by which it was perfected.

Now, to return to the completion of the chapter on pearls:

> *The higher transmutation not only... etc.*

Which has already been explained.

> *But also those things which are strong and robust,*

That is, the **perfect bodies** <note>Alchemists classified gold and silver as "perfect" metals because they do not rust or corrode, while others like lead or iron were "imperfect" or "sick."</note> which he calls "firm" in Book 2.

> *Conserves [them] in the same vigor,*

That is, in that transmutation, the species, form, and virtue of gold is preserved, even though **Raymond** <note>Raymond Lully (c. 1232–1315), a philosopher and polymath to whom many alchemical works were attributed.</note> says it may deviate from its temperament.

> *Hence it happens that pearls are valued more than the remaining seeds*

That is, the **mercury of the moon** <note>original: "hydrargiron lune". In alchemical code, the "moon" (Luna) refers to silver. The mercury of the moon is a refined essence of silver.</note> is more excellent than common quicksilver, or the "seed" of a base solvent material; and it is rightly valued more because that seed also restores health. He therefore established this "healthy life" in the preface of this third book as the foundation of **long life**, that is, of the **Great Work** <term>Great Work: (Latin: *Opus Magnum*) the entire alchemical process of creating the Philosopher's Stone or Elixir.</term>, which takes a very long time compared to "particular" or minor works.

> *Among which I say those of oysters are by far the most excellent.*

I read [this as]: "of oysters," that is, of the moon (silver), which is splendid.

## On the Phoenix and the Basilisk, to incidentally untangle the difficulties of Plutarch and Hesiod, from Pliny and from the books of Albertus Magnus *On Animals*.

<margin>Pliny says these things.</margin>
Regarding the Phoenix of Arabia, I do not know if its story is a fable: there is only one in the whole world and it is not often seen. It is reported to be the size of an eagle, with a golden luster around its neck, while the rest of its body is purple; its blue tail is distinguished by rosy feathers, and its face and head are adorned with a feathered crest. Manilius <note>Marcus Manilius (1st century AD), a Roman author known for his poem *Astronomica*.</note> is the authority for the claim that no one has ever seen it feeding. He says it is sacred to the Sun <note>original: "Soli"; in alchemy and ancient mythology, the Sun and the Phoenix are inextricably linked as symbols of rebirth and gold.</note> in Arabia and lives for six hundred and sixty years. When it grows old, it builds a nest from twigs of cinnamon and frankincense, fills it with perfumes, and dies upon it. From its bones and marrow, a sort of small worm is first born, which then becomes a chick, and so on. Therefore, to wipe away the "sweat" of **Plutarch** <note>Plutarch (c. 46–120 AD) was a Greek philosopher. Suavius uses "sweat" (original: "sudorem") metaphorically to refer to the difficult labor Plutarch spent calculating the Phoenix’s incredibly long lifespan.</note> more carefully than in our short compendium regarding that immense calculation of the Phoenix's years—and so that we do not rashly accuse **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), author of the *Natural History*, a primary source for medieval and Renaissance lore about animals.</note> of being untrustworthy regarding this unique bird—I will bring forth the reasoning for that mystery from **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and polymath who wrote extensively on the natural sciences.</note>, since I hear that his books are rare today and very difficult to find.

<margin>Albertus says these things.</margin>
<margin>Description of the Phoenix.</margin>
Those who investigate theological mysteries rather than natural ones write that the Phoenix is a bird of Arabia in the Eastern regions. They say it is the only one of its species and lives a solitary life for 340 years. They say it is the size of an eagle, with the head of a peacock, a purple body with a golden glow, and a long tail marked with certain rosy feathers, just as the tail [of a peacock] is marked...

And when it feels itself burdened by age, it builds a nest in a tall and secluded tree situated above a clear spring, made of frankincense and myrrh and cinnamon and other precious spices, and it collapses into the nest, and exposes itself to the burning rays of the sun, and multiplies them with the brightness of its feathers until a fire is drawn out: and so it burns itself along with the nest and is reduced to ashes. On the second day, they say a worm is born in the ashes, which, having taken up wings on the third day, is transformed within a few days into a bird of its former shape, and then it flies away. They also report that this once happened in Heliopolis <note>original: "Helyopoli"; the "City of the Sun" in ancient Egypt, a center of solar worship.</note>, a city of Egypt, where this bird, carrying spices, burned itself upon a stack of sacrificial wood, and in the sight of the priest—in the manner previously described—it was formed through two generations of worm and bird, and flew away. These things, as **Plato** says, should not be dismissed as false by us when they are reported as written in the books of the sacred shrines. To these I will add, from the poet **Martial**, an estimation of the Phoenix's riches:

->Whatever the unique bird keeps in its nests.<- <note>A line from Martial's *Epigrams* (6.55.2), referring to the aromatic wealth of the Phoenix's nest.</note>

## ON THE BASILISK.

<margin>Albertus.</margin> <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and polymath whose work *On Animals* is a primary source here.</note>
The Basilisk is a serpent which, according to the Latin interpretation, is called a "little king" <term>regulus: Latin for "little king," a direct translation of the Greek "basiliskos."</term>: which the same word sounds as "Basilisk" in Greek. Moreover, the reason for the name is twofold: one indeed because it is seen to have a crowned head; for it has an appendage upon its head spotted with white and hyacinth-blue...

[in] color, it appears crowned with a royal diadem as if by certain gems shining through. Now, the length of this serpent is two palms <note>A "palm" (*palmus*) was a traditional unit of measurement based on the width of the hand, roughly 3 to 4 inches.</note>, its head is very sharp, its eyes are red, and its color shifts from black toward an ashen gray. Its breath scorches everything it travels over, so that in the circuit around its cavern, nothing grows at all; for it dries up trees, herbs, and shrubs, splits stones, and poisons the air. Consequently, if ever a bird flies over the place where it stays, it immediately falls dead; the same is true for other beasts and other serpents, except only for the **Armene** <note>original: "Armene"; likely referring to the ermine or weasel, which was famously believed in medieval bestiaries to be the only animal capable of killing a basilisk.</note>, which is joined to the Basilisk with great ferocity.

The Basilisk also kills with its hiss, provided it projects it, because the hiss is carried along with its breath <note>original: "spiritu"; here meaning the physical air or "vital spirit" expelled from the lungs.</note>; and the hiss kills at least as far as it is propagated with that breath. In that space where the simple quality of the sound extends without the breath, I do not believe the Basilisk kills. Furthermore, it kills by sight: for everything upon which its gaze falls dies. 

As for what **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), the Roman author of the *Natural History*.</note> and certain others say—that the Basilisk does not kill a man unless it sees the man before it is seen by him, and that the sight of a man will kill the Basilisk if he sees it first—I do not believe this to be true, because it lacks reason. Neither **Avicenna** <note>The Latinized name for Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the influential Persian physician and philosopher.</note> nor **Semeryon** the philosophers <note>Likely a reference to a medieval authority or a corruption of a name like Hermes or Senior Zadith.</note>, who speak from experience, report this. Nor is this the cause by which it kills by sight, which they indeed say is because rays emerging from the eyes...

[the rays of] its eyes corrupt those things upon which they fall. Furthermore, if another person approaches that dead body, they also die; and if the serpent is touched with a long spear or a rod, the person holding that rod dies. Indeed, this once happened to a certain soldier who struck it with a spear; his horse also died when he accidentally touched the horse's leg with that same spear. This serpent multiplies in the land of **Achobor** <note>Likely a reference to a region in North Africa or the Levant, often associated in medieval texts with venomous creatures.</note> and in **Nubia**. The serpent strikes the weasel, but the weasel kills it, and this is true. This is seen as a marvel. They also say that wherever the ashes of a Basilisk have been scattered, spiders will not build nests there, nor do other venomous creatures appear; for this reason, its ashes were anciently scattered in temples.

<margin>Hermes.</margin> **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with alchemy and secret wisdom.</note> also says that silver smeared with the Basilisk's ash takes on the splendor, weight, and solidity of gold. Some also say that there is a certain kind of Basilisk that flies, but I have not read of this in the books of the wise philosophers.

...philosophers. Some even say that it is generated from the egg of a rooster, but this is most certainly false and impossible. And when Hermes <note>Refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> teaches that the Basilisk is generated in the womb, he does not mean a true Basilisk, but the <term>alchemical Elixir</term> <note>original: "Elixir alchimico"; a substance sought by alchemists to transmute base metals into gold or to prolong life.</note>, by which metals are converted.

As for what they say—that a decrepit rooster generates an egg from itself and places it in dung, and that this egg lacks a shell but has a skin so hard that it resists the strongest blows, and that this egg is fertilized by the heat of the dung into a Basilisk, which is a serpent, in all ways like a rooster but with a long serpent’s tail—I do not believe this to be true. Nevertheless, it is a saying of Hermes, and accepted by many because of the authority of the speaker.

<margin>The Pyradum</margin> The **Pyradum** <note>Also known as the Tarandus, often identified in medieval bestiaries as a creature like a reindeer that could change its color like a chameleon.</note> is an animal having the size of an ox, with branched horns like a stag, and having the tracks of a pig or swine. It has a coat of shaggy and thick hairs; they say this animal changes its color when in fear to match the likeness of bodies placed near it. Therefore, when hiding among white stones it becomes white, and while lurking among thickets it becomes green. In this quality, as Hermes says, it agrees with the Basilisk, and because of this kind of change, it sometimes escapes the hunter.

I have taken all these things word-for-word from **Albert**, who was truly **Great** <note>original: "Alberto verè Magno"; a play on the name of Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a dominant figure in medieval science and philosophy.</note>, (lest I be rashly likened to those who are barbaric), and I did so intentionally, lest I be suspected by anyone of corrupting the meaning in a matter of such importance and weight, rather than merely changing the language.

# EXPLANATION
## *of the mysteries.*

<margin>Celestial nature is a supernatural body.</margin>
From these mysteries, I shall conclude that the same entity is presented in parables as the **Phoenix**, the **Basilisk**, **Glaura**, the **Mandrake**, and the **Chameleon**. Regarding this, **Roger Bacon** <note>original: "R. Bacho"; Roger Bacon (c. 1214–1292) was a medieval English philosopher and friar often credited with alchemical secrets.</note> writes: "Take one, which is the secret of the secrets of nature, revealing wonders," etc. Where, a little later, he says: "The celestial nature is weakened," etc., which is that <term>supernatural body</term> <note>In alchemy, this refers to the *quinta essentia* or "fifth essence," a substance that transcends the four physical elements.</note> of which **Paracelsus** <note>Theophrastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), the famous Swiss physician and alchemist.</note> writes in his first book. Thus **Proclus** <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> says: "The Aeon [Eternity] is by itself a living being in the second and middle trinity." (I would understand this second and third trinity to be the same.) Thus also says **Augurellus** <note>Giovanni Aurelio Augurello, whose poem *Chrysopoeia* allegorizes the making of gold.</note>:

*It shall lead at last one work and one thing with it.*

With which **Jean Valentinois** <note>original: "Ioan. Valentianus"; likely Jean de la Fontaine, known as Valentinois, a 13th-century alchemical poet.</note> agrees in *The Strength of Love*. Thus he writes concerning the age of the thing:

*When the seed now completes its own cycles of time.* <note>original: "æui iam compleat orbes"</note>

For what remains in **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, the Roman naturalist whose *Natural History* was the standard reference for the Phoenix legend.</note> regarding the Phoenix:
„ And in the beginning, it pays the due funeral rites to its predecessor and 
„ carries the entire nest to the City of the Sun near Panchaia, 
„ and deposits it there upon the altar. With the life of this bird, 
„ a Great Year <note>A "Great Year" (Magnus Annus) is a vast astronomical cycle after which the planets return to their original positions.</note> is completed, and the indications of the seasons 
„ and the stars return once more to the same point. This, however, 
„ begins around noon on the day when the Sun has entered 
„ the sign of Aries [the Ram].

These things are, as the same Pliny truly says, handed down as fables: lest anyone by chance should understand them falsely, but rather as a fable.

He draws on sources ranging from Roger Bacon to Pliny the Elder to link these symbols to the timing of astronomical cycles.</summary>

<margin>Manilius.</margin>
...handed down by **Manilius** <note>Marcus Manilius (1st century AD), author of the *Astronomica*, the earliest systematic treatise on astrology.</note>, that first and most diligent of the Romans, a senator noble in the greatest teachings who had no [human] teacher. For a falsehood is one thing,
<margin>How a fable differs from a falsehood.</margin>
which posits a thing that truly does not exist; a **fable** is another thing, which according to **Aristotle** covers and veils the truth of a matter, being indeed a truthful sentiment but false in its literal writing. Therefore he said in Book VII: *And the rest more fabulously in the Phoenix and the Nymphs.* Therefore, always understand the <term>earthly Sun</term> <note>original: "Solem terrestrem"; in alchemy, this refers to gold or the "sulfur" of the philosophers, which acts as the sun within the experimental work.</note> here in this fable: take the years to be as they are for the Arabian bird [the Phoenix]—Arabian years, which is to say, days. Understand the "Conversion" according to **Arnaldus** <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note> and **Lull** <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316), the Majorcan philosopher to whom many alchemical works were attributed.</note> as the method of the work derived from the earthly Sun. It is certain in Astronomy and the **Ephemerides** <note>Tables showing the predicted positions of celestial bodies over time.</note> that calculations begin from noon; but as **Trithemius** <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a German abbot, cryptographer, and occultist.</note> writes concerning the East in his
<margin>Trithemius in the Steganographia.</margin>
*Steganographia*, he does not take the East to be where the
<margin>What the East is.</margin>
Sun rises daily, but where it was created at the beginning. Thus the wise Magi of celestial ways judge that observation must be made in the <term>eighth sphere</term> <note>The sphere of the fixed stars, which in traditional cosmology sat above the spheres of the seven planets.</note>, and they warn that those who look to the "new" sphere <note>Likely referring to the contemporary tropical zodiac versus the sidereal zodiac used by the ancients.</note for the effect in forming images and seals are often deceived; a point which **Cornelius Agrippa** <note>Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa (1486–1535), author of *Three Books of Occult Philosophy*.</note> certainly noted. 

<margin>The Sun’s entrance into the signs.</margin>
Thus, in this year 1567, the entrance of the Sun into **Aries** is not to be observed according to the common opinion on the eleventh day of March, at the fourth hour and 39th minute <note>The Julian calendar date of the spring equinox in 1567.</note>, when the moon meets it at 8 degrees and 1 minute of the same sign, at the elevation of the pole at Paris (48 degrees 40 minutes); but rather at the 11th hour of the 27th day of March, at the same time at 1 degree 30 minutes. Regarding this entry of the Sun into Aries, which must be observed in the philosophical work, the same poet sang beautifully:

<margin>Augurellus, Book 3 of the Chrysopoeia.</margin>
> *And if you should desire to hear anything from me,*
> *You shall begin just at the very start of Spring,*
> *When the whole world is in labor...* <note>original: "Ac si me quicquam studeas audire, sub ipsum / Ver adeò incipies, quo totus parturit orbis"; Giovanni Aurelio Augurello's poem *Chrysopoeia* (Gold-making) uses the birth of spring as a metaphor for starting the alchemical process.</note>

### SCHOLIA.

It seems right and orderly for this chapter on **herbs**—that is, vegetable substances—to follow next, according to **Ramon Llull** in his *Vegetable Menstruum* <note>original: "Ray. in mēstruo vegetali"; the "menstruum" is a powerful solvent used in alchemical extraction</note>, by which the things mentioned above are dissolved. Therefore he says: Previously, we made mention of the **Quintessence** <term>Quinta Essentia: The "fifth essence," the purest and most potent spiritual core of a substance, beyond the four elements.</term> which ought to be produced without any extraction; that is, regarding the **ferment of the perfect body** <note>In this context, the "perfect body" usually refers to gold, which serves as a ferment to transform other metals.</note> which is only thinned and refined according to **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), the foundational figure of Arabic alchemy.</note>, or, in the opinion of some, it refers to the body itself, whose substance (which is of a uniform nature) is not separated during the course of the **Mastery** <term>Magisterium: The complete alchemical process of transformation.</term>.

But in the **Herbal Elixir**—that is, herbal and vegetable matter—(just as he said above that gold is the most powerful Elixir), he states that these differ from the "perfect body" because of the diversity of their essences. That is to say, the gold is **Homogeneous** <note>original: "Homogeneum"; composed of parts all of the same kind.</note>, while these vegetable matters are **Heterogeneous** <note>original: "Etherogenea"; composed of different or diverse parts.</note>.

To understand this chapter, one must first recall what was said in Chapter III about gold: If you have understood the nature of gold, you cannot fail to know the nature of other things that are separated from a body. That is, you cannot hold the principle of this gold in the preparation of the ferment or quintessence during the course of the work without knowledge of the **mercuries** <term>hydrargyrorū: literally "water-silver" or quicksilver; the volatile, soulful principle of a substance.</term> extracted from bodies. Regarding these, **Geber**, in his *Book of Investigation*, says: "This is the mercury of mercury, extracted from a spiritual body."

We shall address the rest of those things which are not separated from the body below. When the **treatment of wine** <note>original: "vini tractatio"; referring to the distillation of "spirit of wine" or alcohol, a key solvent in vegetable alchemy.</note> is begun, we shall not forget them. Here, then, he says there is a diversity of substances in herbs; therefore, extraction is necessary to draw out their **Quintessence**. He adds a word of caution: the quintessence must be extracted from herbs in such a way that the "substance" remains, and the herb

*And by which nature reveals itself to the things to be created.* <note>original: "Et quo se rebus aperit natura creandis."</note>

### Ramon Llull in his Testament.

When the matter is entirely confused <note>original: "materia est confusa"; refers to the 'massa confusa' or the initial chaotic state of the alchemical prime matter</note>: then our **Sun** is exalted in the sign of **Aries** <note>The Sun enters Aries in March, marking the spring equinox. In alchemy, this symbolizes the beginning of the "Great Work" when the life-force of nature is most potent.</note>, and there the beginning of our **Mastery** <term>Magisterium: The complete process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</term> must be. For it is the first degree of **sublimation** <term>Sublimation: The process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then solidifies again, used here both physically and as a metaphor for spiritual refinement.</term>, which must be pursued upon the stone. The conversion, however, is described skillfully and cleverly by the same **Arnaldus** <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note> in the "Astrolabic wheel," which I will illustrate for you, if the opportunity is granted. This same "return of the times and the stars" is called by **Augurello** <note>Giovanni Aurelio Augurello (1441–1524), author of the alchemical poem *Chrysopoeia*.</note> himself "the return of Jason to his homeland." Indeed. The author **Manilius** <note>A Roman poet and astrologer.</note> asserts that no one has ever seen the **Phoenix** feeding. Concerning its diet:

### Augurello in the enigmatic *Chrysopoeia*, under the parable of the eggs.

> *The bird fed here and there on leafy herbs*
> *Throughout the sunny fields, where no biting*
> *Winter burns the green crops with ice, nor summer with its suns.*

*And in his lyric poem on the Golden Fleece:*

> *The shepherd, leading him out from the abandoned flock,*
> *Places Alcon in a cave;*
> *And there, diligent, he feeds him alone with*
> *Cut herbs and drawn waters.*

For nourishment is the second and later part of the mystical work. The books of Arnaldus and **Ramon Llull** <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315), a Majorcan philosopher to whom many alchemical texts were attributed.</note> are full of this concept. In the colors of the **Phoenix** and the **Stone**, the similarity is evident.

<header>COMMENTARIES.</header>

It appears correct and orderly that this chapter concerning **herbs**—that is, vegetable matter—should follow, according to **Ramon Llull** <note>original: "Ray. in mēstruo vegetali"; refers to Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315), a Majorcan philosopher and reputed alchemist. The "vegetable menstruum" is a powerful solvent derived from plants, often wine.</note> in his *Vegetable Menstruum*, by which the things mentioned above are dissolved. Therefore he says: "Previously, we made mention of the **Quintessence** <term>Quintessence: The 'fifth essence' or the purest, most concentrated medicinal or spiritual force of a substance, beyond the four elements.</term> which ought to be created without any extraction." This refers to the **ferment of the perfect body** <note>The "perfect body" is gold.</note> which, according to **Geber** <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), the foundational figure of Arabic alchemy.</note>, is merely thinned and refined; or, in the opinion of some, it refers to the body itself, whose substance (which is of a uniform nature) is not separated during the course of the **Mastery** <term>Magisterium: The complete process of the alchemical Great Work.</term>. But in the **Herbal Elixir**—that is, herbal and vegetable matter—(just as he said above that gold is the most potent Elixir), he says there is a *diversity of essences* in these plants, to distinguish them from the perfect body. This means that the former [gold] is **Homogeneous** <note>original: "Homogeneum"; consisting of parts all of the same kind.</note>, while the latter [herbs] are **Heterogeneous** <note>original: "Etherogenea"; consisting of diverse or different constituents.</note>.

To understand this chapter, one must first consider what was said in Chapter 3 regarding gold: *If you have understood the nature of gold, you cannot fail to know the others which are separated from the body.* That is, you cannot grasp the method of this gold in the preparation of the ferment or the quintessence during the progress of the work without a knowledge of the **mercuries** <note>original: "hydrargyrorū"; literally 'water-silver' or quicksilver.</note> extracted from the bodies. Concerning these, **Geber** says in his *Book of Investigation*: "This is the mercury of mercury, extracted from a spiritual body."
We shall not forget the remaining things which are not separated from the body below, where the treatment of **wine** will begin. Here, therefore, he says there is a diversity of substances in herbs; thus, **extraction** is necessary to draw out their quintessence. He adds a caution: that the quintessence should be extracted from the herbs in such a way that the substance remains, and the herb

I establish that this chapter is partly parabolic <note>Written in allegorical or symbolic language.</note> like the preceding ones; that is, it is not only about the human body, but also about the **chaos** <note>In Paracelsian thought, "chaos" often refers to the primordial matter or the atmosphere from which life is sustained.</note>, which I think he called the "physical body." ### ANNOTATIONS.

*He cleanses himself along with the rest which are impure,* <note>original: "Mundat seipsum unà cum reliquis quae immunda sunt"</note>
That is, the liquid is extracted from the substance so that it may be cleansed. And once this "flood" <note>An alchemical metaphor for the distillation process, where the liquid rises as vapor and falls back like rain.</note> is finished, its native or genuine power remains. These remains are called "dregs" <note>original: "faeces"</note> by **Raymond Lull** <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315), a Majorcan philosopher; many alchemical works were pseudonymously attributed to him during the Renaissance.</note> in his *Natural Magic*, or "grape-skins" <note>original: "vinacea," referring to the solid remains after pressing grapes, used here as an analogy for alchemical residue.</note>, in which there is no accidental heat, but a natural or native power, as is described here.

*Therefore, it always directs itself by influence, when its flow or that liquid is returned,* <note>original: "Itaq; sese ex influentia semper dirigit, quando suus fluxus vel liquor ille redditur"</note>
That is, the liquid is brought back again over its foul <term>cohobation</term> <note>The process of repeatedly redistilling a liquid over the solid matter from which it was just extracted to concentrate its medicinal or spiritual "virtue."</note>, so that it may draw that remaining genuine power from the earth. The dregs remain, however, to which the <term>Archeus</term> <note>In Paracelsian thought, the "Archeus" is the internal alchemist or vital force that separates the useful essence of a substance from the waste.</note> finally grants nothing, treating them as impure things from which the pure has been separated. It therefore always directs itself by this flow—that is, it governs itself in different directions—by composing its salt through the extraction of its water (found by earthly or fiery virtue), which is poured at intervals onto the remaining earth.

*Furthermore, if nothing healthy is present at all, it transforms an impure body into a pure one.* <note>original: "Praeterea si nihil sani omnino adest, immundum corpus in mundum transformat."</note>
This refers to "imperfect bodies" <note>In alchemy, metals like lead or tin were considered "imperfect" or "diseased" versions of gold; this passage suggests the medicine can "cure" these metals or the human body.</note> in which nothing healthy exists in actuality or in reality, but they are healthy in potential, and are finally made healthy in actuality. **This is the essence of the preparation.**

<margin>
Mercury of Ore. <note>original: "Ertz Mercury."</note>
</margin>
*Take mineral Antimony, retort it, and distill the retorted liquid, or return it in a twisted cohobation,* <note>original: "R. Stibium minerale retorque, ac retortum liquorem distilla, vel reduc in tortum cohop"</note>
That is, pour it over its black dregs in a third cohobation during distillation through an **alembic** <note>A traditional alchemical still consisting of two vessels and a cooling tube.</note>, where the vessel is triple; and it is received in the third vessel. It is described thus in the German *Book of Surgery* regarding the "Mercury of Ore," <note>original: "Ertz Mercurii."</note> that is, the earth mi- <note>The text breaks off mid-word "mineralis" at the end of the page.</note>

**T**his fourth and final book of Paracelsus on *Long Life*—lest anyone should perhaps falsely add a counterfeit fifth one, as happened with a certain fourth book of **Cornelius Agrippa’s** <note>Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa (1486–1535), a famous magician and occult philosopher. Suavius is warning that just as a fake fourth book was added to Agrippa's "Three Books of Occult Philosophy," readers should be wary of fake additions to Paracelsus.</note> *Occult Philosophy* which was stealthily snatched from the latest works of **Raziel** <note>Refers to the *Sefer Raziel HaMalakh*, a medieval practical Kabbalah grimoire attributed to the angel Raziel.</note>—is by far the most difficult and obscure of this whole work. <header>SCHOLIA.</header>

...the last breath of life, without any sickness, pain, or trouble. Indeed, through medicine devised and prepared by human ingenuity, things that have been weakened can be restored, repaired, and refreshed; this applies to the *quantity* (as physicians say) but not the *quality* of life. Otherwise, we would be establishing a reversal of the ages (as mentioned in **Plato**) <margin>**Plato.**</margin> and paving a way to immortality. For <term>natural death</term> <note>Death caused by the natural exhaustion of the body's radical moisture.</note> can in no way be delayed; <term>accidental death</term> <note>Death caused by disease, injury, or poor lifestyle, which cuts life short before its natural expiration.</note> indeed can be, since it depends on the proportion of the <term>vital heat</term> to the <term>passive moisture</term> <note>The bodily fluids that are acted upon by the heat.</note>, and the power—or lack thereof—to shape that moisture and sufficiently repair the loss for the sake of life. No one but God can have full insight into the limit or span of this duration.

**Nicephorus Blemmidas** <note>A 13th-century Byzantine scholar and monk.</note> published a book of physics stating that a set lifespan is not predetermined for individuals. Similarly, **Petrus Numagen** published another work regarding **Nicolaus Subsylvanus** <note>Also known as Saint Nicholas of Flüe (1417–1487), a Swiss hermit famous for allegedly living for 20 years without eating food.</note>, who lived without food; this confirms **Paracelsus’s** concept of "life in the ether" <note>The idea that life can be sustained by celestial or spiritual forces rather than physical food.</note>. <margin>Life in the ether.</margin> Furthermore, our **Theophrastus** <note>The first name of Paracelsus.</note> <gloss>Theophrastus Paracelsus</gloss> seems to establish this Medicine, which the Arabic philosophers called the **Elixir** <margin>**Elixir.**</margin> in their own language. As I am just now about to approach this subject, my whole mind is shaken by a certain sacred awe (O philosophers!), and a fear like that of one entering the labyrinth of the **Minotaur** strikes me.

### LEO SUAVIUS

<margin>Explanation of the mystery.</margin>
This can be explained as follows: Prepare the *Aniadum* <term>Aniadum: In Paracelsian thought, a celestial or spiritual virtue within a substance that promotes health and longevity.</term>, that is, prepare the perfected thing, and thus acquire it for yourself and make it yours through preparation—specifically through the air alone, that is, through the "broken aerial menstruum" <term>Menstruum: A solvent used in alchemy to dissolve or extract substances; "aerial" suggests a volatile or gaseous state.</term>. Furthermore, *Aniadus* can also be understood as a common virtue, mentioned above: that is, as the "marketable Sun" <note>original: *Sole venali*. This refers to common gold available for purchase, as opposed to the secret "Philosophical Gold" of the alchemists.</note>.

<margin>Arethusa.</margin>
Whence perhaps comes the *Arethusa* of Augurelli <note>Giovanni Aurelio Augurelli (c. 1441–1524) was an Italian poet and alchemist. His poem *Chrysopoeia* often used mythological names like Arethusa to encode alchemical secrets.</note>. It is also said to be the "light of nature," that is, sulfur and alum according to Geber <note>Geber: The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century figure regarded as the father of alchemy.</note>; however, according to Avicenna <note>Avicenna: Ibn Sina, a Persian polymath. Suavius refers to the common alchemical debate over whether the "Stone" can be found easily in nature.</note>, such a thing is not found on earth except for what exists in the Sun and the Moon <note>In alchemical symbolism, the Sun and Moon represent Gold and Silver.</note>. Therefore, along with Paracelsus, it is to be lamented for mortals that it must be sought with such great difficulty within the depths of those bodies.

*Melosine* <note>Melusina: On the previous page, identified as an elemental spirit; here, Suavius links it to the element of air.</note>, or the air, is the sulfur of the Moon, just as *Adech*—derived from Adam with an Arabic suffix—is the red earth or sulfur of the Sun. Pantheus writes most extensively about this in his *Voarchadumia* <note>Giovanni Agostino Panteo's *Voarchadumia contra alchimiam* (1530) was a famous work on "cabala-metallic" secrets.</note>. It can also be called a *Salamandra* because of its fiery nature; hence the philosophers' verse:

> *But the feast dies when the Salamander is the goal.* <note>original Latin: *Sed telon moritur epulum quum sit Salamandra.* This cryptic verse suggests that the alchemical "completion" or feast is achieved through the fiery nature of the Salamander, which consumes or transforms the previous states.</note>

Whatever is not of an aerial nature is removed in this step; this alludes to Bacon <note>Roger Bacon (c. 1214–1292), a medieval philosopher often cited for his experimental approach to alchemy.</note>, but the "stone of air" is placed in a pyramid in a warm location, and so forth. There are therefore three: *Adech*, *Edochinus*, and *Aniadus*, plus a fourth which inclines toward these three; thus *Edochinus* is the *philosophical Mercury*, while the fourth is the *common Mercury*. These four eventually become one. Regarding the concealment or the method of hiding, they agree that it lies hidden under the appearance of "living" [mercury] until the substance thickens; therefore he said that it was hiding—indeed, it is hiding still.

<meta>catchword: Hence</meta>

<summary>Leo Suavius provides an alchemical commentary on Paracelsus's terminology, defining substances like Adech and Melosine as the secret sulfurs of the Sun and Moon. He equates these concepts with the "light of nature" discussed by authorities like Geber and Avicenna.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Leo Suavius’s (Jacques Gohory’s) commentary on Paracelsus's theories of longevity and the "Aniadum." It focuses on the specific alchemical sounds and transformations involved in the creation of a "perfected" substance that extends life.</meta>

### COMMENTARIES

*From this is the birth of that great Aequaster, who was born beyond nature.*

To me, **Aequaster** <term>Aequaster: A Paracelsian term for a being or substance produced through alchemical art rather than natural biological processes; an "artificial" or "equated" star/entity.</term> is a thing crafted by art beyond the powers of nature, which is called by Rhodianus <note>Possibly referring to a follower of the alchemical tradition of the Rhodes school or a specific author like Johannes Rhumelius.</note> "The Equated" <note>original: *Aequatum*</note> from the four natures—that is, either the sulfur of nature, or rather the "absolute stone" <note>The Philosopher's Stone in its final, perfected form.</note>.

*Thus you shall have the longest life,* that is, a life with which—as mentioned above—the [natural] limit of life has nothing in common. For it is, as the **Spagyrists** <term>Spagyrists: Alchemists who follow the Paracelsian method of "separating and recombining" substances to create medicines.</term> say, infinite by way of **multiplication** <term>Multiplication: The alchemical process of increasing the power, quantity, or transmutative virtue of the Philosopher's Stone.</term>, about which he says these words:

*Now, if the same thing has been filled by that which is renewed once again, etc.*

Now, so that the matter remains tranquil, let nothing at all be heard from the bodily substance, and let only the **Aniadum**, then the **Adech**, and finally the **Enochdianum** resound <note>These are Paracelsian terms for spiritual forces: *Aniadum* is the celestial virtue in the body, *Adech* is the "inner man" or archetypal spirit, and *Enochdianum* refers to a state of longevity or celestial existence named after the long-lived biblical figure Enoch.</note>. Some interpret it this way: during **projection** <term>Projection: The final stage of alchemy where the "Stone" is cast upon base metals to transform them into gold.</term>, when the powder is applied, it causes a serpentine hissing to be emitted; then finally the *Aniadum*, etc., "resounds"—that is, it is transformed into a perfect and resonant metal. The mystical books of the Spagyrists mention this sound, as does Augurellus <note>Giovanni Aurelio Augurelli (c. 1441–1524), an Italian poet who wrote the alchemical poem *Chrysopoeia*.</note>:

*By judgment there is also a sound here, dull and not easily caught by the ear.* <note>original: *Iudicio est etiam sonus hinc obtusus & aure Deprehendi haud facilis.*</note>

The author of the *Dangerous Fountain* <note>Referring to *La Fontaine des amoureux de science*, a famous 15th-century alchemical poem.</note> says that a certain melody is produced, which sometimes ceases as if by magic. And elsewhere: "The wonderful sound of an unheard-of little bell strikes my ear." Paracelsus himself in chapter 5 [says]: "and they return to us **anodyne** drums." **Anodyne** <note>original: *anodinica*</note> seem to be those things free from pain. This fourth chapter seems to be about multiplication, which occurs by the addition of the "liquor" or "liquid," which is called the **Horn** <note>original: *Cornu*. Likely referring to the "Cornucopia" or the vessel used for increasing the substance.</note>.

<summary>Suavius explains the alchemical creation of the "Aequaster," a substance born of art that grants infinite life through "multiplication." He describes the mystical sounds—hissing and melodies—that signify the successful transformation of base matter into a spiritualized, "anodyne" state.</summary>

# LEO SUAVIUS

...abundance is what poets call it; here it is the essence itself, which alone is of the greatest value in this place:

*He who treads and he who is trodden upon.* <note>original: *Qui calcat & qui calcatur.* A cryptic reference to the relationship between the active and passive principles in the alchemical vessel.</note>

Therefore, the perfected matter is multiplied by a similar matter, in which the signs are constrained by time; finally, the things remain and persist together. For this reason, Augurellus <note>Giovanni Aurelio Augurello (1441–1524), an Italian humanist and author of the famous alchemical poem *Chrysopoeia*.</note>, in the parable of Glaura, says:

->*The golden Nymph sits.*<-

*The golden bridal chamber shines around and above:*
*Indeed, golden tiles are trodden by the feet of those passing,*
*And the very furniture, cast from gold, gleams.*

Thus, a healthy life is joined in this way to a long life—that is, a purified liquor preserved for renewing the work: which is called the "healthy fountain" by **Johannes Valentinus** <margin>Johannes Valentinus.</margin> <note>Likely referring to the legendary alchemist Basilius Valentinus or a related author in the Paracelsian tradition.</note>.
*As for the place, etc.* The place generates that which is placed within it, and the spirit is said to be the place and the seat of the soul.
*What purpose does it serve to linger on these things in vain, etc.* This is what he said in chapter 2: that we should not labor further in this in vain—namely, in imperfect things in which there is no light, which is to say, <term>digested sulfur of nature</term> <note>original: *sulphur naturæ digestum*; in alchemy, "digestion" refers to the slow ripening of a substance through gentle heat, which matures its inner "sulfur" or spiritual heat.</note>.

> "Furthermore, he who acts with us according to the passion of the mind indicates it, and then deserts us while we are left gaping."
> This seems to be understood as the actions of <term>common mercury</term> <note>original: *Mercurij vulgi*; "vulgar" mercury is ordinary quicksilver, which alchemists believed was useless for the "Great Work" unless it was first transformed into "Philosophic Mercury."</note>, which now approaches and now recedes, leaving us "gaping"—that is, leaving the materials cracked and open due to dryness.

*I set a greater work in motion, philosophers.* <note>A phrase adapted from Virgil’s *Aeneid*, used here to signal a transition to more profound mysteries.</note>

<margin>Chapter 5.</margin> This is chapter 5, to which Paracelsus refers the reader, so that they may not be offended by the previous parables concerning the **Nymphydididic nature** <term>Nymphydidica: A Paracelsian term referring to the spiritual essence of water or the elemental spirits (Nymphs) that inhabit it.</term> and other matters. I shall encompass his meaning in a few words: then the terms for them...

He introduces Chapter 5, which deals with the spiritual essences of the elements, specifically water.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary by Leo Suavius (Jacques Gohory) on Paracelsus. Having previously discussed the spiritual principles of the Aniadum and Adech, Suavius now moves into the specific material classifications of the alchemical process—the "orders" of the work—using terms like Necroli and Scaiolae to describe the progression from raw matter to purified essence.</meta>

### SCHOLIA <note>Scholia are explanatory notes or commentaries on a primary text—in this case, the works of Paracelsus.</note>

I will touch upon these things through my own new and exotic conjecture. The **Necroli** <note>original: *Necrolij siue Necrolici*. In Paracelsian terms, these refer to a specific class of spiritual or material entities associated with the "first order" of alchemical work.</note> mentioned in chapter 4 are excluded from the boundaries of the "long life"—that is, the Great Work <note>The *Magnum Opus*, or the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note>—which is called the "third order" by **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), a foundational figure in alchemy.</note>. 
<margin>The mystical summation of the philosophical work. The Necroli.</margin>
For the raw and black elemental matters, which **Raymond Lull** <note>A major medieval philosopher and alchemist (c. 1232–1315).</note> calls "Blacker than black" <note>original: *Nigrum nigrius nigro*. A classic description of the *nigredo* or blackening phase, symbolizing the death and dissolution of the starting material.</note>, bring about the dissolution of death. 
<margin>The Scaiolæ.</margin>
The **Scaiolæ** <term>Scaiolæ: A Paracelsian term referring to the four elements once they have been separated and purified.</term> seem to be the four elements in a purified state. Within the **Necroli**, that is, the first order of the work, there are "hypermenic" fictions, or sophisticated <note>In an alchemical context, "sophisticated" usually means "adulterated" or "fake"—imitations that look like gold but are not.</note> preparations that do not withstand the judgment of the cupel <note>original: *cineritij*. A cupel is a shallow, porous cup used in assaying to separate precious metals from base metals like lead.</note>.

*Yet they open a window in Cyphantus,* <note>original: *Cyphanto*. This refers to a specific alchemical vessel or a strainer used in the process.</note>

This means they lead toward the formation of our **Embryo** or **Infant** (as **Arnaldus** <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note> and **Lull** call it), which Geber explains in this way: Without the preparations of the first order, the mastery cannot be completed. Those who fix their foot in these early stages and do not progress to the higher orders are called **Allaeani** <term>Allaeani: A term used by Paracelsus for "superficial" alchemists who only change the appearance of metals rather than their true nature.</term> by Paracelsus—that is, superficial changers of forms, such as those who merely whiten copper <note>original: *veneris*. In alchemy, Venus represents copper.</note> or use deceptive tints to make silver <note>original: *lunæ*. Luna (the Moon) represents silver.</note>. Regarding other philosophers, he says:

*Nevertheless, both will remain.*

In the **Scaiolæ**, if we suspect something "sinister" <note>Suavius is playing on the Latin *sinister*, which means "on the left" but also "ill-omened" or "wrong."</note> from the sound of the word, it would agree poorly with **Roger Bacon** on this very argument: *Let the distillation be repeated so that the "right" of the good may receive you sufficiently*—unless we understand "right" <note>original: *dextrum*.</note> as referring to more perfect matter, and "left" <note>original: *sinistrum*.</note> as referring to imperfect bodies. This is similar to how others speak enigmatically of the "Eastern part" and the "Western part."

*The Hydros envies the Scaiolæ, hiding from them the liquor to be drawn out: he who holds the extraction of this is a **Hydromantic**, and he who softens it by fire is a **Pyrotongus**.* <note>These are Greek-derived titles. A Hydromantic (from *hydro*, water) masters the liquid aspect, while a Pyrotongus (from *pyro*, fire) masters the heat.</note>

<summary>This page analyzes Paracelsus's technical terminology for the stages of alchemy, distinguishing between the "first order" (Necroli) and the purified "Scaiolae," while warning against "Allaeani" who perform only superficial chemical changes.</summary>
<keywords>Necroli, Scaiolae, Geber, Raymond Lull, Alchemical orders, Nigredo, Allaeani, Arnaldus de Villa Nova, Roger Bacon, chemical purification</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Leo Suavius’s (Jacques Gohory) commentary on the alchemical "orders" of Paracelsus. Following the discussion of the Necroli and Scaiolæ on page 315, Suavius now critiques those who fail to achieve "fixation" in their chemical work and explains the role of the higher spiritual principles like Adech in the final stages of the Great Work.</meta>

# OF LEO SUAVIUS

He mocks the Sophists <note>In this context, "Sophists" refers to "pseudo-alchemists" or those who possess theoretical knowledge without practical experience or true understanding.</note> who, being endowed with little experience, act in such a way:

> *As the pulsating Necroliæ fall asleep.* <note>original: "Vt Necroliæ indormiscunt pulsatiles." The Necroliæ are spiritual or material entities associated with the first stage of the work.</note>

This means they do not entirely "fix" the tincture <term>Fixation: The process of making a volatile substance stable under heat so it does not evaporate.</term>, which still lives in some manner and flies away from the fire. He uses the phrase "fall asleep," as poppy seed often does, which induces sleep; I understand this to refer to the coagulation of Mercury—sometimes light, sometimes firm—which the Spagyrists <note>Alchemists who follow the Paracelsian method of "separating and recombining" components.</note> call fixation. <margin>Mandrake</margin> Similarly, the **Mandrake** is sleep-inducing, and it was held in high regard among women in the Old Testament <note>A reference to Genesis 30, where Rachel and Leah trade mandrakes to facilitate conception.</note>; thus, it was rightly removed <margin>Master Nostradamus.</margin> from the book of Master Nostradamus <note>Michel de Nostredame (1503–1566), the famous physician and seer, who also wrote on cosmetics and medical preparations.</note> concerning ointments, along with the rest of the potion’s preparation. As he refuses shortly after, it is so that the "fictions" <note>original: *figmenta*. Likely referring to unstable or false chemical results.</note> may be fixed.

> *The Aequaster shall not infringe upon the place of the Scaiolæ.* <note>original: "Scaiolarum locum non infringet Aequaster." *Aequaster* is a Paracelsian term for a spiritual star or influence corresponding to the human constitution.</note>

Perhaps the "Anatic" <note>Related to the *Aniada*, or spiritual life-forces.</note> matter of the perfect work delights in this spiritual seat of the **Scaiolæ** <term>Scaiolæ: In Paracelsian thought, these are the four elements once they have been purified and separated from their coarse material shells.</term> or of the philosophical Mercury. If Gold or Silver <note>original: *Sol vel Luna*.</note> were inserted into these through a crude preparation, something would need to be excepted—that is, a preparation of the matter receiving the "projection" <note>The act of throwing the alchemical powder onto a base metal to transform it.</note> would be necessary, but only in the medicine of the "second order."

> *But the greatest Adech precedes them.* <note>original: "Sed maximus Adech anteuertit." *Adech* is the "inner alchemist" or the spiritual mind that directs the formation of things.</note>

That is, in the medicine of the third order, Mercury, philosophically prepared and circulated, leads the proposed work precisely in all its aspects (according to Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the 8th-century "father" of chemistry.</note>) into the progress of the work. However, this does not apply to the "mode" or method, because in that order there is a difference in the specific method and the subtlety of the preparation. Finally, the Silver <note>original: *Luna*.</note>, having left behind the simple first "Nymphididic" water <note>original: *Nymphididica*. Likely water associated with the Nymphs, or the elemental spirits of water, representing a raw or initial liquid state.</note>, passes through the "water of the Scaiolæ" <note>original: *hydor scaiolarum*.</note> into another transformation, in which it shall remain.

<summary>Suavius critiques inexperienced alchemists for failing to achieve "fixation" and explains the transition from the second to the third order of the alchemical work using Paracelsian concepts like Adech and Scaiolæ.</summary>
<keywords>Fixation, Mercury, Nostradamus, Mandrake, Adech, Scaiolæ, Geber, Alchemical Orders, Gold and Silver</keywords>
