### SCHOLIA

...[the thief would] steal, if the difficult and, as it were, insoluble Sun <note>In alchemy, the "Sun" usually represents Gold or the masculine, fixed principle of the work.</note> should assent: which indeed is death through fixation <term>Fixation: The process of making a volatile substance stable under heat so it does not evaporate.</term>, and life through the illumination of the *scaiolae* <note>Paracelsian terms for spiritual forces or entities that govern certain natural phenomena.</note>. He assents; however, in the first stages, in conjunction with the moon <note>The "Moon" represents Silver or the feminine, volatile principle; their "conjunction" is the union of opposites.</note> he is whitened, but toward the end, he transforms himself, because the King is made red at the completion of the work <note>The transition from the "White Work" (Albedo) to the "Red Work" (Rubedo), the final stage of the Great Work.</note>. These things he discusses at the end of the book regarding "figments," and then concerning *Nymphididica* <note>Likely referring to Paracelsus's teachings on elemental spirits, specifically Nymphs or water spirits.</note>. This is a *hysteron proteron* <note>original Greek: "υστέρον πρότερον," meaning "the last first"—a rhetorical device where the natural order of events is reversed.</note>, using a backwards order of teaching to cast darkness [over the subject]: a thing which the masters of this science frequently do (as Augurello <note>Giovanni Aurelio Augurello (c. 1441–1524), an Italian humanist who wrote the alchemical poem *Chrysopoeia*.</note> testifies).

---

->Devoted to the laws of a complex art.<- <note>original: "Addicti perplexæ legibus artis." A quote from Augurello's poetry regarding the difficulty of alchemy.</note>

*But to return to the Nymphididica. So that it may be conceived in our minds, etc.*

That is, so that this water may attract perfect souls into itself.

*I shall finally conclude this most obscure discussion on the joining of three materials into one through the mysteries of the ancient sages: In vain will he approach Palaemon and Leucothea <note>Sea deities in Greek mythology; here they represent different states or components of the alchemical "Sea" or mercurial water.</note> who has not first attracted Nereus <note>The "Old Man of the Sea," often representing the "First Matter" or the primordial state of the substance.</note>: nor will he attract Nereus, who has not worked concerning the primary animal trinity. Furthermore, he will possess nothing stable in the work who has not attracted Vesta <note>Goddess of the hearth; in alchemy, she represents the central, "fixed" fire or the earth principle.</note>. Then, from Plato, who received it from Diotima <note>The text reads "Diotina," likely an error for Diotima, the priestess who instructs Socrates in Plato's *Symposium*.</note>: that Love was born from the union of Penia and Porus—that is, Poverty and Plenty—in the gardens of Jupiter, during the birth of Venus, while the gods were feasting; Porus himself, she explains, is the son of Counsel.* <note>Suavius is using this famous allegory from Plato’s *Symposium* to explain the alchemical "marriage" or the combination of "void/need" (Penia) and "resource/abundance" (Porus) to create the "Love" (the Philosopher's Stone).</note>

These things concern the ambiguous meaning; now receive the explanation of the writing.

Suavius uses the allegories of sea deities and Plato’s account of the birth of Love to describe the complex attraction and union of alchemical materials.</summary>

### Let this be a conjecture regarding the terms traced back to the Greek language.

*Necroly.* From <note>original Greek: "νεκρὸς"</note> *dead* and <note>original Greek: "ὄλλυμι"</note> *I destroy* or <note>original Greek: "ὅλος"</note> *whole*.

*Scaiolae.* From <note>original Greek: "σκαιὸς"</note> *left-handed* or *wicked* or *obscure* and *I destroy* or *whole*, as above. <note>In the Paracelsian system, these often refer to spiritual forces or "shadows" of things.</note>

*Aniadus.* From <note>original Greek: "ἀνία"</note> *pain* and <note>original Greek: "δίδωμι"</note> *I give*. <note>Aniadus refers to the spiritual fruits of the earth or stars.</note>

*Adech.* From the privative <note>original Greek: "α"</note> <term>Privative alpha: A Greek prefix (a-) that negates the word following it, like "un-" or "non-".</term> and <note>original Greek: "δέχομαι"</note> *I receive*, or from <note>original Greek: "αδην"</note> *much* and <note>original Greek: "ἔχω"</note> *I have*. <note>Adech often signifies the inner "archeus" or invisible director of the body.</note>

*Ilech.* From <note>original Greek: "ἰλη"</note> *a troop* and *I have*.

*Ceduini.* From <note>original Greek: "κῆδος"</note> *care* and <note>original Greek: "οὖρον"</note> *urine* or *wind*.

*Gnathius.* From <note>original Greek: "γνάθος"</note> *jaw*; for the teeth of the dragon sown by Jason <note>Referring to the myth of the Argonauts where Jason sows dragon teeth that turn into warriors.</note> were in the jaw, and the earth is the bony element. Hence to Bacchus: "Take from the bones of Adam." <note>This is a cryptic alchemical instruction linking the biblical "First Man" to the primary material of the work.</note>

*Spagyri.* <term>Spagyric: The alchemical method of "separating and recombining" components to create medicines.</term> From <note>original Greek: "σπάω"</note> *I draw out* and <note>original Greek: "ἄγυρις"</note> *an assembly*.

*Prothoneus* From <note>original Greek: "πυρ"</note> *fire*, <note>original Greek: "ὠθῶ"</note> *I push* and <note>original Greek: "ὄγκος"</note> *swelling*.

*Melosyne.* <note>original Greek: "μελοσύνη"</note> *the sweetness of song*.

---

->OR RATHER.<-

1 *See whether **Iliastes** <note>A Paracelsian term for the prime matter of the universe or the "chaos."</note> is actually **Hiliastes**, from the sun <note>original Greek: "ἀπὸ τοῦ ἡλίου"</note>; as if to say, solar; or **Iliastes** from mud <note>original Greek: "ἀπὸ τῆς ἰλυὸς"</note>. The former is more approved by the words of Paracelsus in chapter 4: "the nature of the sun is from **Iliastes**."*

--- Page 355 ---
<meta>This page continues Leo Suavius’s (Jacques Gohory) commentary on Paracelsus's terminology. On the previous page, Suavius began a list of "conjectures," attempting to find Greek roots for the obscure, often invented, vocabulary used by Paracelsus. This page continues that list, focusing on terms related to life, death, and celestial influences.</meta>

<page-num>317</page-num>
<header>C O M M E N T A R Y.</header>

2 **Aniadin** & **Aniadum**: consider whether it is derived from <note>original Greek: "ἀπὸ τῆς ἀνίας"</note> *from distress* or *sorrow*, and <note>original Greek: "ᾄδης"</note> *Hades* or *the underworld*. This is because it seems, in a way, to bring pain to the inhabitants of the underworld by raising the dead or by liberating them from death. <note>In Paracelsian thought, "Aniadus" refers to the spiritual powers of the stars that influence human life and longevity.</note>

3 **Melosyne**: if it is derived from <note>original Greek: "ἀπὸ τῶν μήλων"</note> *from sheep* (or *apples*), it is nothing other than the method of finding the Golden Fleece. It would be formed in the same way as **Eleemosyne**, which is the method of showing mercy, or the work of **Mnemosyne**, which is the method of recalling or reporting. <note>The "Golden Fleece" was a common alchemical metaphor for the successful creation of the Philosopher's Stone.</note>

4 **Alliani**: perhaps should be read as **Alleani**. That is to say, "changers of forms or substances," from <note>original Greek: "ἀλλοίωσις"</note> *alteration* or *changing*.

7 **Cyphanto**: from <note>original Greek: "κυέω"</note> *to carry in the womb* and <note>original Greek: "φαίνω"</note> *to show* or *appear*; you may relate this to the embryo.

8 **Necrolium**: seems to be the opposite of **Amado**, because it is spoken of as if "killing the whole," from <note>original Greek: "νεκρὸς"</note> *dead* and <note>original Greek: "ὅλος"</note> *whole*.

9 **Scaioli**: that is to say, "entirely sinister" or "completely on the left," from <note>original Greek: "σκαιὸς"</note> *left-handed* or *ill-omened* and <note>original Greek: "ὅλος"</note> *whole*.

**Hypermenica**: that is to say, "things above the moon." For <note>original Greek: "μήνη"</note> is the *moon*, from <note>original Greek: "μὴν μηνὸς"</note> *month*.

**Pyrotonus**: seems to be a corruption for **Pyrotongus**, that is to say, a "Fire-pourer," one who softens metals with fire; hence the reference in <note>Giovanni Aurelio Augurello (c. 1441–1524), an Italian poet and alchemist famous for his poem "Chrysopoeia," which compared alchemy to poetry.</note> **Augurellus**.

Yet, when they infect through the mediation of a vapor, the spirits alone can be infected, alongside the fact that the "mines" [organs] are infected by the mixing of evil vapors with the spirits.

# S C H O L I A.

...the organs <note>original: "membra"</note> according to which they change by their properties; sometimes the organs are changed before the spirit. For a property is sometimes directly opposed to an organ and not to the spirit, and sometimes the reverse: just as some complexioned thing <note>A "complexioned" thing is any physical substance or body defined by its specific balance of the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry</note>, by reason of its property, resists or benefits one organ and not another. Moreover, to every mixture or complexioned thing, another in the category of mixtures or complexions is directly opposed by the power of its property. For since the degree of mixing in all mixtures prepares <note>original: "disponat"; disposes or readies the material</note> them for the reception of a property at every level, and since every degree of mixture or complexion has another that is its natural opposite, it is necessary that this opposite exists in reality just like its counterpart. Consequently, it is necessary that there are things possessing the property to which that degree has prepared them, since matter is never without form. Therefore, since the spirit belongs to the category of complexioned things, something may be <margin>On the property.</margin> directly opposed to the organs through its property. This could be not just one thing, but many, the reason for which is clear from the causes of the property. For although a property naturally comes to a generated thing from a celestial impression <note>The influence of the stars and planets believed to "stamp" a thing with its unique characteristics at the moment of its creation</note>, nevertheless, that which prepares the generated thing to receive it is sometimes the entire range <term>latitude</term> <note>The "latitudo" refers to the span or spectrum of allowable variation within a specific category or species</note> of mixture or complexion that belongs to the species. In this case, the property is a **specific power**—that is, one that follows the species <note>The "species" here refers to the biological or metaphysical category, such as "human" or "lion"</note>—and therefore it belongs to all individuals of that species. But at other times, that which prepares the generated thing to receive a property is some particular degree of mixture, which [falls] under the [latitude] of the species...

This is the source from which the tricks of magicians, the deceptions of enchanters, the harassments of sorcerers, and even swift impressions derive their efficacy, even if **demons** assist them.

### SCHOLIA.

...they cannot exercise their accustomed functions, or they are not remembered. In such cases, the operations of **sorceries** <term>original: "maleficiorum"; specifically referring to harmful magic or "binding" spells intended to inhibit a person's natural powers.</term> and similar arts are most effective, especially when the aforementioned power is present not only in the objects that the practitioner uses as tools, but also when a similar, assisting power resides within the practitioner himself. This power is imprinted upon him by his **birth chart** <term>original: "figura suæ natiuitatis"; an astrological map of the heavens at the moment of one's birth, believed to bestow specific innate talents or occult strengths.</term>. Since the entire period of his life is related back to this chart—in terms of his various perfections or defects—it is possible for the power imprinted at the hour of his birth to be strengthened or weakened later by a **celestial aspect** <note>In astrology, an "aspect" is the angle planets make to each other, which practitioners believed could activate or suppress the potential found in a person's birth chart.</note>, depending on how that aspect relates to the different parts of his birth chart. 

From this, it happens that the impressions or works of certain **magi** <note>Practitioners of "natural magic," which sought to use the hidden properties of nature and the stars.</note>, sorcerers, or **charmers** <note>original: "fascinantium"; those who influence others through "fascination" or the power of the gaze.</note> are exceedingly effective, while the works of others are not effective at all. It also explains why, for those same practitioners, their efforts are sometimes of no efficacy—or at least very little—while at other times they achieve wonderful results. Therefore, if a person’s power acquired from the heavens is contrary to soft and pure bodies (such as a child or fresh wax), and if they approach such things at the proper distance, they will corrupt them by the spirits and vapors they emit, and by the very air being infected or shaped—especially if at that hour their power is strengthened by a celestial aspect.

# LEO SUAVIUS

### *On gold. An addition to the explanation of Iliastes.*

<margin>Albertus.</margin>
Regarding **Iliastes** <term>original: *Iliastes*; in Paracelsian philosophy, this refers to the primordial life-force or the "star" within matter that governs growth and health.</term>, in which Paracelsus said the nature of the **Sun** resides—that is, the nature of gold—let this addition be made from those things which **Levinus Lemnius** <note>A Dutch physician and author (1505–1568) known for his work on the secrets of nature.</note> recently wrote about gold. This comes from the recently published second part of his book *On the Hidden Miracles of Nature*—which perhaps he might have more rightly titled *On the Wondrous Works of Nature*, because "miracles" properly belong to God, according to **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and philosopher who wrote extensively on the natural sciences.</note> in the book *On the Miraculous Science of God*. Regarding gold, I say, he first wrote in general terms those things which can also be said of copper and silver regarding the common greed for them.

Now receive what he discusses concerning the medicinal powers of gold, after I have again warned that it is against philosophical reason to suggest that gold contributes anything medicinally when it retains everything within itself—that is, when it is in no way worn down or consumed. Something else might indeed be said of fragrant things or others from which a "thin spirit" <note>An exhaled essence or volatile vapor.</note> exhales, by the loss of which a tiny amount is taken from the weight of the matter, though it can scarcely be perceived by the senses. How then does he dare to speak of a **liquid of gold** <term>original: *liquamen auri*; often referring to "potable gold," a medicinal oil or solution made from gold.</term> when its **gold leaf** <term>original: *bracteæ*; thin sheets of beaten gold.</term> is boiled in foods? But since gold, which is pure and unadulterated, cannot cause harm when applied externally, the cure of a disease is oftentimes ascribed to it (as is the case with physicians who are more lucky than they are skilled) which **nature itself** has actually accomplished. 

<margin>L. Levinus.</margin>
But leaving these things aside, we must discuss the nature of this metal, which is imbued with many and great powers. Indeed, gold is especially effective, possessing a most immediate power...

# COMMENTARY

Gold prevails in conquering the most savage diseases and in restoring health where it has collapsed or suffered damage. For those who have conceived a blemish from venereal and foul contact <note>A reference to syphilis, which was often described in early modern medicine as a "foul contact" or "stain."</note>, and have been infected by a contagion of the groin, they are manifestly relieved by its use. It also expurgates **Elephantiasis** <margin>Gold cleanses leprosy</margin>—which is considered common leprosy—or at least mitigates it. It firms up loose and unstable teeth that have been spoiled by rotting moisture, and it suppresses all ulcers and pustules of the mouth. 

Thus, for those whose breath is foul and exhales a heavy odor, I have been accustomed to advise that they keep rings made of pure and unadulterated gold in their mouths from time to time. This is especially helpful for those who, having been anointed for the "French disease" <term>original: *morbus gallicus*; a common historical name for syphilis</term>, are plagued by ulcers of the lips and gums; for gold washes away the poison and dries out the eruptions. 

Furthermore, if one wishes to mix plates, segments, or leaves of gold into boiled meats <margin>The use of gold in food.</margin> and offer the broth of this to the sick, it can scarcely be said how much it lifts the strength and vital spirits. Therefore, I restore those consumed by emaciation and wasting, or those exhausted and weary from immoderate Venus <note>Excessive sexual activity, named after the goddess of love.</note>, with decoctions of this kind, and I renew their strength. Nor does the gold become any worse in any part of itself by this method, nor is it taken out thinned or diminished. <margin>Gold is not worn away by boiling.</margin> 

Sometimes I order a capon cut into small pieces, or veal, along with several egg yolks, to be cast into a rounded vessel which they call an **alembic** <term>original: *alembicum*; a chemical still or vessel used for distillation</term>, placed upon a hot hearth. This is drenched with three or four **sextarii** <margin>A *sextarius* contains a pound and eight ounces.</margin> <note>A Roman unit of volume, roughly equivalent to a pint or half a liter.</note> of cow’s milk, mixed together with segments of the purest gold (which they call **obrizum**) <term>original: *obrizum*; highly refined or pure gold</term> or a gold necklace, along with the most effective herbs—namely,

# LEO SUAVIUS.

<margin>*A cruder method for artificial salt.*</margin>
Therefore, the cruder method of making salt from all things is as follows: Collect any substance or herb you like, and burn it in a hearth that has been swept clean of all filth with brooms (some sun-dry the plants first, others dry them in the shade). The method of burning continues until the scorched herb clings together in a sort of loaf; but if you go further by burning it until it reaches **incineration** <note>original: *incinerationem*; the process of reducing a substance to ashes</note>, you will obtain a greater measure of salt. 

Afterward, pour clear and limpid water over this "loaf" or ash in a lead-glazed earthenware vessel, and place it on the fire so that it boils for several hours. Finally, pour it off into another vessel where it may settle, leaving the dregs behind. At last, pass it through a linen cloth, and return that which has passed through to a slow fire of a few coals, so that the water evaporates and the salt settles at the bottom of the "philosophers' vessel."

<margin>*A more refined method for artificial salt.*</margin>
Another method is more refined: place the previously dried herb in an earthenware vessel closed with its own lid and burn it with a long and intense fire until it is reduced to the whitest ash. For this color is the sign of perfect **calcination** <note>original: *calcinationis*; heating a substance to high temperatures to remove volatile impurities</note>. 

Afterward, make it boil in rainwater or distilled water within a glass vessel. This vessel should be placed in an earthenware pot full of sifted ashes. Let it boil until a fourth part of the water is consumed. Then, let it settle for some time and pour it into another large glass vessel—perhaps a **Beauvais vessel** <note>original: *Bellouacenſe*; referring to the famous glassware produced in Beauvais, France</note> of a concave shape—into which you insert the "tongues" of a new and pure filter. Through these tongues (by the principle that a **vacuum is not possible** <note>original: *ratione vacui non dabilis*; a reference to the Aristotelian belief that nature abhors a vacuum, which here explains the siphon-like action of the filter wicks</note>), the clear salty water will ascend and then descend into other receiving vessels. When the filtration has ceased, evaporate that liquid [with fire...]

### SCHOLIA.

...with a gentle fire in a glass vessel, and the salt will remain at the bottom, clear and pure.

<margin>*The most subtle method for artificial salt.*</margin>
The third method is the most subtle: Collect the herb and grind it while it is green. Distill the water through an **alembic** <term>alembicum: a distilling apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube or neck</term>, and **calcine** <note>original: *calcina*; to reduce a substance to ash through high heat</note> the dregs in a closed vessel with moderate fire until they are turned into dry ash. Great care must be taken with the fire, lest the matter be deprived of its own **radical moisture** <note>original: *radicali humiditate*; in alchemy, the essential life-sustaining fluid inherent in a substance</note>, for if this is lost, it could yield nothing more than a **glassy fusion** <note>original: *vitrificatoriam fusionem*; turning into slag or glass rather than soluble salt due to excessive heat</note>. Return the distilled water to its own earth [the ashes], bury it in dung or a water bath for several days, then pour it off cautiously as described above so that the dregs are not disturbed. Finally, filter it and evaporate the filtered liquid.

These are the various ways of preparing artificial salt from all things that are subject to fire, which have been hidden by philosophers both ancient and modern. Their use can be wonderful for treating more delicate patients who shrink from every other kind of medicine; this salt can be placed in meat broth or in a salt cellar to season their meals. On the other hand, I shall not omit the method for extracting fresh water from sea and salt water—a technique most useful for long voyages—handed down by **Cardinal Cusanus** <note>Nicolaus of Cusa (1401–1464), a German philosopher, mathematician, and astronomer</note> in his book *On Static Experiments*, namely by means of a wax globe immersed in sea water.

<margin>*Cardinal Cusanus.*</margin>
However, the chemical method is more convenient, involving the distillation of sea water on a ship's hearth. Regarding such navigation, I marvel that the very recent invention of the **mariner’s compass** <term>pixidis nauticæ: literally "nautical box," the housing for a compass</term> with its **magnetic needle** <note>original: *acu magnetica*</note> is attributed to antiquity by that same Levinus <note>Levinus Lemnius (1505–1568), a Dutch physician who argued that the ancients possessed the compass</note> without any sound reason or authority. For it is ridiculous that he cites testimony from **Plautus** <note>Titus Maccius Plautus (c. 254–184 BC), a Roman playwright</note> concerning the "versoria" <note>A Latin term for a rope used to turn a sail; Levinus mistakenly interpreted this as a reference to a magnetic needle</note> in the play *The Merchant*.

*Now the wind is favorable this way, just take up the tack* <note>original: *Huc secundus ventus nunc est, cape modo vers*; likely a reference to Plautus’s *Mercator*, line 875. The author is debating whether "vers" refers to a "turn" of a sail or a line of verse</note>.

Therefore, reader, accept all these things—written by me not from a desire for victory or contradiction, but from a zeal for uncovering the truth for the common benefit of the **Republic of Letters** <term>reipublicę literarię: the international community of scholars who exchanged ideas through Latin texts</term>—in a fair and kindly spirit.

<meta>This page continues the introductory epistle by Leo Suavius (Jacques Gohory). In the preceding text, the author expressed his humility and his aspiration toward the "sacred rites" of Paracelsian philosophy despite his modest means. Here, he begins to describe this hidden philosophy through a series of classical metaphors and lists the great figures of history and contemporary France who have sought this ancient wisdom.</meta>

-> E P I S T L E <-

...who excel here might easily grasp a specimen of it through conjecture. This, moreover, is the *Golden Chain of Homer* <note>original: "Homeri catena aurea"; a classical metaphor for the divine connection between heaven and earth, frequently used in alchemical literature to describe the chain of being or the sequence of creation.</note>, this is the *marriage of Heaven and Ops* <note>Ops was a Roman goddess of the earth and fertility; her marriage to the god of the heavens symbolizes the union of celestial and terrestrial forces.</note>, these are the *rings of Plato* <note>original: "Platonis annuli"; likely referring to the celestial spheres or the mythological rings, such as that of Gyges, discussed in Platonic philosophy.</note>, and this is the philosophy *hidden in the innermost sanctuaries of nature*. These things indeed were noticed and understood from the monuments of ancient philosophers and poets by the most wise and learned Chancellor of France, **Michel de l’Hôpital** <note>A famous French statesman and humanist (1505–1573) known for his efforts to maintain peace during the Wars of Religion.</note>; by the most learned Grand Almoner to the King, **Jacques Amyot** <note>Jacques Amyot (1513–1593) was a renowned translator of classical Greek texts and a high-ranking cleric.</note>, and by other such sublime minds. They know that for the sake of attaining this knowledge, **Democritus** of old, **Plato**, **Pythagoras**, and **Apollonius** traveled to Egypt to the **pillars of Hermes**, and to the **Brahmans** and **Gymnosophists** <note>original: "Gymnosophistas"; meaning "naked philosophers," ancient Greek terminology for the ascetic sages of India.</note>. Furthermore, they know from the ancient writers how much caution must be exercised in announcing mysteries; if I have perhaps caught a scent of them, I shall whisper it in a few words into the ear of those present, just as the ancient **Kabbalah** <note>original: "Cabala"; referring to the Jewish mystical tradition, which was traditionally passed down orally from teacher to student.</note> of the Hebrews was handed down from hand to hand: the others...

<meta>catchword: ...others</meta>

<summary>The author describes the hidden "philosophy of nature" using classical metaphors and cites famous ancient and contemporary figures who have sought this secret wisdom, emphasizing the need for discretion and oral transmission in the manner of the Kabbalah.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the introductory epistle by Leo Suavius (Jacques Gohory) to his commentary on Paracelsus. It follows a list of ancient and contemporary seekers of wisdom, ending with the Brahmans of India. This final section provides instructions on how to read esoteric or "mystical" texts, emphasizing spiritual and allegorical understanding over literal interpretation.</meta>

# E P I S T L E

...the **Brahmans**, it will be enough to have warned others not to linger on the naked coverings of words, and that we have provided them some understanding based on the practices of similar writers. That is to say: when they read *mystical books* <note>original: "mysticos libros"; in this context, Gohory refers to alchemical, Hermetic, or Paracelsian texts that use allegory and "Decknamen" (cover-names) to hide their true meaning from the uninitiated.</note> of this kind, they should neglect the literal writing, and instead choose and follow the inner meaning. 

This is consistent with what is handed down in the established state by the precepts of the Rhetoricians, and what legislators have judged must be practiced in human laws: that the reasoning of the divine mind must be grasped. This follows the example of that sacred word: *The letter kills, the spirit gives life* <note>original: "Litera occidit, spiritus viuificat"; a quote from 2 Corinthians 3:6, frequently used by Renaissance occultists to justify allegorical interpretation of nature and scripture.</note>; and that other saying: *Milk for infants, wisdom among the perfect* <note>original: "Lac paruulis, sapientiam inter perfectos"; drawing from 1 Corinthians 3:2 and 2:6, where St. Paul distinguishes between basic teachings and advanced spiritual mysteries.</note>. "Hear the mystery in secret," they say, "keep it with you; you would scarcely tell it even to your dearest friend." For while all other arts are tossed about among the common people, these secrets are told quite privately among a few; and although they are most true, it is nevertheless in the interest of the Commonwealth that they be
->kept silent<-
->in some way.<-

->At Paris <note>original: "Lutetiæ"; the Latin name for Paris.</note>, on the Calends of January,<-
->In the year 1567.<-

<summary>In this concluding part of the preface, Gohory instructs the reader to look past the literal text of mystical works to find their inner spiritual meaning, citing both legal theory and Pauline scripture. He argues that these high philosophical secrets must remain hidden from the public to protect the stability of the Commonwealth.</summary>

<keywords>allegory, mystical books, biblical interpretation, secrecy, Commonwealth, Paris 1567, Jacques Gohory, Hermeticism</keywords>

# THE POISON, WHICH A LION (I KNOW NOT WHICH), SUAVIUS, ATTEMPTS TO VOMIT UPON THE THEOPHRASTIANS, IS TURNED BACK INTO HIS OWN BREAST, by GERARD Dorn
<note>original: "Theophrasticos"; referring to the followers of Theophrastus Paracelsus, the Swiss-German physician and alchemist.</note>

## An Apologetic Retort.

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial 'N' containing a figure in a landscape with architectural elements and foliage.</image-desc>I rejoice that it has turned out happily—and not contrary to my omen and expectation—that the incautious Lion, nearly two years after the publication of my "offspring," <note>Dorn refers to his published book as his "offspring" (fœtus).</note> has stepped forward to devour it. What could ever have happened to me that was more pleasant <note>A pun on his opponent's name: "Suavius" is the Latin word for "sweeter" or "more pleasant."</note> than this: that by engaging in a duel with such a fierce beast, I might achieve a victory (of which I have no doubt). But I do not quite see by what art of metamorphosis a Rooster <note>original: "Gallus"; this is a double entendre. In Latin, *Gallus* means both "a rooster" and "a Frenchman." Dorn's opponent, Jacques Gohory, was French.</note> has been transformed into a Lion to rush forth into battle; for the former [the Rooster] excels the latter [the Lion] in solar influences, and the Lion is said to dread the Rooster. <note>Dorn alludes to a common bit of Renaissance natural lore: that the roar of a lion is silenced by the crowing of a rooster, because the rooster is more closely aligned with the power of the Sun.</note> This secret seems to have escaped that "Suavius," the supposed investigator of nature's secrets: otherwise, he would not have changed his Rooster-form, under which he might have overcome even lions. In perhaps a—

<summary>In this opening of a polemical defense, Gerard Dorn uses wordplay and alchemical symbolism to mock his critic, Jacques Gohory (Suavius), for attacking his Paracelsian writings. Dorn highlights the irony of a Frenchman (a "Gallus" or Rooster) assuming the persona of a Lion, noting that in natural magic, the rooster actually holds power over the lion.</summary>

<keywords>Gerard Dorn, Jacques Gohory, Suavius, Paracelsus, alchemy, polemic, Lion and Rooster symbolism, solar influences, natural magic</keywords>

--- Page 410 ---
<meta>This page continues Gerard Dorn’s polemical attack on "Suavius" (Jacques Gohory). In the previous page, Dorn mocked his opponent for hiding behind the pseudonym of a "Lion" despite being a "Rooster" (a play on Gohory being French, as *Gallus* means both Rooster and Frenchman). Dorn now questions the cowardice behind this disguise.</meta>

->### APOLOGY<-

...with a dejected spirit, no doubt, he feared the enmity of foxes toward roosters. Striving to strike fear into those foxes and other animals, he chose to cloak his degenerate and timid **Rooster** <note>original: "Gallum"; a pun on Gohory’s nationality (French) and the bird.</note> in a **Lion's skin**. Nor did he think himself sufficiently safe with that defense, for he added another fashioned under the sign of a triangle.

What sort of man—or what other fierce animal—lurks under the veil of the initials **I. G. P.** <note>These initials stand for *Iacobus Gohorius Parisiensis* (Jacques Gohory of Paris).</note> is unknown to me. Therefore, let whoever he is not take it badly if I happen to respond more sharply to his "Lion’s roars" than his true persona deserves. I have attempted to obtain an interpretation of this hidden name from certain learned men. Among them, some understand it as: **The Envious Parisian Rooster** <note>original: "Invidus Gallus Parisiensis"; Dorn is mocking Gohory by turning his initials into an insult.</note>. They judge that because of his not insignificant academic learning, one should spare his name and surname, and that I should rage against him more moderately than he himself does.

Meanwhile, however, so that you may see—and that others may judge—how foolish it is to make claims about things little known or not sufficiently understood, and then (what is worse) to impudently accuse others of lying based on one's own dreams: this is a foul habit. It is only fair that he who, beyond the bounds of fairness...

GERARD DORN.

...fairness <note>The text completes the word "fairness" (original: *equitatem*) from the previous page.</note> toward others, he should hear even worse things said of him. And so that the trophy of victory may stand more grandly for me, I shall let this **Lion** <note>Dorn's opponent, Jacques Gohory, wrote under the pseudonym "Leo Suavius" (The Smooth Lion).</note> tear himself apart with his own claws, rather than anyone saying I took up my own weapons in self-defense against his various insults. Nor will it seem enough that I defend myself from enemies through my enemy; rather, so that the victory may be greater, the greatest friend of this enemy of mine shall vindicate me. The **Rooster** <note>original: "Gallus"; a pun on Gohory’s nationality (French) and the bird.</note>, who changed himself for a Lion, has for this reason become his own enemy. I shall add thorns to his spurs, so that the Rooster riding the Lion—namely, Suavius—may recognize that it is very hard to kick against the prick <note>A biblical idiom (Acts 9:5) meaning to struggle uselessly against an unstoppable force or the truth.</note>. For that "prick" is the truth. Let us set these things aside and join the battle in earnest.

You are not ashamed to hurl your first spear at me under a rather arrogant warning to the readers, and with false statements, in these words:

> "Now (you say) we must treat the principal preparations of Paracelsus <note>original: "Parac."; referring to the famous Swiss-German physician and alchemist Theophrastus Paracelsus.</note> from herbs, stones, and metals, which I shall set down as they have been handled <note>original: "contritæ"; literally "worn down" or "rubbed," suggesting these recipes have been corrupted by frequent use or poor copying.</note> by the hands of some, so that..."

# DEFENSE
<meta>catchword: queris</meta>

*...at last, let me call the readers away from the errors of Gerard Dorn.* <note>Dorn is quoting a heading or statement made by his opponent, Leo Suavius.</note>

Falsely (by your leave, or rather, by the readers' leave, I should say) you dream, **Lion**, that the tinctures <term>tincturas: liquid medicinal extracts, often alchemical in nature</term> of **Theophrastus** <note>Theophrastus Paracelsus (1493–1541), the famous Swiss-German physician and alchemist whose work Dorn edited.</note>—which you first call "confections" <term>confectiones: a term Dorn considers "pharmacopolico" (belonging to common druggists), usually referring to medicines mixed with sugar or honey</term> using a clumsy apothecary’s term, though they are the simplest of medicines—were crushed by my hands, or as you later suggest, defiled and mutilated. Any Germans who read the German books of the **Great Surgery** <note>original: *Chirurgia magna*; Paracelsus’s most famous and widely circulated medical text.</note>, especially those oldest copies, will judge much better than you—a **Frenchman** <note>original: *Gallus*; a pun on Suavius's nationality and the word for "Rooster."</note> who is completely ignorant of the German language—whether those errors you try to attribute to me belong to you rather than to me. Meanwhile, even as you rebuke the translation which I made faithfully, you do not refuse to use that same translation, inserting a portion of it word-for-word into your own summary <note>Dorn is accusing Suavius of plagiarism—criticizing Dorn's work while simultaneously copying from it.</note>. This you do wrongly to the doctrine of **Theophrastus**, as you shall hear later. It is proof of your failure that you have not provided a better translation of your own, which would have shown plainly whether the lie belonged to you or to me. Afterwards, in your reasoning concerning the "confections" which you say were wrongly described by certain people, you proceed thus—

# OF GERHARD DORN

As for why I used the word "Venetian" in place of the German phrase and adjective **the best** <note>original: des besten</note>, let the readers understand that I did this because, in this century of ours, no better theriac is found than that which is exported from Venice and prepared there. You see, therefore, Leo, that there is no place here for the epithet or the summary imagined by you.

...the term *Lilig* <note>A Paracelsian term, likely referring to a specific alchemical state or substance</note>, which is to be explained from the German *Surgery* of Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus Paracelsus</note>, which I find used in no language, etc. Unless (you add) we read *sibi* instead of *lilli*, as Gerard Dorn reads, who erroneously places saffron-colored <note>original: "croceum"</note> after yellow <note>original: "flavum"</note> in calcination <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder or change its chemical state</term>, etc.

You say, Leo, that you are unable to find the word *Lilig* in various commentaries on languages, or among many experts in them. Truly, if you had read my little book with attention, it would have led you onto the right path by warning you that one should not look for it where what is sought cannot be found. Why did you not look for it among the coals instead? Perhaps you would not have found it there either; but they would have referred you to the fire, in which the *lilli* <note>Dorn suggests these are technical terms born of laboratory practice, not linguistics</note> are born. You complain later that I read *lilli* in place of *lilig*. Those who read the German text will find this to be false, and that both are nevertheless contained in it successively. Therefore, I will not be loath to add the German:

<note>Dorn here quotes the original German text of Paracelsus to prove his accuracy</note>
Take antimony / transformed in the very best way into the alcohol <note>In alchemical texts, "alcohol" refers to an extremely fine, purified powder, not the liquid we associate with the word today</note> / thereafter reverberate <term>reverberate: to heat a substance in a furnace where the flame is reflected or "reverberated" onto the material</term> it in a closed reverberatory furnace for a month / and thus it will become a volatile [substance] /

->GERARD DORN.<-

...of your knowledge of the German language, [showing] that you wanted to boast before those Frenchmen who are equally ignorant of it. Ask any German whether these German color names (**white, yellow, red, and brown**) <note>original: "weiß/gel/rot vñ braun"</note> do not mean—following the order observed in the text—white, yellow, red, and saffron-colored <note>original: "album, flavum, rubeum atque croceum"</note> in Latin? What kind of philosopher do you reveal yourself to be, when you admit to being ignorant of the "philosophical colors" <note>the specific sequence of color changes observed during the alchemical Great Work</note> and the intermediate stages that follow in order between the extremes? I could discuss more of these matters with you, were I not so weary of your follies. It remains for me to show from your own words, to those who know the Spagyric art <term>Spagyric art: the alchemical practice of separating and recombining the essential components of a substance (salt, sulfur, and mercury)</term>, what kind of alchemist—or rather, "Theophrastist" <note>a follower of Theophrastus Paracelsus</note>—you are, since you cannot distinguish between calcination <term>calcination: heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder or ash</term> and sublimation <term>sublimation: the process of heating a solid so it turns directly into vapor and then solidifies again as a purified substance</term>. Tell me, I pray: what metals or minerals become volatile through calcination? For that is what you seem to believe here, when at the end of the preparation of *silig* <note>original: "silig," likely a variant of the "lillig" or "lilli" discussed on the previous page</note> you add this: "(in calcination)." For the rest, you should be ashamed to appear even among the most unskilled distillers, let alone to thrust yourself into the ranks of the Spagyrics. Truly, it would have been better for you to have remained asleep than to undertake such a difficult task. I wonder if you will dare to open your mouth again after this, unless you have a hardened brow <note>original: "perfrictam [frontem]," a Latin idiom for being shameless</note>...

<meta>This page concludes Gerard Dorn’s "Apologia" (Defense), continuing his sharp-tongued rebuttal against Leo Suavius (the pseudonym of Jacques Gohory). In the preceding text, Dorn critiqued Suavius’s ignorance of the German language and alchemical terminology.</meta>

# DEFENSE

...that you have any forehead at all <note>original: "frontē omnino habeas"; a Latin idiom meaning "to have no shame" or to be bold-faced</note>. But those who have put on a mask for themselves, as you have done, are terrified of being recognized because of their own ignorance. Lay this [mask] aside; let us see what kind of man the initials J. G. P. <note>referring to Jacques Gohory Parisiensis, the man behind the pseudonym Leo Suavius</note> have so greatly hidden. You attempt to attack men while remaining unknown: in Germany, this is considered the office of traitors, and furthermore, changing one's name brings the greatest suspicion. 

But why should I imitate the noble Lion (not yours), who, as soon as victory is achieved, spares the submissive cub? The "Mocking Lion" <note>original: "Leo Sannius," a pun on his opponent's name, Leo Suavius</note> would not have acted thus with me if I had not vigorously resisted his mockeries; had I not, I might perhaps have fallen into his nets as the prey he sought. Nevertheless, I must act more "suavely" <note>original: "Suauius," a pun on the name Suavius, meaning "more gently" or "more pleasantly"</note> than he has acted, so that he might repent of his deed and come to his senses in the future. 

Excellent reader, farewell, and if perhaps I have acted less agreeably than you would have wished to hear, I pray you forgive me: it is permitted to defend one's reputation.

->THE END.<-

# THE PRINTER TO LEO
## SUAVIUS, J. G. P. <note>J. G. P. stands for Jacques Gohory Parisiensis, the true identity of the man using the pseudonym Leo Suavius.</note>

I have no dispute or controversy with you, Leo Suavius, concerning Hippocratic <note>traditional medicine based on the Ancient Greek physician Hippocrates</note> or Paracelsian <note>original: "Theophrastica," referring to Theophrastus von Hohenheim, better known as Paracelsus</note> medicine—neither as to whether you, failing to understand the latter, try to undermine it, nor whether you truly strive to promote the former. Indeed, I call nothing into doubt, since I profess neither of them, nor do I understand even the slightest bit of either. 

But, by the laws of humanity and prudence and the law of nations <note>original: "iuris gentium"; a concept of international law or natural law common to all people</note>, I must summon you to court for the slander you have inflicted. You are not unlearned in these laws, yet you have most shamefully offended against them by indulging your passions more than is fair. For that natural fickleness in you was more effective than the learning of philosophy and skill in the laws, which you display so magnificently in your writings with words scattered here and there. 

For what can be more flighty or more foreign to a philosopher than to provoke other men who are not unlearned—and perhaps often even more learned than you—when they teach and dispute about the most serious matters? What is more alien than to tear them apart with insults and to spare no one, if they happen to have said anything that does not entirely please you, or if somewhere (as the saying goes) **the good Homer nods** <note>original: "bonus dormitarit Homerus"; a reference to Horace’s *Ars Poetica*, meaning that even the greatest creators make mistakes</note>? Is it philosophical to rage without discrimination against both the living and the dead, even while they have disputed learnedly and decreed wisely? 

One also acts most impudently if, snatched away by mere spite and a depravity of character, he not only rebukes but even criminally accuses the reasoning of deeds unknown to him, or the things themselves. Will you, Leo Suavius, judge such a man to be a philosopher—the kind of man you desire to seem everywhere in your writing? I, however, judge him worthy of neither the name of philosopher nor the name of man; such a...

<meta>Catchword: talem. This page continues the Printer's address to Leo Suavius (Jacques Gohory). # THE PRINTER

Indeed, whoever reads this writing of yours against Paracelsus will discover you to be an empty boaster, a liar, a shameless person, and most ignorant of the things about which you write. And so that I may bring into the open what I feel, and what I have heard from learned physicians of both sects <note>Referring to the competing schools of traditional Galenic medicine and the new Paracelsian system.</note>, you satisfy no one. Both sides affirm that you are utterly ignorant of Theophrastic <note>Referring to Theophrastus von Hohenheim, known as Paracelsus.</note> matters, and they say you boast of knowing both kinds of medicine rather than actually being skilled in either. 

In fact, you have achieved two things with this single piece of writing: you have become hated by both sides, and you have gained no favor with the Hippocratics <note>Traditionalists following the ancient Greek physician Hippocrates.</note> and Methodics <note>A medical sect that sought to simplify medicine into a set of "methods" or rules.</note> except a bad reputation. On the other hand, you are poorly received by the Spagyrics <note>Alchemists or chemists who used the "spagyric" art of separating and recombining substances to create medicine.</note> and Paracelsians as one who is completely ignorant of their art—even if you were to buy up and possess all the Paracelsian books yourself—since you are ignorant of the language in which he wrote almost all his works, with few exceptions. <note>Paracelsus wrote primarily in German, while many scholars of the time, like Suavius, preferred Latin and looked down on vernacular languages.</note>

But since I have not undertaken the patronage of anyone here, I will leave aside those whom you treat so inhumanely. Even so, you appear to have acted most impiously and flippantly, because you most shamelessly attack—without distinction, as if they were uneducated asses—both the dead and those illustrious philosophers who have served literature and the study of natural and divine things so well, and who have until now been held in high regard by the common consensus of all good and learned men. 

I come now to myself, and I shall speak of me: since you do not know me, nor do you know the truth of the lies you tell about me, you involve and drag me along in the flood of your slanders—together with the noble and illustrious pupil of Paracelsus, **Master Adam von Bodenstein**—calling me an impostor and a thief through your lies, all so that you might appear elegant and eloquent. This is not the behavior learned in the school of the greatest philosophers, to whom you [consider] yourself not only equal...

# TO LEO SUAVIUS.

...to be held, but you also boastfully imagine yourself superior when you despise them. You have learned this not from Christ our master, but from a fellowship of scoundrels and sycophants. But lest I seem to act slanderously toward you, as you have done toward others, I call you as your own witness and make you the judge, so that you may judge from your own words. For this is what you write in the preface of your commentaries on the four books of Paracelsus *On Long Life* <note>Original: "De vita longa." A foundational work by Paracelsus on longevity and alchemy.</note>, which you have stuffed almost entirely with insults and slanders, on page 136 of your edition:

> To these four books *On Long Life*, [Adam] <note>Referring to Adam von Bodenstein (1528–1577), a physician and the primary editor responsible for bringing Paracelsus’s German manuscripts into print.</note> inserted a fourth one as if it were a fraudulent offspring <note>Original: "supposititium partum," suggesting the book was a forgery or "fake" heir.</note>, while the true and legitimate fourth book was forcibly cast into the fifth place and unjustly driven out of its rightful possession. In the remaining books, almost ridiculous changes to certain words or syllables were made so that the work would appear more saleable, appearing to the buyer to be something new in this regard (for today the book fairs in Germany <note>Referring to the massive international book markets in Frankfurt and Leipzig.</note> are large and wealthy). The physician Adam was not ashamed to foist upon us this fourth book, overflowing with empty trifles, which neither connects with the others in any logical sequence, nor reflects the subtlety of Paracelsus’s thoughts, nor the gravity of his style. I wonder, I say, that he, out of hope for profit or a bit of glory, was so complicit in the printer's deception—those who, in the manner of street-vendors, give a stolen thing a new appearance by altering it to cover up the theft, etc.

These are your own words, you *most shameless man*, spewing out your malice! You ought to be far more ashamed of these things, if you had even a grain of modesty, since you say them so maliciously...

->THE PRINTER<-
<meta>catchword: per</meta>

*...faking <note>Original: "fingentem." Completing the thought from the previous page where Suavius accused Adam von Bodenstein of faking or "shaping" Paracelsus's words.</note> things, rather than Master Adam producing the true works of his master [Paracelsus]. Is this how you play the philosopher—the very figure you described as someone who abhors all deception and lies? But you are a philosopher in name only; in reality, you are a most lying slanderer, deserving of a public flogging for your shame—to say nothing worse—rather than respect. But lest I, too, should seem to speak out of emotional agitation and a desire for revenge rather than truth, come, let us demonstrate the facts clearly for all who wish to see.*

*About five years ago, more or less, the aforementioned Master Adam, out of his goodwill toward me as his neighbor and for the sake of our friendship, handed over to me the five books **On Long Life** <note>Original: "De vita longa."</note> by Theophrastus Paracelsus. These were written by the hand of the now-famous printer Johannes Oporinus <note>Johannes Oporinus (1507–1568) was a major Basel printer who famously served as Paracelsus's secretary or amanuensis around 1527.</note>, who was once Paracelsus’s own <term>amanuensis</term> <note>A secretary or clerk who writes down what another dictates.</note> while the author himself dictated. They were in the exact same order in which they were printed by me, without so much as a single <term>stroke of the pen</term> <note>Original: "apice," referring to the smallest mark or "tittle" in writing.</note> added or removed; he delivered them to me uncorrupted. Of this matter, not only is Johannes Oporinus himself a reliable witness for us, but so is the manuscript itself, which is still preserved at Master Adam’s house. For, as if he had foreseen this "tragedy" <note>The printer uses "tragedy" ironically to describe the public controversy sparked by Suavius.</note>, Adam wanted the original, uncorrupted copy returned to him for safekeeping. If anyone wishes to deny what I am now saying, let him come and see it, and let him employ his own eyes as witnesses.*

*What need was there then, you most frivolous man, to rave against us so tastelessly and to lie? Who will believe you hereafter, even if you should happen to tell the truth? But you—if one may "judge a lion by its claws" <note>Original: "ex unguibus Leonem." A Latin proverb meaning that one can judge a person's entire character or talent by a single small sample of their work.</note>—you claim to know the teaching and customs of Paracelsus as well as I do. You shall learn the truth from me today, whether you like it or not, even though I am neither a doctor, nor a physician, and much less a disciple of Paracelsus. His custom was such that if he wrote on a subject several times, he used neither the same method, nor the same...*

### TO LEO SUAVIUS.

*...of the words, but in the same sense, as is well known he did in many books. This is especially clear in this work **On Long Life** <note>Original: "de vita longa."</note>, which you will see written in that same hand of Oporinus at the home of the same Doctor [Adam von Bodenstein]. That manuscript contains only four books, yet you will see that the version we have printed consists of five.*

*And now I have under the press a book by the same author on **Anatomy**, likewise written in the hand of Oporinus, although it has been printed before (by whose hand, I do not know). I am also printing the book on **Degrees** <note>Original: "de Gradibus." A fundamental Paracelsian text on the intensity and properties of medicines.</note>, which I see is familiar to you, including the preface and commentaries of the same Adam, in which he answers you sufficiently in few words. Learn, therefore, having been struck and convicted, to hold back your shallow judgment and your tongue.*

*As for your calling me a thief and an impostor: if you turn those words back upon yourself and your own circle, it may be that you are not lying. We, for the sake of profit—as you have heard—have deceived no one, nor have we stolen anything from anyone. Rather, in good faith, we have shared what we found with our readers for the sake and benefit of the **Commonwealth** <note>Original: "Reipub[licae]." In this context, it refers to the "Republic of Letters," the international community of scholars and physicians.</note>. But the profit we hoped for from this work was stolen from us by your people, who have imposed themselves upon us. Nor are we triflers <note>Original: "nugamur," meaning to talk nonsense or play the fool.</note> here like you; rather, to our own misfortune, we speak the truth.*

*But by hurling the weapon back at you, you shall be called an impostor with the best of reason. For what else is an impostor, except one who displays what is fabricated and false, while hiding and suppressing what is true? From this comes the idea of a **changeling** <note>Original: "supposititius aut imposititius partus." Literally a "substituted or imposed birth," referring to the folkloric belief in a baby being swapped for a false one.</note> or a fraudulent birth, where the true child is secretly removed and you substitute a bastard in its place, or secretly impose it. Have you not also, most "upright" man, omitted your own name, leaving behind only the traces of a true name in the manner of **Hieroglyphics** <note>The printer is mocking Suavius's use of a pseudonym and his interest in occult symbols.</note>, and substituted a fictitious and illegitimate **Leo** [Lion]? You did this so that if, by chance, your writing had found favor, you would not lack that **vain little glory** <note>Original: "gloriola."</note> among the wise and the searchers of Hieroglyphics...*

### THE PRINTER

*...who would shout your name to the rest of the common crowd; and though you indicated it more covertly in the initials **I.G.P.** <note>Original: "I.G.P." These initials stand for Iacobus Gohorius Parisiensis, the Latin name of Jacques Gohory, who used the pseudonym Leo Suavius.</note>, you most openly numbered yourself among the most famous and learned men in two places. Meanwhile, behind the shield of obscurity, you wished to remain unknown to those whom you publicly accused of ignorance, imposture, theft, and so forth. I do not wish to pursue the rest of the matter, since I have both cleared myself and hurled the slanders and accusations back at you. It would remain for me, as a printer, to speak of your book, so "artfully" and "well" edited—or rather, to speak of my excellent and most kind friend, who I believe contributed nothing to the book besides his name and the expense, and that only to gratify you (such is his kindness toward everyone). Since he does not print at his own home, some lazy person—a slave, I should rather say—printed it, so that **a fitting lid might be matched to the pot** <note>Original: "ut patella dignum aptaret operculum." A Latin proverb used to suggest that a poor-quality cover or "lid" is a perfect match for a poor-quality "pot" or book.</note>. But I am called to better things.*
